and sign-in in direct chats, groups and cloud routines. For an API connection,
choose a model that supports both images and tools. Screenshots reach that model
at native resolution; tool approvals and Take control still apply. A model
without computer tools can't use the cloud computer: choose another model, or set
Works on to Auto.
On Auto, a conversation works on the Boat only after the bot moves it there
(it asks to switch with `select_computer`). Auto by itself never reads, wakes or
creates a Boat, so it adds no cloud computer calls to an ordinary message.

sections.title: Cloud computer and your own VPS: Bring your own VPS
sections.text:
Sagax can control Docker on an x86_64 Linux server through an SSH config alias. The agent process stays on your local machine; only Docker commands and the managed desktop container run on the VPS.
Your SSH alias should include connection multiplexing, keepalives, and a connect timeout. Connect manually once to approve the host key, then verify:
 
The SSH user needs Docker access, which is root-equivalent on that server. Use a dedicated VPS and firewall inbound traffic to SSH only.
The managed container publishes no ports, has no host mounts, and is checked before every attach. Its filesystem should be treated as disposable; move important results out before deleting or upgrading the container.
Take control opens the VPS desktop inside Sagax through a temporary SSH tunnel. noVNC remains on the container's private bridge network; only a random loopback port is opened on your computer, and the tunnel closes with the viewer.
Auto reuses an already-ready VPS without changing its lifecycle. To let Auto create or wake this bot's managed container, enable Start VPS automatically for that bot. This permission is off by default. When neither the VPS nor a local fallback is available, Sagax shows the exact VPS failure instead of silently omitting computer tools.

sections.title: Cloud computer and your own VPS
sections.text: Choose a managed Boat desktop or a hardened container on a Linux server you own.

sections.title: Give a bot a computer: Auto, local, and cloud selection
sections.text: Computer selection is explicit per bot. Auto may reuse a ready, verified backend, but it does not silently provision every backend or turn on host control.

sections.title: Give a bot a computer
sections.text:
Choose the right desktop or isolated environment for a task.
A bot can work without a computer, use the computer running Sagax, or work inside an isolated desktop.
 
| Backend | Isolation | Best for |
 
| This computer | None | Working with local apps and files you explicitly approve |
| Local VM | Containerized desktop | Repeatable browser and desktop work on your machine |
| Boat cloud computer | Hosted remote desktop | Always-available isolated Linux work |
| Self-hosted VPS | Hardened container over SSH | Using infrastructure you own |

sections.title: Give a bot a computer: Preview and takeover
sections.text:
The Computer panel can show live frames while an agent works. Supported cloud desktops also provide an interactive viewer. Sagax opens that viewer in the app when possible, with a browser fallback for external join flows.
 
 Starting a screen preview does not grant the bot control. Local input requires a separate opt-in and remains subject to the computer-use safety boundary.

sections.title: This computer: macOS
sections.text: The packaged app can request Accessibility and Screen Recording permission. After granting either permission, restart the control session when prompted so macOS applies the new grant.

sections.title: This computer: Safety model
sections.text:
- Enabling local control globally does not assign it to a bot.
- Choose This computer for each bot that should receive the capability.
- Risky actions still surface through the approval flow.
- Missing permissions, unexpected binaries, unsupported desktop sessions, and failed health checks fail closed.

sections.title: This computer
sections.text:
Let a supported agent control the local desktop through the bundled CUA boundary.
Local control is off by default. The Electron main process owns the bundled CUA driver lifecycle so operating-system permissions are attributed to Sagax rather than a background helper.

sections.title: This computer: Ubuntu
sections.text: Ubuntu 24.04 GNOME host control is temporarily disabled while the real-seat input-safety blocker in issue #345 is resolved. Packaged builds retain the pinned runtime for reproducible review, but Sagax does not start it and clears legacy opt-ins. Chat, screen preview, Cloud, and Local VM remain available. Do not start the bundled driver manually as a workaround.

sections.title: Local VM
sections.text:
Run desktop work inside an isolated Docker or Podman environment.
The Local VM gives each bot a containerized Linux desktop on the same machine as Sagax. It is useful for browser work, downloads, and repeatable automation that should not run directly on your host desktop.

sections.title: Local VM: Ownership and reuse
sections.text: Local VM ownership uses a renewable lease. Sagax validates the resolved image and container safety contract before reuse instead of trusting only a mutable image tag.

sections.title: Local VM: Persistence
sections.text: The bot's workspace and browser profile live in a durable mounted directory. Recreating the desktop can repair stale runtime state without deleting the durable workspace.

sections.title: Local VM: Requirements
sections.text:
- Docker Desktop, Docker Engine, or a supported Podman setup
- Enough local memory and disk for the desktop image
- A healthy container runtime available to the Sagax process
On Windows, Podman is the preferred Local VM runtime. Sagax checks Podman before Docker and validates the exact Windows-to-VM workspace mount before reusing a container.
Before starting two desktops on Windows, confirm the Podman machine is running and has enough shared CPU, memory, and disk for both. Podman Desktop exposes that machine under Settings → Resources; both Sagax desktops consume the same machine budget.

sections.title: Local VM: Run two bot desktops
sections.text:
1. Open App Settings → Local VM, prepare the managed desktop image, and choose Per bot.
2. Set Maximum per-bot desktops to `2`.
3. Give two bots Local VM as their computer and create each desktop from that bot's Computer panel.
4. Choose Open two desktops from either bot to watch both in one workspace.
Both desktops may keep running, but only one pane can hold interactive control at a time. Switching control releases the previous pane first; opening the two-up workspace never creates or starts a VM.
The equivalent source configuration is:
 
Local VMs always run on the same physical host as the Sagax desktop process. `maxInstances: 2` does not pool one VM from a Mac and another from a Windows PC. To use Windows capacity today, run Sagax on Windows with its supported Podman lane and create both per-bot desktops there. The BYO-VPS backend is limited to an x86_64 Linux Docker host; do not point it at Windows as a substitute remote Local VM. Cross-host Mac and Windows pooling is tracked in issue #508.

sections.title: Capabilities
sections.text:
Everything a bot receives on top of its engine: plugins, skills, MCP servers, engine connectors, Perspicax roles and Pulsatrix Flow.
A capability is anything a bot receives on top of its engine: a plugin, a skill, an MCP server, a connector of the engine account, a Perspicax role, or Pulsatrix Flow. Sagax manages them on one page, Capabilities (Discover, Installed, Providers, Sources), opened from the pill at the foot of the sidebar. Every capability is described the same way:
- Source: where it comes from (a Git marketplace, Perspicax, the engine account of the person, a file of the person, the Sagax catalog).
- Scope: who gets it. Today a plugin installs for one bot or for everyone on the server; the scopes This bot, Me and Organization are coming.
- State: available, installed, on, to connect (an account or a key is missing), update offered, set by the organization, or not served by this engine.
No provider key is ever written into bot prompts or the renderer.

sections.title: Capabilities: Disconnecting
sections.text: Disconnecting an account revokes the upstream grant on the engine. It does not only hide the account in the local UI. Other accounts for the same service remain connected.

sections.title: Capabilities: Engine-provided connectors
sections.text:
A Claude bot uses the connectors on the person's own Claude subscription, and a bot on Grok uses the connectors managed on the person's own xAI account. Sagax lists Grok's connectors from Grok's own catalog and cannot check whether they are connected, so they show as not verifiable. You authorize each connector once with the engine, in the browser, and the bot can then use it:
1. Sign in to the engine the bot runs on (Claude or Grok/xAI).
2. Authorize the connector you want on that account.
3. Return to Sagax and ask a bot to use the service.
The authorization stays with the engine. Sagax never holds the provider's OAuth tokens.

sections.title: Capabilities: Multiple accounts
sections.text: Connect more than one account for the same service and give each a clear alias such as `work`, `personal`, or `client-acme`. When several accounts could perform an action, Sagax requires explicit selection instead of silently replacing the first connection.

sections.title: Capabilities: Pulsatrix MCP
sections.text: Workspace tools that are not engine connectors come from Pulsatrix MCP servers. A mounted MCP server exposes its own tools to the bots that are allowed to reach it, under the same approval rules as any other outward call.

sections.title: Capabilities: What each engine receives
sections.text:
| Engine | Plugins | Skills and commands | MCP servers |
 
| Claude | the whole plugin, hooks left out | yes | yes |
| Codex, Pi, OpenCode and other engines that work with files | skills and commands in the prompt, no agents | yes, in the prompt | yes |
| Grok | not yet | not yet | through Sagax's tools |
| API engines (OpenAI-compatible, Mistral, Groq...) | not yet | not yet | not yet |

sections.title: Multiple accounts: Add an account
sections.text:
1. Open Capabilities.
2. Find the toolkit you want to connect.
3. Choose Connect (or Add account if you already have one).
4. Enter a unique label such as `work`, `personal`, or the workspace name.
5. Complete authorization in your browser.
Sagax asks for a label on every new account, including the first, so the Connected tab shows your chosen name instead of a generated id. When more than one account could execute a tool, Sagax requires explicit account selection. A new authorization does not silently become the default for the old one.

sections.title: Multiple accounts: Disconnect safely
sections.text:
Each connected account appears separately with its alias and status. Disconnect removes only the chosen account and leaves the others active.
Sagax caps each service at five usable accounts. If a provider policy prevents another authorization, use a separate Sagax installation or configuration rather than reauthorizing over a working account.

sections.title: Multiple accounts: Grants apply to tools, not accounts
sections.text: Per-bot tool grants say which tools a bot may call on a service; they do not pick an account. When several accounts could run a tool, the bot still selects one explicitly, and a grant covers every account of that service on the installation. To keep one bot away from a specific account, put that account in a separate installation or configuration.

sections.title: Multiple accounts
sections.text:
Connect work and personal accounts without silently replacing either one.
Sagax supports several labeled accounts for the same toolkit. This is useful for two Gmail inboxes, several Slack workspaces, or separate personal and work services.

sections.title: Writing documentation: Add a page
sections.text:
Create a `.mdx` file with a title and description:
 
Add the page filename to the nearest `meta.json` so it appears in navigation.

sections.title: Writing documentation: Documentation standard
sections.text:
- Describe shipped behavior, not an open PR as though it has been released.
- Lead with user outcomes and include exact recovery steps for known failure modes.
- State platform and security boundaries plainly.
- Prefer links to stable public docs over duplicating long internal design records.
- Keep unreleased claims out of the changelog. Entries are read from GitHub
 only after a release is published.

sections.title: Writing documentation: Preview locally
sections.text:
From the repository root:
 `pnpm docs:dev` 
Open `http://localhost:3000`. Before submitting:
 `pnpm docs:build`

sections.title: Writing documentation
sections.text:
Add and review Fumadocs pages in the same pull request as the feature.
Public documentation lives in `apps/docs/content/docs`. Internal design notes and implementation plans can remain in the repository's top-level `docs` folder.

sections.title: Contributing: Before building
sections.text:
- Search open and recently merged issues and pull requests.
- Link overlapping work and coordinate with the current contributor.
- Extend the existing harness, renderer, companion, and provider boundaries instead of adding a parallel system.
- Open an issue before a large cross-platform change.

sections.title: Contributing
sections.text:
Work with the project architecture and keep changes reviewable.
Sagax welcomes focused fixes and features. Read the repository's CONTRIBUTING.md before opening a pull request.

sections.title: Contributing: Keep PRs narrow
sections.text: One concern per pull request is easier to review, test, revert, and release. Large prototypes are useful integration branches, but upstream submissions should be split into independently green slices.

sections.title: Contributing: Local checks
sections.text: Run the platform-specific package or native tests when your change touches macOS, Windows, Ubuntu, Cloudflare, or iOS.

sections.title: Approvals and inspector: Approval cards
sections.text: When an engine supports approvals, Sagax surfaces the request instead of hiding it in terminal output. Read the requested action and scope before approving it. Denying an action sends control back to the agent so it can choose a safer path.

sections.title: Approvals and inspector
sections.text:
Stay in control when agents ask questions, request access, or perform risky work.
Sagax renders structured agent events as native conversation cards. Questions, choices, permission requests, tool activity, and failures remain attached to the task that produced them.

sections.title: Approvals and inspector: Changes a bot makes to itself
sections.text:
A bot can change its own routines, skills, profile, and default model without asking, at every approval level, including engines such as Pi that have no Full access. Each change shows in the conversation as one plain line, for example "Scout scheduled a routine: Check before dentist, today 2:30 PM", with Details for the full text and Undo to put it back. After you undo it, the line ends with "Undone". If the thing changed again since, Undo says so and changes nothing.
A change for another bot, such as a Chief editing a teammate's profile or scheduling a routine for it, still asks unless the conversation has Full access. Creating, deleting, or moving bots and messages between bots keep their usual approvals. A bot that already has 20 routines on asks before it turns on another one, and a bot asks before it moves its own working folder, since that changes which files its tools can read and write without asking. In a conversation a guest drives on My Cloud, every change still asks.
Full access applies every change as it always has, with the same one-line receipt and Undo.

sections.title: Approvals and inspector: Inspector
sections.text: Use Inspector when you need more detail than the conversation provides. It is useful for following tool calls, reconnect attempts, engine output, and long-running work.

sections.title: Approvals and inspector: When a run disconnects
sections.text: Sagax retries transient streaming failures. If retries end in an authentication or configuration error, fix the underlying engine rather than repeatedly retrying the task. See Agent engine troubleshooting.

sections.title: Attachments, search, and message tools
sections.text: Add visual context and find, preserve, or reuse important parts of a conversation.

sections.title: Attachments, search, and message tools: Files and large media
sections.text:
Documents, audio files, and archives can be up to 250 MB. Videos can be up to 1 GB. Each picture can be up to 32 MB on an organization server or 90 MB on a personal one, and the pictures in one message can total 200 MB (at most 32 pictures). Other files have no per-message count. Uploads larger than 4 MB resume from the last acknowledged chunk after a network interruption or app restart.
Open a video from its message or the conversation's Files tab to stream it on demand. Playback and seeking request only the needed byte ranges, including for encrypted-at-rest files. Download and Save a copy hand the opaque conversation URL to the browser's download manager instead of holding the whole file in memory.
PDF and compatibility previews stay intentionally bounded to protect memory. If a preview is too large or the format cannot play in the browser, use Save a copy. The original file remains available through the same conversation authorization.

sections.title: Attachments, search, and message tools: Image attachments
sections.text: Paste a screenshot directly into the composer or attach an image from disk. Add a short instruction explaining what the agent should inspect—the highlighted UI, an error message, a layout mismatch, or the whole image.

sections.title: Attachments, search, and message tools: Message actions
sections.text:
- Pin durable decisions or instructions.
- Copy a response without selecting the message manually.
- React to leave lightweight feedback in shared conversations.
- Retry when a transient provider or connection failure interrupts a response.
- Read aloud when voice output is configured.
 
 Crop tokens, email addresses, private repository names, and customer data before attaching an image to any cloud-backed model.

sections.title: Attachments, search, and message tools: Search
sections.text: The sidebar search finds bots and conversation content. Use distinctive project names, issue numbers, or exact error fragments to narrow results quickly.

sections.title: Attachments, search, and message tools: Voice notes
sections.text: Voice notes an agent sends are audio attachments: mp3 files in the same attachments store as images and documents, with their text kept as the visible caption and transcript. They share the attachment quota, and playback can seek without downloading the whole clip.

sections.title: Routines and webhooks: Reaching a local webhook
sections.text:
On My Cloud there is nothing to set up: webhooks use the workspace's own address. The Webhooks panel shows `https://` plus the workspace's hostname followed by `/hooks/` and the endpoint, and only those hook paths are passed to the receiver. The same is true of a hosted workspace.
On the desktop app the receiver listens only on this computer. To accept events from the public internet, proxy only the webhook receiver through a narrowly configured relay or tunnel. Do not expose the main harness port.
 
 Local routines and webhook deliveries are not hosted jobs. Closing the desktop app stops the local executor and receiver.

sections.title: Routines and webhooks: Routines
sections.text:
A routine runs once, at a repeating interval, or on selected weekdays. Each run starts a fresh execution using the selected bot's model, permissions, tools, and computer configuration.
 
Run receipts distinguish queued, active, waiting, completed, missed, failed, and cancelled work. Sagax must be running when a local routine becomes due.
### Reports land in the bot's conversation
Each run works in its own execution context, then posts its whole report into the bot's one conversation, dated, with View run for the run's detail (its conversation, approvals and logs). There is no separate results thread. Post results in the conversation turns that report on or off; approvals, questions and errors always reach you. In a run's detail, Continue in the conversation opens that conversation with the report quoted, ready for your reply. Run logs keeps the execution history, including failures and waiting runs.
A bot schedules, changes, pauses, resumes, and deletes its own routines from chat without asking, and each change shows as one line with Undo (see Changes a bot makes to itself). A routine for another bot asks first unless the conversation has Full access.
### Remember the last run
Each run starts fresh by default. For work that builds on last time, such as a QA pass, monitoring or follow-ups, turn on Remember the last run under the routine's instructions. Each run then starts with the previous run's report (up to 2,000 characters), so the bot knows what it found before. It is available for repeating routines that one bot runs; team goals don't carry it yet. You can also ask the bot in chat to turn it on.
### Clear a folder's unread dots
Right-click a folder or open its … menu, then choose Mark folder as read. This clears unread dots without opening each thread. It does not answer approvals, dismiss questions, or stop any running work.

sections.title: Routines and webhooks
sections.text: Run agents on a schedule, collect their reports in one thread, or trigger work from an external event.

sections.title: Routines and webhooks: Webhook triggers
sections.text:
Webhooks start the same queued task executor from an external HTTP request. They are independent from schedules and use a dedicated receiver on `127.0.0.1:8800` by default.
The receiver exposes only health and secret hook routes. It does not expose the broader Sagax API.
Bearer authentication is preferred because it keeps the secret out of URLs and most access logs. A capability URL is available for senders that cannot set headers.

sections.title: Bots, folders, and threads: Bots are persistent teammates
sections.text:
A bot keeps its identity, instructions, memory, approved skills, connected tools, and computer preference. Create separate bots when the role or access should differ. You do not need another bot just to start a different project or choose another model.
- A coding bot attached to one repository
- A research bot with browser and document tools
- An operations bot with Gmail, Calendar, and Slack
- A local-model bot for private or offline work
New bot opens an editable draft before anything is created. Review its profile, model, permissions, memory, skills, and routines, then select Create bot. App settings → General → Defaults for new bots → Edit sets the starting values for future creation dialogs without changing existing bots. See Create your first bot for the full flow.

sections.title: Bots, folders, and threads
sections.text: Share one agent profile across organized, independent conversations.

sections.title: Bots, folders, and threads: Delegation
sections.text:
Delegation asks another bot to handle a bounded subtask. The delegated task keeps its own activity and returns a result to the originating conversation. Give each delegate a narrow outcome and avoid assigning two bots ownership of the same files.
| Need | Use |
 
| Ongoing relationship and memory | Bot |
| Related conversations organized together | Folder |
| An independent conversation and running state | Thread |
| Several bots sharing context | Group |
| A specialist handling one branch of work | Delegation |
| Repeated work at a known time | Schedule |

sections.title: Bots, folders, and threads: Folders keep related threads together
sections.text:
Folders are optional organization under a bot. For example, Pepper can have an Email folder containing Triage Gmail and Triage iCloud, alongside a Website folder.
A thread can choose its own model in the chat header and its Ask/Auto setting inside the composer. Folders have no model or permission settings. Moving a thread does not change its model, account, or access, or interrupt it. Removing a folder leaves its conversations ungrouped; it does not delete their history.
All the bot's threads share its saved memory and skills; they do not automatically receive every sibling transcript. Folders are not separate accounts or privacy boundaries. Bot profiles can carry different access preferences, but app organization is not an operating-system sandbox.
Threads can converse independently, but a physical computer, browser session, or shared project folder cannot safely have two agents changing it at once. Sagax reports contention instead of allowing overlapping managed actions. New local-agent threads use separate working folders by default; existing pinned folders are retained.

sections.title: Bots, folders, and threads: Groups and teams
sections.text: Groups are the conversations previously called channels or rooms. They let multiple bots share context. Use a group when several specialists need the same brief or should hand work to one another. Membership, instructions and thread history are retained. The existing multi-bot turn-taking behavior is unchanged.

sections.title: Bots, folders, and threads: Primary Bot
sections.text:
Your Primary Bot (formerly Chief of Staff) is your main contact among your bots: it receives requests, delegates focused tasks to your other bots, and summarizes the results. It wears a small orange star on its avatar in the sidebar, the pickers, the team map and the chat header.
You have one Primary Bot (on an organization server, one per person, since bots belong to their owner). Right-click it in the sidebar and choose Replace with different Bot to pick another one in Choose a primary Bot: search, select one of your bots, then Confirm. On any other of your bots, Make primary bot hands the role over directly. The server keeps exactly one per person; the previous one steps down.
Your Primary Bot can also hand the role over in a team setup plan: the plan must step it down and appoint the new one together. It coordinates its own team and the additional teams you allow in its settings. It does not inherit the creator's access to other teams or execution permissions. Stepping down also removes its additional managed-team access. Existing conversations and model selections remain intact.
When you upgrade from a version with one Chief of Staff per team, each person keeps one: the General team's Chief, else the oldest. The teams the others led are added to its managed teams, so coordination still reaches them.

sections.title: Bots, folders, and threads: Threads are independent conversations
sections.text:
The conversations previously called Tasks are now Threads. Expand a bot in the sidebar and choose New thread, or use All threads to find an older conversation. Existing history is preserved.
Each thread has its own progress, approvals, and Stop control. Start another thread while one is working; stopping one does not redirect its siblings. Up to three direct threads can run per bot, including threads waiting for your approval.

sections.title: Bots, folders, and threads: Threads use their bot's model
sections.text:
Every thread runs on its bot's model. Change the bot's model and its threads change with it, including old ones a routine, a delegation or a hand-off opens again. A thread keeps a model of its own only when you pick one in that thread; choose the bot's own model in that thread's model menu (for a bot named Ada, Use Ada's model) to put it back on the bot's. A thread that follows the bot shows (bot's model) beside that model.
When some threads use their own model, the bot's model setting says how many, with Switch them too. That moves them all back onto the bot's model once; it is not a setting. A thread that is working keeps its model until it finishes.
If a thread's own model can't run (its engine was removed, turned off, can't start, or isn't allowed), the turn runs on the bot's model instead, the thread uses the bot's model from then on, and one line in the thread says so. A thread whose engine is signed out does the same only when the bot's model is on another engine that can run; on the same engine you see the sign-in prompt.

sections.title: Threads, groups, and collaboration: Bots and threads
sections.text:
A bot is a durable agent identity. A thread is one conversation with that bot and has its own transcript, provider session, approvals, costs, and running state. It runs on the bot's model unless you pick another model in that thread. Optional folders organize related threads without duplicating the bot's memory or skills.
Use separate threads when you want fresh context or independent work without duplicating the bot. Messages sent to a busy thread are queued, and supported providers can be steered while they work. Other threads can continue independently. See Bots, folders, and threads for limits and shared-resource behavior.

sections.title: Threads, groups, and collaboration: Delegation
sections.text:
Bots can hand work to other bots. Delegated runs carry explicit status back into the parent conversation, including completion, failure, and cancellation.
### Creating a specialist with a chosen model
A Primary Bot can create a specialist in its own team with `create_bot`. Ask for a particular engine, model and reasoning effort if you want to choose them. The Primary Bot can look up exact available choices with `list_team_setup` and pass `modelSelection` with `instanceId`, `model`, and optionally `effort` or a supported `variant` (not both).
When no model selection is supplied, the new bot uses the workspace's default model selection, including its reasoning effort; it does not copy the Primary Bot's model. An invalid explicit choice is rejected rather than silently replaced. The new bot starts with capabilities and automatic approvals disabled, and existing bots keep their models. Combined team changes still use the reviewed team-setup flow.

sections.title: Threads, groups, and collaboration: Deleting a team
sections.text: To delete a team, right-click its name in the sidebar and choose Delete team, or use its Manage menu in Team map. The confirmation explains that bots (including archived bots) and group chats move to General with their conversations intact. The team's shared instructions are removed; General's instructions stay unchanged. Stop active work and unassign any team computer first.

sections.title: Threads, groups, and collaboration: Groups
sections.text:
Groups bring several bots into one conversation. Each participant keeps its own provider state. Group timeouts prevent a participant from blocking the whole group indefinitely. Existing channels and their thread histories remain intact; the new label does not change turn-taking or delegation.
When a bot sends the same request to several group members, the group shows one shared message addressed to those members. Each member runs with its own model and permissions and can reply in that conversation. Different assignments remain separate.
### Group token usage
After a group participant finishes a turn, the group header shows the current thread's reported cost, or input tokens when no cost is reported. Hover over the compact badge for uncached input, cached input, and output, plus the latest participant's turn. Switching threads switches these figures too; other group threads and private chats are excluded.
The figures come from the existing usage ledger and survive restarting the app. A missing cache figure is shown as an unknown split, not zero cached input. If some turns omit cost, the dollar amount sums only reported costs.

sections.title: Threads, groups, and collaboration: Memory and working folders
sections.text: Bot memory is visible and editable. A bot may also have a dedicated working folder; groups can use a shared working folder. Cloud workspaces use a stable default so generated files remain discoverable across threads. A sidebar folder is only organization, not a working directory or a permission boundary.

sections.title: Threads, groups, and collaboration: Renaming teams
sections.text: Right-click a named team heading in the sidebar and choose Rename team, or use the team's menu on the Team map. Enter the new name and save. Bots (including archived bots), group chats, shared instructions, and an assigned team computer stay together. Existing management access to a populated team follows its new name; an existing team's name cannot be used to merge teams. Finish active work before renaming.

sections.title: Threads, groups, and collaboration: Rewind and branches
sections.text: Editing an earlier message creates a new conversation path. Sagax avoids resuming stale provider sessions after a rewind, so the next turn follows the visible branch rather than hidden abandoned state.

sections.title: Threads, groups, and collaboration: Team membership
sections.text:
Every named team keeps an Add bots button in the sidebar. Once it has members, the button reads Add or remove bots. The dialog lists current members as checked alongside other available bots. Check a bot to move it into the team; uncheck one to move it to General, then save. Conversations stay with the bots.
Choose New bot inside this dialog to open bot creation for that team. The new bot is created directly in the selected team and appears checked when you return to the membership list. Creating it does not discard your other unsaved checkbox edits.

sections.title: Threads, groups, and collaboration
sections.text: Organize agents like contacts and let them collaborate without losing control of each task.

sections.title: Threads, groups, and collaboration: Token usage
sections.text:
Hover over the usage chip in a bot's chat header to see the totals and the latest message's usage. Input and output are separate:
- Uncached input is input the provider did not report as served from its prompt cache.
- Cached input is input the provider reported as served from its prompt cache.
- Output is the generated token count reported by the provider.
Uncached input plus cached input equals total input. If the provider does not report a cache split, the tooltip shows total input and output instead. A missing cache count is not treated as zero.
The compact chip shows cost when the provider reports it. Otherwise, it shows uncached input when known, or total input. Generated output is listed separately in the tooltip and is not added to either input figure.

sections.title: Bots on the desktop: Activity level
sections.text: App settings → Appearance → Activity level (also in the right-click menu) sets how often the mascot moves on its own: Calm, Normal or Lively.

sections.title: Bots on the desktop
sections.text: Put a bot on your desktop as a living mascot that chats, plays, walks around, and flies off while it works.

sections.title: Bots on the desktop: Choose its character
sections.text:
Each bot picks its character in Edit persona > Appearance (click the big avatar in the bot's panel to open it there). Under Mascot, a gallery lists the characters with a search and filters (All, Owned, To unlock, and one per family: Classics, Shapes, Animals); the column beside it previews the one you pick with its colors, skins and moves. Generate and Upload set a picture instead, and Reset brings the owl back. By default the bot can wear the Owl, with its colors, skins and wing moves. Shapes (eight shapes: circle, pebble, rounded square, capsule, triangle, hexagon, cloud, droplet, shaded like clay, with two eyes cut through the body that look around, blink and follow your pointer, a color and a skin, and fourteen moves such as Thinking, Wink, Orbit or Comet) appear after you link a Grok account. A bot that wore one of the earlier shapes now shows the nearest of the eight. Trombi and Bunbu (our own little collectible monster with long ears and a toothy grin, in the bot's color and a Bunbu skin; its signature move is the ear flop) appear when you unlock them. Shiba (a dog drawn in flat tones with one outline, in the bot's color or a coat of its own, with sixteen faces) is a Mastery character: the achievement Hands Off unlocks it, and its coats and premium skins come from the Mastery achievements (see Achievements). Frog (a smug, heavy-lidded frog with wide flat lips, its green taking a tint of the bot's color, with sixteen faces) is one too: Polyglot unlocks it. A locked character shows on the To unlock shelf with the achievement that unlocks it and how far you are: you can preview it, not wear it yet (Trombi stays a secret until you find it). A locked skin stays out of the list until then. A bot that already wears one keeps it. The preview plays the moves you pick and the equip animation of a skin you choose. The choice is stored with the bot, so it shows everywhere the bot appears (the sidebar, the chat, the panels, the desktop mascot) and on your other devices.
Skins come in four rarities, one tab each in the popover (with how many skins it holds), and the popover opens on the tab of the current skin: Common (Owl: classic, snowy, barn, carbon; Shapes: clay, pastel, glossy, night; Trombi: classic, retro 98; Bunbu: plain, pastel, night, plush), Rare (Owl: gold, ice; Shapes: outline, gold; Trombi: gold; Bunbu: velvet, gold), Epic (Owl: neon, lightning, chrome; Shapes: neon, chrome, crystal, circuit; Trombi: neon, chrome, glitch; Bunbu: neon, chrome, crystal) and Legendary (Owl: inferno, holographic, galaxy, spirit; Shapes: holographic, molten, galaxy; Trombi: holographic, molten; Bunbu: holographic, galaxy, molten). Shiba wears the bot's color (Plain) for free; its coats (cream, black and tan, red, sesame, white) and Retro 98 and Gold are Rare, Neon, Chrome and Glitch Epic, Holographic and Molten Legendary.

sections.title: Bots on the desktop: Fly away during tasks
sections.text:
When the bot starts working, the mascot crouches, spreads its wings and flies to the nearest edge of its screen, flapping all the way, and waits there as a small badge with a turning ring. Click the badge to open the thread. When the work is done it flies back to the spot it left, lands and celebrates; if a message could not be sent it comes back looking sad, and if the bot needs your approval it comes straight back.
Turn this off in App settings → Appearance → Fly away during tasks, or from the mascot's right-click menu. With it off, the mascot stays put and thinks while the bot works.

sections.title: Bots on the desktop: Motion and battery
sections.text:
- With Reduce motion on in your system settings, the mascot stays calm: no walks, flights or big moves, only breathing, blinking and gentle looks.
- It draws only as fast as it needs, and not at all while hidden or covered.
- Clicks pass through the empty space around the mascot to whatever is underneath.

sections.title: Bots on the desktop: Play with it
sections.text:
The mascot has a little life of its own: it breathes and blinks, follows your pointer with its eyes, looks around, preens, scratches, pecks, stretches a wing, hoots, walks a few steps along the desk (turning to face the way it goes) and now and then hops or flies a short way. After a quiet while it yawns and naps until you come back.
- Stroke it by moving the pointer back and forth over it: it hugs itself and leans into your hand; keep going and it shows hearts.
- Rush the pointer past it and it jumps; rest the pointer near it and it waves.
### Shiba on the desktop
Shiba lives like a dog. It sits, breathes, blinks, wags its tail and twitches an ear, and now and then it sniffs, lies down for a nap, turns in circles or barks. Every few minutes it wanders: it walks off to a spot (always within its room on the screen, never while its chat is open), sniffs it, turns around and walks back. It walks on four legs while the mascot moves along the desk and runs while it flies off for a task.
- It barks when someone nudges you, turns in circles when you unlock an achievement and gets excited when a reply lands.
- It sits up, head tilted, while its bot waits for your approval, and droops its ears after an error.
- Hide for 1 hour makes it lie down and fall asleep before it goes.
- Drop it somewhere new and it goes to sniff the spot, then comes back to it.
- Its Moves menu (and the Appearance gallery) offers Bark, Turn in circles, Wag, Sniff, Head tilt, Stretch, Lie down, Shake off, Wave and Excited.
- Its bark is silent unless you turn on Settings > Appearance > Shiba barks out loud.
With Reduce motion on it stays still and a move only changes its face.
### Frog on the desktop
Frog sits with its heavy lids half closed, breathes with its throat and blinks one eye, then the other. Now and then it catches a fly, nods smugly or croaks. Every few minutes it hops about, and more rarely it takes a long jump to another spot on the screen (never while its chat is open). It hops along while the mascot moves along the desk and long-jumps while it flies off for a task.
- It puffs its throat while its bot works.
- It gives a slow side-eye, then sinks into its pond up to the eyes while its bot waits for your approval, and shivers after a refusal or an error.
- It nods smugly when a task goes well.
- It croaks when someone nudges you, celebrates an achievement and catches a fly with its tongue when a reply lands.
- It naps on a lily pad and stretches its legs when it wakes up.
- Its Moves menu (and the Appearance gallery) offers Hop, Long jump, Catch a fly, Croak, Smug nod, Lazy blink, Stretch, Side-eye, Shiver and Wave.
With Reduce motion on it stays still and a move only changes its face (the pond and the lily pad still show).

sections.title: Bots on the desktop: Put a bot on the desktop
sections.text: Right-click a bot in the sidebar and choose Put on the desktop. The bot leaves the window and stands on your desktop as its mascot, above your other apps. In a browser or on a phone it floats over the app instead. Choose Put back in the window from its right-click menu to bring it home.

sections.title: Bots on the desktop: Talk to it
sections.text:
- Click the mascot, or press Enter while it has focus, to open its balloon, ready to type. The reply streams into the balloon; Open in Sagax jumps to the full thread.
- Double-click it to open Sagax on the bot's thread.
- The balloon grows with the answer (up to about 60 % of its screen, then it scrolls, earlier exchanges above) and never runs off the screen: it opens on the side of the mascot that has room, below it near the top of a screen and to its right near the left edge, and stays on the mascot's screen. It shows lists, bold, code, tables and links like the chat, your messages in the same bubbles. Its composer is the app's: the paperclip and the model chip open the app on the bot's thread (its file picker, its model picker), the voice button starts a call. Drag its corner grip to resize it, drag its header to move it anywhere, right up against the mascot (it never covers it), and use the pin button to put it back; its size and place are remembered per bot. Enter sends, Shift+Enter starts a new line, Esc closes it. With Trombi it wears the Windows 98 look.
- Call it: where voice mode is on for the bot, the voice button in the balloon's composer (or Start a voice call in the right-click menu) starts a voice call through the bot's thread, the same call as in the app. A small call pill stands under the mascot: the live waveform, Settings, Transcript, Mic and the red button to hang up. The mascot bounces while its bot talks and leans in while you speak (not with Reduce motion on); click it to cut the bot short. Only one call runs at a time: starting one in the app or on another mascot ends the other.
- Click it to chat: a plain click on the mascot opens its chat balloon and never starts a call (use the call button that shows when you hover it, or the hotkey). A drag still moves it and a double click still opens the app. During the call a click only cuts the bot short while it talks; it never hangs up (the pill's red button does). The call is the same as the app's call bar: both show it.
- Hover it: after a moment three round buttons appear beside it (never over it): quick chat (the balloon), voice (start or end the call) and activity, a small tray of what its bot is running now with Allow and Stop for anything waiting on you; click a row to open it in the app. They fade away a moment after the pointer leaves (without a fade with Reduce motion on).
- Captions: during a call the mascot shows the call's status (listening, thinking, speaking) and the live words beside it, yours as you speak and the bot's word by word as it says them, three lines at most. Turn them off in Settings > Appearance > Call captions beside the mascot.
- Hotkey: press Control+Option+Space (Ctrl+Alt+Space on Windows and Linux) anywhere to call the mascot's bot, press again to mute or unmute, and, when the call is set to push to talk, hold it to talk (macOS). Change the keys or turn it off in Settings > Appearance > Call hotkey; it is off while no mascot is on the desktop.

sections.title: Feature overview: Agents and conversations
sections.text:

- Queueing and steering while an agent is already working
- Per-task token and cost visibility
- Readable, editable bot memory

sections.title: Feature overview: Automation
sections.text:
- One-time and weekday routines
- Webhook-triggered tasks with dedicated secret endpoints
- Fresh task context and durable run receipts for each automated run
- Notifications for work that needs attention

sections.title: Feature overview: Computers and tools
sections.text:
- Local computer control with explicit opt-in and approval boundaries on supported hosts; Ubuntu currently fails closed under an input-safety hold
- Isolated Local VM desktops through Docker or Podman
- Hosted Boat cloud computers
- A self-hosted Linux VPS backend over Docker's SSH transport
- Live previews and in-app desktop takeover where the backend supports it
- USB Android control through the Phone Harness skill

sections.title: Feature overview: Desktop experience
sections.text:
- macOS, Windows, and Ubuntu packages
- Theme switching and accessible contrast
- Sidebar sections, compact headers, pinned messages, spoilers, and image attachments
- Automatic updates on macOS and Windows
 
 macOS has the broadest native integration. Ubuntu chat, preview, Cloud, and Local VM are available, while host control is temporarily disabled under an input-safety hold. Windows installers are not yet signed, and the iOS companion keeps sensitive workspace configuration on the computer.

sections.title: Feature overview
sections.text:
A map of the capabilities currently available in Sagax.
Sagax turns agent CLIs into a messaging-style workspace. The harness normalizes each provider into one event stream, so the interface can treat different agents consistently while preserving their native strengths.

sections.title: Feature overview: Voice and access
sections.text:
- Spoken replies and per-bot voices through ElevenLabs, Fish Audio, built-in Mac voices, or Chatterbox
- Native macOS dictation and half-duplex call mode
- Paired iOS companion with chat, approvals, search, transcript controls, and opt-in computer viewing

sections.title: Voice, dictation, and memory: Call mode
sections.text:
On macOS, call mode combines native on-device speech recognition with the configured voice. It is deliberately half-duplex: the microphone pauses while the bot speaks to prevent the app from transcribing its own audio.
Tool progress and approval requests can be narrated during a call so long-running work does not sound disconnected.
### Take turns or Live
On the desktop, the call button starts the kind of call you picked last; the arrow next to it picks Take turns or Live and starts that call.
- Take turns is the call described above: on-device listening, the bot's own voice, one side talks at a time. It needs the macOS app on This computer.
- Live runs the conversation through OpenAI GPT-Live. You can talk over it and interrupt at any time. It works on the desktop, iPhone and Android.
A Live call keeps the chat open: a call bar above the composer shows the call time and a caption of what the voice says, with a settings gear, Mute and Hang up. On the desktop, Cmd+Shift+M mutes or unmutes and Cmd+Shift+H hangs up (Ctrl+Shift+M and Ctrl+Shift+H on Windows and Linux).
The voice speaks as the bot, in the first person, but the bot does the work: each request goes to it as a normal message, marked "via call", with the bot's own engine, tools, memory and approvals, and the voice reads the answer back. The voice's own words appear only as captions and are not saved. While the bot works, the voice gets a quiet status note every 30 seconds, so it can say the bot is still busy instead of guessing; if a turn ends without an answer, it says the result is in the chat.
When a call that connected ends, the chat keeps one record of it: a small row with the call's length and what the bot did for the requests you spoke, its steps by name and the permission requests it raised, such as running a command, with how each was decided. The record reads "Call with" and the bot's name. With generated thread titles turned on (`"features": { "llmThreadTitles": true }` in `~/.sagax/config.json`), the bot's own engine, which already saw those requests, gives it a short title from what you asked on the call; the call sends nothing more to OpenAI. The requests you spoke and the bot's answers stay in the chat as before. The record holds no speech: the voice's own words are still not saved. A call that never connected leaves no record, and a phone app that does not know the record yet shows it as one short line, such as "Call with Ada · 1:42".
A permission request, such as running a command, can be answered with a clear spoken yes or no, decided by Sagax, not by the voice model; the card stays on screen too, and a card decided on the call is marked "by voice" there and in the decision log. On a Live call the microphone stays open while the voice speaks, so "okay", "sure" or "fine" on their own do not count as a yes, and words heard while the voice itself was talking are left out; say "yes" or "no".

sections.title: Voice, dictation, and memory: Dictation
sections.text: The composer microphone uses Apple's local speech recognition in the macOS desktop build. Linux and Windows dictation are not currently shipped.

sections.title: Voice, dictation, and memory: Memory
sections.text: Each bot can keep plain-text memory that you can inspect, correct, or delete. Memory is not a hidden remote profile; it lives with the local Sagax data.

sections.title: Voice, dictation, and memory: Spoken replies
sections.text:
Pick a voice engine in App Settings, choose a voice, and use the speaker control on a response. Auto-speak can read new replies as they arrive. Four engines are available:
- ElevenLabs — cloud voices, needs an API key.
- Fish Audio — cloud voices from the Fish Audio library, needs its own API key.
- Built-in Mac voices — the voices already installed on macOS, no key.
- Chatterbox (local) — an open-source, MIT-licensed engine reached through an OpenAI-compatible server you configure. With a server on your own machine there is no cloud call; the address can also point at any HTTP(S) server you choose.
The harness rewrites code-heavy Markdown into speech-friendly text before synthesis. Keys remain on the harness and never reach the renderer.
### Fish Audio
1. Create a key in Fish Audio API Keys.
2. In an agent profile, choose Fish Audio, paste the key, and save it.
3. Pick one of the voices returned by your Fish Audio account, then use Try before enabling spoken replies.
Fish Audio and ElevenLabs keys are stored separately, so switching engines does not replace the other provider's credential. The picker combines popular public voices with voices owned by your Fish Audio account. Only use a voice when you have permission to do so.
### Chatterbox (local)
Sagax speaks through any OpenAI-compatible server that runs Chatterbox behind `POST /v1/audio/speech` — for example LocalAI with a Chatterbox model installed, or a small wrapper service around `pip install chatterbox-tts`.
1. Start your Chatterbox server locally and note its address, for example `http://127.0.0.1:4123`.
2. In App Settings, pick Chatterbox (local) as the voice engine, paste the server address, and set the model id your server expects (the default is `chatterbox-turbo`).
3. Pick a voice. Voice ids come from the server's `/v1/models` listing when it has one, or `/v1/audio/voices` when it doesn't; otherwise a Default entry uses the server's built-in voice.
There is no API key. Sagax sends the text to the configured server address, so synthesis stays on your machine only when that server is local. Per-agent voice overrides work the same as with the other engines, and a dead or unreachable server is reported as a clear error instead of a hang.

sections.title: Voice, dictation, and memory
sections.text: Listen to agents, talk to them, and inspect what they remember.

sections.title: Voice, dictation, and memory: Voice notes
sections.text:
An agent can send a voice note: a short spoken message it writes itself, synthesized with the configured voice engine and attached to its reply when the turn ends. The same text becomes the note's visible caption and transcript, so the conversation stays readable — and searchable — without playing anything. Notes are limited to 1000 characters, and the same limit is enforced again at synthesis.
A note posted to a shared room works the same way: the agent records the note, then attaches it to its room post, where the room members can play it inline.
Voice notes can be turned off per agent. The switch sits with the voice settings in the agent profile; while it is off, the agent is not offered the voice-note tool at all, even with a voice configured.
The audio itself is an mp3 file in the attachments directory on your computer, with a generated name and owner-only permissions. It counts against the same 512 MiB attachment quota as images and documents.

sections.title: Configuration
sections.text:
Understand engine paths, credentials, and the local configuration boundary.
Most users configure Sagax from the app. The packaged desktop validates credentials before saving them and stores supported secrets with the operating system's secure storage.

sections.title: Configuration: Engine discovery
Configuration: Environment configuration
sections.text:
Source and headless runs can set supported environment variables before starting the harness. The app-level settings are preferable for normal packaged use because they validate inputs and keep secret values out of the renderer.
### Per-instance Claude tool scope
Source and headless installations can give separate Claude instances different built-in tool sets in `~/.sagax/config.json`:
 
`tools` selects Claude's available built-ins; an explicit empty array disables every built-in, while omitting it keeps Claude's default set. `disallowedTools` applies Claude tool-name patterns as an additional deny list. These settings do not grant or pre-approve MCP integrations, which remain controlled by the instance's mounted integrations and Sagax permission flow.
### Claude Code isolation
A bot on the Claude engine sees only what its owner gave it: the MCP servers under Settings → MCP servers, its integrations (computer, browser, agents, phone), and its own project's `.mcp.json`. It does not load this machine's Claude Code setup — the MCP servers and claude.ai connectors in your user or local Claude config, your skills and agents, your hooks, or your personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Loading those into every turn of every bot cost one measured desktop about 407 extra tools and 10k tokens per model call.
`SAGAX_CLAUDE_INHERIT_USER_CONFIG=1` on the Sagax process turns that isolation off again, for every Claude bot, until the variable is removed. It exists to recover a bot that genuinely depended on a user-scope server, and it is easy to forget: nothing in the chat looks different, only the token usage does. While it is set, Settings → Engines shows a warning on the Claude engine and the server logs one line at startup. The supported fix is to add the server the bot needs under Settings → MCP servers or to the bot project's `.mcp.json`, then unset the variable and restart.
### ACP session reuse
Every ACP engine (Antigravity, Grok, Gemini CLI, Kimi, Droid, Cursor, OpenCode,
Qwen, Hermes, custom ACP CLIs) keeps one agent process alive per conversation
thread and reuses it across turns, so the ACP handshake — which can take tens of
seconds for a heavy runtime like Antigravity — is paid once per thread instead of
once per message. The process is closed after 10 minutes of quiet, and sooner on a
spawn-contract change (different model flags, working directory, or approval
level), a crash, or app shutdown; the next turn then resumes the
recorded session over a fresh process. Integration credentials rotate every turn,
so a follow-up re-establishes the native session over the wire (`session/load`)
on the same process — the handshake is still paid only once.
An agent that refuses `session/load` for a session already live in its own
process gets exactly one replacement process for that turn: Sagax closes
the pooled child, starts a fresh one, pays the handshake again, and resumes the
recorded session there. The conversation is never traded for a blank

sections.title: Configuration: Optional credentials
sections.text:
| Credential | Enables |
 
| Boat API key | Hosted Linux computers |
| ElevenLabs API key | Spoken replies and voice mode |
| Fish Audio API key | Spoken replies and voice mode with Fish Audio voices |
| Chatterbox server address | Spoken replies and voice mode without a cloud key |
| OpenCode API key | Optional alternative to an existing OpenCode provider login |
Local agent chat works without these credentials.

sections.title: Configuration: Shared user profile
sections.text:
Open Settings → General → Profile → About me to save information you want every bot to know, such as your preferences, background, or working hours. It saves automatically and shows Saved when the server confirms the update. The question mark beside the field explains where it is shared.
The text is included in the instructions for subsequent private-chat and group-chat turns, across model providers. Existing bots receive it too; an already running turn keeps the instructions it started with. Clear the field to stop including it in future prompts. Clearing does not erase information already present in conversation history.
This is workspace-wide context, not a private note for a single bot. It is stored in the workspace configuration and sent to the model provider with bot requests. Use credential settings for secrets. The field accepts up to 24,000 characters.

sections.title: Create your first bot: Before you start
sections.text: Install and sign in to at least one supported agent CLI. Sagax detects installed engines during onboarding and again from App settings → Agent engines.

sections.title: Create your first bot: Create the bot
sections.text:
1. Select New or share in the sidebar.
2. Choose New bot.
3. Review the New bot dialog. Its settings start from your saved defaults, and the suggested name remains editable.
4. Give the bot a clear name and purpose in Identity, then select its engine and model in Model.
5. Review the other sections: Soul, Skills, Memory, Routines, Access, Permissions, and Voice & alerts. Choose a working folder in Access if it should edit files or work in a repository.
6. Select Create bot. Closing or cancelling the dialog discards the draft without creating a bot.
The working folder matters: it becomes the bot's starting context and limits accidental edits elsewhere. Use a dedicated project folder for coding, research, or content work.
In Identity, Random female name and Random male name insert a local
suggestion into the editable name field. Click again for another suggestion
or type your own. The lists contain 4,944 female and 3,897 male names from
stdlib's English-language Moby Word II datasets. Choosing a name does not
create a bot, call a model, or change any other profile setting.

sections.title: Create your first bot
sections.text: Choose an engine, folder, and working style for a useful first agent.

sections.title: Create your first bot: Give it a useful first task
sections.text:
Start with a concrete outcome and the constraints that matter:
 
Once you trust the diagnosis, ask the bot to implement the change. This keeps review and mutation as separate, easy-to-check steps.

sections.title: Create your first bot: Set defaults for future bots
sections.text:
Open App settings → General → Defaults for new bots → Edit. This opens the same editor as bot creation. Save the identity, model, instructions, access preferences, memory, skills, and routines you want future bots to start with. Leave the name empty for a random suggested name each time.
Saving defaults does not change existing bots or start routines. When creating a bot, you can override or clear any inherited value. Full access and local-computer Auto still require their normal confirmation when the bot is created; a saved default is not a permission grant.
These full templates apply to the creation dialog and the HTTP bot-creation endpoint. Bot-driven team setup keeps its own reviewed setup flow; it does not automatically copy template memory, skills, or routines.

sections.title: Create your first bot: Tune the bot
sections.text:
Open Bot settings to change its name, avatar, instructions, engine, model, working folder, and computer setup. Different bots can use different engines and folders at the same time.
 
 Sagax launches agent tools you installed. If an engine returns a 401 or asks you to sign in, finish that engine's own CLI login, then refresh detection in App settings.

sections.title: Installation: Build from source
sections.text:
Requirements: Node.js 24 or newer, pnpm 10.34.6, and at least one authenticated agent CLI.
 
Run the harness, web UI, and Electron shell in separate terminals:

sections.title: Installation: Download a released build
sections.text:
Choose your computer below. Each link always downloads the latest published build.
| Platform | Recommended package | Notes |
 
| macOS Apple silicon | Download `.dmg` | Signed and notarized. Drag to Applications. |
| macOS Intel | Download `.dmg` | Signed and notarized. |
| Windows x64 | Download installer | Per-user installer; Windows signing is not yet available. |
| Ubuntu 24.04 x64 | Download `.deb` · AppImage | The `.deb` is recommended; the AppImage is portable. |
 
 The Windows installer is not code-signed yet. Windows may show “Unknown publisher.” Verify that you downloaded it from the official OpenMausBot releases repository before choosing More info → Run anyway.

sections.title: Installation: Install an agent CLI
sections.text:
Sagax needs at least one supported agent engine installed and signed in. Claude and Codex are the most common starting points.
1. Install the CLI from its official provider.
2. Run it once in a terminal and complete sign-in.
3. Restart Sagax.
4. Open the model picker. Available engines appear normally; unavailable engines explain what is missing.
See Agent engines for the complete list and explicit path overrides.

sections.title: Installation
sections.text: Install Sagax on macOS, Windows, or Ubuntu.

sections.title: Installation: Using Sagax at work
sections.text: To use Sagax with your organization, join its Perspicax server from Settings. See Use Sagax at work.

sections.title: Installation: Where data lives
sections.text: Sagax stores its application data under `~/.sagax`. Electron window and browser data use the normal per-platform application data directory.

sections.title: Use Sagax at work: A shared installation
sections.text: Some organizations give you a link to a shared installation instead of the desktop app. It runs in your browser. Sign in through the invitation your administrator sent. Bots, chats and files on that installation are shared with your team.

sections.title: Use Sagax at work: Join a Perspicax server
sections.text:
1. Open Settings → Organization.
2. Under Join a Perspicax server, enter the server address your administrator gave you.
3. Optionally choose which of your bots to copy, with or without their conversations and memory. You can preview the copy before you join.
4. Choose Join. The desktop opens that server and starts Sign in with Pulsatrix.
On a server that is already signed in with Perspicax, Settings → Organization shows the organization, your role, and a link to manage it in the Perspicax console. People, models and billing for the organization are managed there, not in a separate Admin portal.

sections.title: Use Sagax at work
sections.text:
Join your organization's Perspicax server. Sagax does not sign in to a hosted Admin portal.
Sagax at work is your organization's Perspicax server. There is no hosted Admin portal, no Company model catalog, and no company cloud backup.
 
 Joining does not upload this computer's chats unless you choose specific bots to copy. Your own engines, accounts and local models stay on this computer.

sections.title: Quick tour: 1. Sidebar
sections.text: The sidebar holds your bots, groups, automations, capabilities, profile, and app settings. Search looks through bot names and message history. Use New or share to create a bot or start a shared room.

sections.title: Quick tour: 2. Conversation
sections.text: Messages are the work log. Agent replies, questions, approval requests, tool progress, attachments, and failures stay together in the conversation. You can pin, copy, react to, search, and retry messages.

sections.title: Quick tour: 3. Task mode
sections.text: The Task button starts a separate unit of work without losing the main conversation. A task keeps its own status and result, which is useful for parallel or delegated work.

sections.title: Quick tour: 4. Model picker
sections.text: Pick an agent engine and model per bot. The picker separates cloud-backed agent CLIs from local engines and shows what is installed on this machine.

sections.title: Quick tour: 5. Computer and inspector
sections.text: Open Bot's computer to choose where visual work runs. Open Inspector to follow lower-level activity when a task is executing.

sections.title: Quick tour: 6. Capabilities and automations
sections.text: Capabilities (plugins, skills, MCP servers, connectors) give bots authenticated tools. Automations turn a good prompt into scheduled or webhook-triggered work.
