sections.title: Sagax documentation
sections.text:
Build a team of AI agents that can talk, use tools, operate computers, and keep working on a schedule.
 Local-first agent workspace 
Sagax turns agent CLIs into a familiar desktop chat app. Each bot can have its own model, instructions, working folder, capabilities, computer, and recurring work.
 
 Many engines Claude, Codex, Grok, Cursor, local models, and more 
 Real tools Apps, files, terminals, browsers, VMs, and cloud desktops 
 Your machine Local data and bring-your-own agent subscriptions

sections.title: USB Android control: Requirements
sections.text:
- A physical Android device connected over USB
- USB debugging enabled on the device
- The computer trusted from the device's debugging prompt
- The packaged Android platform tools or a compatible local ADB installation
Phone access is a separate capability from desktop computer use. Keep the device unlocked and visible while testing, and review actions that may send messages, change accounts, or expose private content.

sections.title: USB Android control
sections.text:
Let a bot inspect and operate a physically connected Android phone.
Sagax can expose a USB-connected Android device through its Phone Harness skill. A supported agent can inspect the screen, open apps, tap, type, swipe, scroll, and capture screenshots.

sections.title: iOS companion
sections.text:
Pair an iPhone directly with the Sagax instance running on your computer.
The native iOS companion is a thin client. Your computer remains the only machine that owns agent processes, credentials, transcripts, SQLite data, and computers.

sections.title: iOS companion: Network options
sections.text:
- Same trusted Wi-Fi: Bonjour discovery and direct HTTP.
- Away from home: Tailscale on both devices with the computer's MagicDNS name.
- Hosted HTTPS: sign in by email on the desktop to provision a private
 Cloudflare Tunnel address; the phone still pairs to that specific computer.
LAN and Tailscale remain available without a Sagax account. The hosted
control plane stores account/installation metadata, not transcripts; Cloudflare
proxies phone traffic to the user's computer. Bonjour does not cross Tailscale,
so that direct remote option uses manual address entry.
Your computer must remain on, awake, and running Sagax. In desktop Companion Settings, Keep this computer awake can prevent system sleep while Companion is enabled; it is off by default, allows the screen to turn off, and may use more battery. A sleeping or powered-off computer cannot be reached even through hosted HTTPS.

sections.title: iOS companion: Pairing
sections.text:
The desktop opens a two-minute pairing window with a high-entropy QR credential and a six-digit manual fallback. Redeeming either closes the window and returns a separate per-device token stored in iOS Keychain.
The computer stores only a digest of the device token. Revoking the phone from desktop Settings invalidates future requests.

sections.title: iOS companion: Security boundary
sections.text:
The companion sidecar uses a default-deny route allowlist. Provider keys, pairing administration, Local VM lifecycle, webhook secrets, team import/export, and internal peer-agent routes remain unreachable from the phone.
 
 Live and replayed events can produce alerts while the companion is connected, but a terminated iOS app cannot be awakened without a future APNs relay.

sections.title: iOS companion: What it can do
sections.text:
- Discover and pair on the same LAN, connect through Tailscale, or use an
 optional account-provisioned HTTPS address
- List bots and rooms, read paged transcripts, send messages, and interrupt work
- Answer approvals and questions, including narrow always-allow grants
- Search, manage tasks, react, share, and navigate message versions
- Follow resumable live updates and optionally view a bot's managed Boat cloud computer. The loopback-only VPS SSH viewer currently opens in the desktop app.

sections.title: Google Antigravity: After upgrading from the older agy integration
sections.text:
Version 0.1.51 switched from the community `agy` CLI to Google's official ACP runtime. An existing Antigravity app or `agy` login does not sign this separate runtime in. Complete Install official Antigravity and Sign in with Google in the model picker, then refresh and choose a model available to that account.
Saved legacy `agy` paths, including Windows `.cmd` shims, now resolve to the official runtime. Genuine custom ACP executable paths are still respected. The migration does not copy credentials from another app, remove the old CLI, or change which Google account you authorize.
The Google sign-in belongs to the engine instance, not the runtime version, so ordinary app updates do not require signing in again. Cold starts can be slow, particularly on Windows; setup and model discovery allow up to 90 seconds. If Google expires or revokes the saved session, sign in again when prompted.

sections.title: Google Antigravity
sections.text:
Install Google's official ACP runtime and use your Google subscription in Sagax.
Sagax connects to Google Antigravity through Google's official Agent Client Protocol server. It does not ask for your Google password or copy a login from another app.

sections.title: Google Antigravity: Multiple Google accounts
sections.text: Create another Antigravity engine instance for another account. Each instance has a separate private `GEMINI_HOME`, token, settings file, and model catalog. Signing one instance in never replaces another instance's account.

sections.title: Google Antigravity: Permissions and tools
sections.text:
Antigravity uses the same Sagax approval cards as other ACP engines. Capabilities, custom MCP servers, the browser, computers, and teammate tools are mounted only for the active session; Sagax no longer edits the user's global Gemini MCP configuration.
The normal mode asks before protected actions. Full access maps to Antigravity's native `yolo` mode, but native questions still wait for a person instead of being guessed automatically.

sections.title: Google Antigravity: Remote servers
sections.text: When the Sagax server and browser are on different computers, Google's final redirect points to the server's loopback address and may show a page that cannot load locally. Expand Signing in from another computer?, copy the complete redirect URL from the browser address bar, and paste it into Sagax. The server accepts only the loopback port and OAuth state created by that exact in-progress sign-in.

sections.title: Google Antigravity: Set up
sections.text:
1. Choose an Antigravity model in the model picker.
2. Select Install official Antigravity. The download comes from `dl.google.com` and Sagax verifies its pinned size and SHA-256 before installing it.
3. Select Sign in with Google and finish in your browser.
4. Return to Sagax, open the model picker, and select Refresh. The account's available models appear after discovery completes.
The runtime download is large because Google ships the ACP server and its local computer harness together. Sagax stores it in its own data directory; it does not modify a system installation.

sections.title: Agent engines
sections.text:
Use the agent subscriptions and CLIs you already have.
Sagax does not proxy every message through its own model account. It starts supported agent CLIs on your computer and normalizes their output through the local harness.

sections.title: Agent engines: Built-in engines
sections.text:
| Engine | Authentication shape | Notes |
 
| Claude | Claude CLI login | Strong support for tools, approvals, sessions, and local computer use |
| Codex | Codex CLI login | Model discovery, approvals, steering, and computer tools |
| Grok | Grok CLI login | ACP-based local model catalog and session support |
| Cursor | Cursor Agent CLI login or API key | ACP driver with live model discovery |
| Kimi | Kimi CLI login | ACP integration |
| Droid | Factory Droid CLI login | ACP integration |
| Antigravity | Google account through the official ACP server | Managed install, isolated accounts, live models, and approval cards |
| OpenCode | Existing OpenCode provider login or optional API key | Live Zen, Go, third-party, and local model discovery through ACP |
| Qwen | Qwen CLI login | ACP integration |
| Hermes | Hermes CLI login | ACP integration |
| Pi | Pi CLI login | Native driver |
Additional driver instances can be declared in local configuration. Unavailable engines remain visible with a reason instead of crashing the provider fleet.
To use OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, DeepSeek, Cline, or your own OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible service, see Other model providers.
Codex models come from the signed-in CLI's live model list. If that list cannot be read, the picker shows an offline fallback that includes GPT-6 Astra, Sol, and Luna with availability marked unverified. An older CLI may not expose newer models; Sagax checks for a newer stable Codex release and offers an update command for the configured executable. Updating the CLI does not grant model access to an account.

sections.title: Agent engines: Codex browser tools
sections.text:
Codex bots use the browser and computer selected in Sagax. Desktop-only Codex
browser/computer features and their bundled plugins are disabled for those bot
processes, so bots do not select a native desktop connection that is unavailable
inside the CLI. This does not uninstall plugins or change the standalone Codex app.
Native web search keeps its configured mode.
After built-in browser navigation, Sagax collects a snapshot in the same
browser session. A sign-in page or redirect is evidence of where navigation landed,
not confirmation that the requested task finished. Connection failures retain the
selected computer/account and do not automatically replay uncertain actions.

sections.title: Agent engines: Detection
sections.text:
Sagax checks common installation directories and the login shell in the background. Restart the app after installing or authenticating a CLI.
If detection fails, use Settings → Engines to set an explicit executable path. This is supported for every engine and is the most reliable solution for version managers, wrappers, custom builds, and Windows installations outside the normal path.

sections.title: Agent engines: Mistral API
sections.text:
Open Settings → Connections, save your Mistral API key, then choose Mistral (API) in a bot's model picker. No CLI installation is needed. The Test button checks catalog access without sending a chat message.
The model list refreshes from Mistral's `/v1/models` endpoint, including versioned models and aliases. Archived and non-chat models are excluded. Use Refresh models after new models become available to your account; an unsuccessful refresh preserves the previous list. Mistral bills requests to your API account.
For a server deployment, set `MISTRAL_API_KEY` or save `mistral.key` in the server configuration. Advanced users can declare additional `mistral` instances with a `config.model` default and endpoint URL. A saved workspace key is shared by those instances. The connection supports streamed replies and structured tools through the shared chat-completions runtime; it does not launch a local agent CLI or grant filesystem access.

sections.title: Agent engines: Model selection
sections.text: The model picker groups models by provider and marks defaults. Supported engines can refresh their model catalog from the installed CLI. Changing the model affects future turns; it does not rewrite earlier transcript history.

sections.title: Agent engines: Multiple Claude accounts
sections.text:
Open Settings → Engines → Add Claude account and give the account a name, such as Work or Personal. Sagax creates a separate configuration-directory setting for it; it does not copy your existing login. Under Manage account and sign-in, copy the sign-in command and run it on the computer hosting Sagax, then choose Check account. On Windows, use PowerShell. Claude handles the browser sign-in and stores its own credentials.
In a bot's model picker, choose Claude, select Work or Personal in the Account dropdown, then choose a model to save the selection. Claude appears only once in the provider list. Each bot keeps its own selection, and the chat header shows the account name. Account changes apply to future turns and are blocked while that bot is responding; other bots are unaffected. Conversation history is not erased when you change the selection.
The original Default entry keeps using your existing CLI login. Advanced users can supply an existing, separate Claude configuration directory. Once an account has been used by bots or conversation history, add a new account instead of repointing its directory. Removing an account from Sagax does not delete its files or sign it out; first move any bots using it to another account.
This does not require a CLI proxy, and there is no automatic account rotation or fallback. Named account management currently supports Claude only.
 
 Your existing CLI login or provider API key determines access and billing. Sagax does not turn one subscription into access to another provider.

sections.title: Other model providers: Current limits
sections.text:
There is no shared provider list that configures every engine. Use each
engine's setup above, and do not assume a key saved for one engine changes
another engine's sign-in or model list.

sections.title: Other model providers: OpenCode 2.x
sections.text:
Sagax installs and tests OpenCode 1.x (the `opencode-ai` npm package).
OpenCode 2.x is a separate package, `@opencode/cli`, and it also installs a
command called `opencode`.
- If you installed OpenCode from Sagax's Settings, bots use that copy.
 Otherwise they use the first `opencode` on your PATH, which is 2.x if you
 installed `@opencode/cli`. Settings → Engines shows the version in use.
- 2.x works on a best-effort basis. Version-specific differences:
- Some 2.x releases have reported missing configured providers in new
 ACP sessions (upstream report #50236).
 If a provider is missing, check the installed version and upstream
 updates before changing your credentials.
- When a provider key is set in the environment (for example
 `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` on a server), 2.x hides OpenCode's free models and
 makes a paid model the default.
- 2.x keeps its sign-ins apart from 1.x, so a sign-in made with one may not
 be seen by the other. Run `opencode auth login` with the version your bots
 use.

sections.title: Other model providers
sections.text:
Use OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, DeepSeek, Cline, or your own OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible service.
This page covers what works today in each engine and version-specific
differences with OpenCode 2.x.

sections.title: Other model providers: What works today
sections.text:
| Provider | OpenCode | Chat engine | Claude Code | Codex |
 
| OpenRouter | Yes | Yes | Only through Claude Code's own settings | Not yet |
| Fireworks AI | Yes | Yes | Only through Claude Code's own settings | Not yet |
| DeepSeek | Yes | Yes | Only through Claude Code's own settings | Not yet |
| Cline | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Your own OpenAI-compatible address | Yes, in OpenCode's config file | Yes | No | Not yet |
| Your own Anthropic-compatible address | Not tested | No | Only through Claude Code's own settings | No |
"Chat engine" is Sagax's built-in engine for OpenAI-compatible services.
In a bot's model picker it is called OpenAI-compatible (OpenRouter / Groq)
and, for now, sits in the Local group.
The Cline row lists its hosted model service. To run Cline's own coding agent,
use the Cline engine.
Other engines (Antigravity, Cursor, Gemini, Qwen, Grok, Droid, Kimi, Hermes,
Pi and custom agents) use their own sign-in.
Keys you export in your shell (`~/.zshrc`, `~/.bashrc`) don't reach the
desktop app when you open it from the Dock, Finder or an app menu: it copies
only `PATH` from your shell. Use the steps below instead.
### OpenCode
OpenCode already supports OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, DeepSeek and ClinePass. It
just needs your key.
1. In a terminal, run `opencode auth login`.
2. Pick OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, DeepSeek or ClinePass and
 paste your key.
3. In Sagax, open a bot's model picker, choose OpenCode and press the
 refresh button (Refresh models). The provider's models appear in the
 list. Sagax reads the model list from an ACP session on both
 OpenCode 1.x and 2.x.
Sagax uses your normal OpenCode sign-ins and settings, so there is
nothing to set up inside the app. Sign in with the same OpenCode version that
your bots use (see OpenCode 2.x).
Your own OpenAI-compatible address (this includes Cline credits, at
`https://api.cline.bot/api/v1`):
1. Run `opencode auth login`, pick Other, type a short ID such as
 `myrouter`, and paste your key.
2. Add the provider to `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`
 (`%USERPROFILE%\.config\opencode\opencode.json` on Windows):
 
 Keep this file plain JSON, with no comments or trailing commas.
 Sagax edits it when an OpenCode bot uses a model running on this
 computer.
3. Refresh OpenCode's models in Sagax.
OpenCode's provider guide has more
examples. OpenCode can also use Anthropic-compatible addresses, but we haven't
tested that with Sagax.
On a self-hosted server that you start from a terminal, OpenCode also reads
provider keys exported in that terminal, such as `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`,
`FIREWORKS_API_KEY` or `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`. Keys exported
this way reach every engine on that server, and any bot that can run commands
can read them. On OpenCode 2.x this also has a side effect; see below.
`CLINE_API_KEY` is scoped to the Cline and OpenCode engines. For ClinePass in
OpenCode, `opencode auth login` also keeps its sign-in in OpenCode's own settings.
### Chat engine

sections.title: Engine troubleshooting: A selected model fails
sections.text:
- Refresh the model picker after updating the CLI.
- Choose a model actually available to that provider account.
- Confirm a custom wrapper forwards the model argument and preserves the provider's expected environment.
- Try the provider CLI directly with the same model to separate an account problem from a Sagax integration problem.

sections.title: Engine troubleshooting: Authentication failures
sections.text:
Run the provider's own status or login command in a terminal. Sagax uses the CLI's authenticated session; installing the binary alone is not enough.
A `401 Unauthorized` response from `api.openai.com` means the launched Codex process did not receive valid authentication. Confirm `codex login status`, sign in again if needed, then restart Sagax. Do not paste a ChatGPT password into Sagax.

sections.title: Engine troubleshooting: “CLI not found”
sections.text:
1. Open a terminal and run the CLI directly.
2. Confirm the command is an executable, not only a shell alias or function.
3. Restart Sagax after installation.
4. Set the exact executable in Settings → Engines if automatic detection still fails.
Desktop applications often inherit a different environment than a terminal. This is common on Windows shortcuts, macOS Finder launches, and Linux application menus.

sections.title: Engine troubleshooting: Codex sandbox mismatch
sections.text:
Sagax preserves Codex's resolved network and writable-folder settings when
starting a turn. If Codex returns no resolved sandbox or a different mode from
the one requested, the turn stops before sending your message. Check the native
Codex sandbox setup and selected access mode, then retry. Sagax does not
silently replace that policy with broader access.

sections.title: Engine troubleshooting
sections.text: Fix missing CLIs, failed authentication, model errors, and path differences.

sections.title: Engine troubleshooting: Windows notes
sections.text: Use a real `.exe`, `.cmd`, or resolvable command path in the engine override. If a CLI was installed in WSL, the Windows desktop app cannot treat that Linux binary as a native Windows executable without an explicit bridge or wrapper.

sections.title: Security model: Core boundaries
sections.text:
- The harness owns agent processes and listens on loopback.
- The renderer receives configured-or-not credential state, not secret values.
- Provider-specific credentials are injected only into the process that needs them.
- Risky actions become approval cards rather than implicit permission.
- Local computer control is a separate opt-in and per-bot selection.
- Paired phones use a default-deny API allowlist and per-device bearer tokens.
- Cloud and VPS backends are validated before reuse.

sections.title: Security model
sections.text:
The boundaries that keep agents, credentials, computers, and paired devices scoped.
Sagax is designed around a local owner, explicit capabilities, and narrow process boundaries. Local-first does not mean risk-free: an agent with tool or computer access can still act on the resources you grant it.

sections.title: Security model: Your responsibility
sections.text:
- Review approvals, especially shell commands, file writes, and actions in connected services.
- Use dedicated environments for untrusted or destructive work.
- Keep provider accounts and capabilities scoped to what a bot needs.
- Revoke lost companion devices immediately.
- Keep Sagax and agent CLIs updated.
Security reports should be filed through the repository's documented security channel rather than disclosed in a public issue before a fix is available.

sections.title: Permissions and secrets: Approval cards
sections.text:
Supported providers emit permission requests and questions through the local harness. Sagax displays these inline and records the outcome. Cancellation closes outstanding requests so stale approvals cannot be answered after a turn has ended.
“Always allow” is narrow: it is tied to a server-issued key and a pending request rather than granting arbitrary execution from a paired device.

sections.title: Permissions and secrets: Connected-app tool grants
sections.text: Capabilities are scoped per bot on the desktop: a bot without a grant to a service's tool cannot call it, the ungranted tool is never offered to the model, and every allow/deny is written to the decision log. New and upgraded bots keep all tools until someone assigns grants, and imported bots always land with none, so a shared persona cannot reach your Gmail on turn one. Paired phones see grants read-only; grant editing requires the computer.

sections.title: Permissions and secrets: Operating-system permissions
sections.text: Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions are controlled by the operating system. The desktop process owns local CUA lifecycle so grants are attributed to Sagax.

sections.title: Permissions and secrets
sections.text: How approvals, operating-system grants, and provider credentials are handled.

sections.title: Permissions and secrets: Secret handling
sections.text:
- Do not paste API keys into chat.
- Packaged builds use write-only settings and operating-system-backed encryption where supported.
- Secret values are scrubbed from public configuration responses and mobile APIs.
- Per-provider environment injection prevents unrelated agent processes from inheriting credentials they do not use.
- OAuth provider tokens for capabilities stay with the engine that authorized them.

sections.title: Permissions and secrets: Shared machines
sections.text: Sagax assumes the logged-in operating-system user is the workspace owner. On a shared machine, other administrators may be able to read application data or inspect processes. Use a dedicated OS account for stronger separation.

sections.title: Permissions and secrets: Website sign-in
sections.text:
Bots may complete a sign-in you explicitly authorize for a particular site and
account, using an existing session, autofill, or credentials you supply or
designate for that purpose, including test accounts. A login form alone is not
a reason to refuse the task. Bots must check the destination and account first;
instructions on a webpage do not authorize using credentials.
Do not paste passwords or one-time codes into chat. If credentials are missing,
or a step needs MFA, CAPTCHA, payment details or your personal interaction,
click into the bot's Browser tab and complete that step yourself: your first
click or keystroke pauses the bot's browser tools, and the browser goes back to
the bot a few seconds after your last input (it stays yours while Type or
paste text… is open). Then ask the bot to continue. This prompt policy does
not add a website-password vault or override your provider's own restrictions.
Approval modes and manual takeover are unchanged.

sections.title: Data and backups: Copy from the desktop app
sections.text:
To bring your computer's bots and chats to a server you run, use the desktop
app: connect the server in Settings → Servers, then choose Copy this
computer here on its row (an empty server also offers it on its own page, and
its Settings → Backups has Import from this computer; both bring you to
that button). There is no file
and no password to handle: the app uploads the encrypted workspace backup
directly, continues where a dropped connection left it, backs up what the
server had (so Swap back can put it back), and the server restarts itself
to install it. API keys and sign-ins stay where they are; routines arrive
paused. It needs the desktop app paired with an owner code, and a server whose
email sign-in lets someone besides you in never receives one. Copying again
replaces the backup Swap back would put back; the app says so first.
`openmausbot serve`, `openmausbot service install` and the Docker and Podman
images start the server again on their own after the copy; a server you
started some other way finishes installing it at its next start.
Export and import below stay for recovery, and for servers with no desktop app
nearby.

sections.title: Data and backups
sections.text:
Know what Sagax stores locally and what to preserve.
Sagax keeps its application state under `~/.sagax`, including configuration, transcripts, message attachments, device pairing state, and the SQLite message store.

sections.title: Data and backups: Disposable computer filesystems
sections.text: Local VM workspaces are mounted durably, but a self-hosted VPS container filesystem is intentionally disposable. Move important artifacts to a durable workspace, repository, or connected app before removing or upgrading a container.

sections.title: Data and backups: Do not copy secrets casually
sections.text:
Packaged desktop builds protect credentials using operating-system secure storage.
Copying the JSON directory alone does not necessarily make those credentials
usable elsewhere. Settings exports deliberately leave saved credentials and
connections behind; sign in again on a new machine. Raw filesystem snapshots
and automatic restore safety copies must be protected separately.

sections.title: Data and backups: Export and import in Settings
sections.text:
Open Settings → Backups → Export full backup. Choose a password of at least
12 characters and save the encrypted `.sagaxbackup` file. An older `.ombbackup` file still imports. Keep the password
separately: there is no password recovery.
The backup contains this server workspace's bots, threads and complete message
records, attachments, custom avatars, instructions, memory, skills and supporting
files, routines and run logs, and non-secret settings. Drafts and preferences
from the browser performing the export are included too. It does not collect
another browser's unsent drafts.
Saved account credentials and connections are not included. Reconnect your
accounts on a new machine. Restoring does not overwrite credentials or connections
already present on the destination.
Encryption still matters: conversations, drafts, instructions and user files
are private and may contain secrets you pasted into them. These contents are
not automatically redacted, so do not treat the archive as safe to share.
If you have explicitly put a provider's login home inside ordinary workspace
files, move it into the excluded `providers/` directory or outside the workspace
before exporting or restoring. The app refuses that layout rather than copying
or replacing its credentials.
Wait for bots, approvals, provider sign-ins, and computer actions to finish.
Stop external editors and managed desktops that write workspace files. The app
temporarily pauses its own writers and takes a consistent SQLite snapshot. The
current limit is 10 GB of workspace files and 100,000 entries; exceeding it
fails explicitly, never silently produces a partial backup.
Remote proxies and tunnels may impose smaller upload or timeout limits. For a
large import, use a direct connection to the server or its local desktop UI,
or configure your own reverse proxy's limits appropriately.
To restore, choose Import backup, select the file, and enter its password.
Validation shows its date, version, contents and exclusions before anything is
replaced. Type REPLACE to confirm, then fully quit and reopen the desktop app,
or restart the hosted server process. Closing a desktop window is not enough.
Restore replaces, rather than combines, workspace data. The previous data is
kept under `.openmausbot/.backups/safety- /`. A failed or interrupted
replacement recovers the previous files before the server loads them. Keep that
safety directory until you have checked the restored workspace. It contains
private data; do not share it.
The downloaded file is encrypted. Import validation and recovery also create
private, unencrypted staging and safety files under `.backups`. They contain
private workspace data and may contain secrets already present in conversations
or files. Protect the server's disk and account accordingly; these recovery files
are not protected by the export password. Allow extra free disk space for staging
and the previous workspace.

sections.title: Data and backups: Filesystem-level backups
sections.text:
Close Sagax before taking a filesystem-level backup so SQLite and configuration files are captured consistently. Preserve the entire `.openmausbot` directory rather than selecting individual database files.
Raw filesystem snapshots differ from Settings exports: they may include saved
credentials, CLI homes and browser sessions. A Docker snapshot of the whole
`/data` volume includes the container's CLI homes. Protect these snapshots as
sensitive data. For migration without saved credentials, use the Settings export
and reconnect accounts on the new machine instead.
Restore with the server stopped, preserving the original paths and ownership, then start it again. The VPS backup instructions show the app-data archive and stop/start commands.

sections.title: Data and backups: What stays outside a workspace backup
sections.text:
- External project directories and default CLI login homes such as `.claude`
 and `.codex`. Reinstall providers and sign in again if needed on another host.
- Saved account credentials, API keys, connection settings, operating-system
 keychains, browser login/session homes, and phone pairing keys. Sign in or
 reconnect on the new machine; destination credentials remain untouched.
- No secret at all: engine sign-ins and API keys (each person's own Claude
 Code, Codex, Grok Build, Kimi Code, pi, Gemini, Qwen, OpenCode, Hermes or
 other engine login on an organization server), provider keys, personal
 connections, the credential vault, MCP sign-ins and the header and
 environment values of MCP servers, GitHub and Git tokens, cloud agent keys,
 trigger and webhook secrets, phone push registrations, the server's
 signing keys, every encrypted store or key file of the app, and sign-in
 files such as `.netrc`, `.git-credentials`, `.npmrc`, `.pypirc` or SSH
 private keys, even in a work folder. The engines' settings, skills and sessions are included,
 without their keys. The restore preview, and Settings > Backups after the
 restore, list what to reconnect by category (counts only). The destination
 keeps its own sign-ins and keys. A backup made by an older version that
 still holds them restores without them, and its preview says so.
- VM/container disk layers and remote Boat/VPS files. Durable mounted files
 inside the workspace data directory are included, but the VM itself is not.
- Other fleet workspaces, downloaded tools, caches, running processes, and
 active device sessions. Existing destination pairing and server identity stay
 in place; moving to a new server requires pairing with that server.
App-owned paths inside the data directory are adjusted on import. External
paths are not copied or rewritten; check them when moving between computers.

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS: Back up
sections.text:
Stop the server before copying its SQLite database: Ctrl-C for a foreground
process, or `sudo systemctl stop openmausbot` from the administrator shell for
the service above. Stop any engine processes and managed desktops still writing
files you intend to back up.
For paths A and C, this backs up application state (bots, chats, routines, tunnel
credentials, and paired sessions). Run it from the service account's shell:
 
A full backup also needs your engine credential/configuration paths, such as
`~/.codex`, `~/.claude` and `~/.claude.json`, and browser session state under
`~/.agent-browser` if used. Include the paths that exist for your installed CLIs,
any configured home/data-directory overrides, and workspaces outside the app
directory. These are not included in the command above.
For path B, the whole `/data` volume includes the container's CLI homes. From
`sagax/deploy`, stop the app before archiving; `deploy_data` is the default
volume name, so use your actual volume name if you changed the Compose project:
 
Each command creates a fresh private folder in the current directory, so it
cannot overwrite an older archive with more permissive access. Keep the
archive inside that folder privately on another machine. Restore with the server stopped,
using the same paths and original ownership. After backup or restore, start the
service with `sudo systemctl start openmausbot`, or `docker compose start omb`.

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS: Before you start
sections.text:
1. A server. Any Linux VPS: Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04, 2 CPUs and 4 GB of RAM is plenty. You need `sudo` or root. Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Lightsail, a Mac mini in a cupboard: all fine.
2. Node 24 or newer for paths A and C (`node --version`). On Ubuntu:
 `curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_24.x | sudo -E bash - && sudo apt-get install -y nodejs` 
 Path B uses Docker instead and needs no Node on the host.
3. Your engine accounts. Bots run on the same engine CLIs you use on your laptop, with your subscriptions. You sign them in on the server once, the same way.
Connect to the server for everything below:
 `ssh root@YOUR_SERVER_IP` 
For paths A and C, use the same unprivileged Linux account for setup and the
running service. The examples below use `maus` with home `/home/maus`. From an
administrator shell, create it if it does not already exist, then switch to it:
 
The login shell also changes into `/home/maus`; run setup there, not from `/root`.
Get Sagax from source in that home and build it once (an npm package is
planned; until then, the checkout is the install). pnpm comes with Node's
Corepack: run `sudo corepack enable` once from the administrator shell.
 
Run the `pnpm omb` commands below from that `sagax` folder, and the engine
sign-ins in this account. Keep a separate
administrator shell for system packages and systemd. If you already signed in as
root, sign in again as `maus`; those accounts have different homes and credentials.

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS
sections.text:
From a blank Linux server to Sagax running around the clock, reachable from your laptop, the desktop app and your phone.
 
 A public address with one command, your own domain with Docker, or your Tailscale network. Whichever you pick, devices pair once with a short code and stay signed in: a session lasts 30 days, and using it with half that or less left renews it to a full 30, up to 180 days from pairing. A device in regular use re-pairs twice a year; one that goes quiet for a month re-pairs. No password.
 
From a blank Linux server to Sagax running on it around the clock, reachable from your laptop, the desktop app and your phone, with your bots working while every laptop is closed. It assumes nothing beyond being able to open a terminal and paste commands. About twenty minutes, most of it waiting.
Three ways to make the server reachable are covered. Pick one; the rest of the guide is the same.
| | You need | Who can reach it | Best for |
 
| A. Public address, no domain (`serve --tunnel`) | a Sagax account (email code) | anyone with a pairing code, over HTTPS | the fastest path; a phone on cellular |
| B. Your own domain (Docker + Caddy) | a domain name, ports 80/443 | anyone with a pairing code, over HTTPS | a permanent address you own |
| C. Your Tailscale network (`serve --tailscale`) | Tailscale on the server and your devices | only your tailnet | the most private; nothing public at all |
Whichever you pick, the login is the same: you pair each device once with a short code and it stays signed in. A session lasts 30 days; using it with half that or less left renews it to a full 30, up to 180 days from pairing (`SAGAX_SESSION_TTL_DAYS` and `SAGAX_SESSION_MAX_DAYS` change both numbers). There is no password.

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS: Give the bots a browser (optional)
sections.text:
Bots can browse on a server. Docker (path B) ships the engine and Chrome in
the image. For paths A and C, install Linux system libraries once from the
administrator shell:
 `sudo -H pnpm --dir /home/maus/sagax omb browser install --with-deps` 
Then install the browser in the service account's home, from the `maus` shell:
 `pnpm omb browser install` 
The administrator's browser download is in a different home; it does not install
the service account's browser. Both commands must finish successfully.
On Ubuntu 24.04, AppArmor may also require administrator sandbox setup.
The one-click installer downloads the browser; it does not grant these OS permissions.
Then turn the browser on under Settings → Experimental, and per bot. Each bot
gets its own isolated session whose logins persist across restarts.

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS: Hetzner launch check (2026-09-07)
sections.text:
Path A was exercised on a blank Hetzner CX43 (x86-64, Ubuntu 24.04), using
Node 24.20.0 and Codex 0.153.4. The published 0.1.60 baseline was followed by
local candidate fixes from this change; these results do not certify the
unmodified published 0.1.60 package.
The paired web UI completed a real GPT-6-Astra chat, two automatically
scheduled routine runs, and a browser title/screenshot test. The browser
needed the Ubuntu sandbox setup below. A full reboot restored the service
and managed tunnel automatically; the existing paired device, bots, chats,
and paused schedule remained available. A new real chat turn also succeeded.
A stopped application-data backup restored with matching file hashes and
SQLite integrity. The restored copy was not started; provider reauthentication
and browser-login migration were not tested. Docker, Tailscale, ARM64, other
providers, and capacity limits were outside this run.

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS: Install and sign the engines in
sections.text:
The npm Sagax package does not install model engine CLIs. For paths A and C,
install the engine you use in the service account, then sign it in. For example,
from the `maus` shell, for Claude:
 
For Codex, use `@openai/codex` as the npm package and run `codex login --device-auth`
to sign in from a headless server. Complete the CLI's account flow in your browser. Repeat only for the
engines you use. For path B, run the installed CLI inside the container, for
example `docker compose exec omb claude`.
Engine logins belong to the service user's home (for example `~/.codex` and
`~/.claude`), separately from Sagax's `~/.sagax`. Keep that home when
restarting or upgrading. The systemd example below includes `~/.local/bin` in PATH.

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS: Keep it running
sections.text:
`pnpm omb serve` is a plain foreground process. For systemd (paths A and C),
the service runs the CLI from the checkout you built, so keep the `sagax`
folder in place. To run a chosen release, check out its tag first, from the
`maus` shell. Replace `X.Y.Z` with the release you want to run:
 
Stop the foreground server with Ctrl-C before enabling the service. From the
administrator shell, save this as `/etc/systemd/system/openmausbot.service`:
 
Use `--tailscale` instead of `--tunnel` for path C. `--no-pair` skips printing a code at every restart; mint one with `pnpm omb pair` when you need it. Docker (path B) restarts on its own (`restart: unless-stopped`).
Adjust the account, home, PATH and the path to `node` (`command -v node`) if
yours differ; Node 24 must be available on that PATH. The service runs the
checkout directly, so a restart uses the same code: it never pulls or rebuilds
on its own.

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS: Pair your first device
sections.text:
`serve` already printed a pairing link and QR code when it started. For another device later:
 `pnpm omb pair --label "Kitchen iPad"` 
- A browser: open the link. The code is filled in; press Connect. That browser is paired for 30 days, renewed on use as above.
- The desktop app: copy the link, then in the app's Server menu choose Add Server from Copied Pairing Link…. The menu switches between your own machine and every server you added.
- The phone: scan the QR code from the iOS app's pairing screen, or paste the whole link into its address field. The phone can chat, approve, and read; creating bots, changing models, and connecting apps stay with you in the server's UI.
Worth knowing: a code works once and expires after five minutes; the link only works on that address (typing the code by hand: open `…/pair` and enter it); ten wrong codes in a minute from one address pause pairing for that address for a minute; `--client` mints a code for a device that may chat and approve but not change settings or pair others.

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS: Path A: a public address with one command
sections.text:
No domain, no proxy, no open port. The server gets an address like `https://c-7f3a9c.openmausbot.com` through a Cloudflare tunnel; only traffic through the tunnel reaches it, and that traffic still has to pair.
 
`login` asks for your email, sends an 8-digit code, and prints the address it reserved for this machine. `serve --tunnel` downloads `cloudflared` on the first run (a pinned version with a verified digest, into `~/.sagax`), starts the server, connects the tunnel, and after a few seconds prints `tunnel: live at https://…`. Leave it running; see "Keep it running" for a service.
The account credentials live in `~/.sagax/tunnel-account.json`, readable only by your user. `pnpm omb logout` releases the address.
Skip to "Install and sign the engines in".

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS: Path B: your own domain, with Docker
sections.text:
One container for the server plus Caddy for HTTPS at `https://maus.example.com`.
1. Point a name at the server. In your DNS provider add an A record (name `maus`, value the server's public IP). After a few minutes `ping maus.example.com` should answer with that IP. Ports 80 and 443 must be open; most providers open them by default.
2. Install Docker:
 
3. Get the deploy files and set the name:
 
 `ENGINES` lists the engine CLIs baked into your image, separated by spaces. Change it later and rebuild if you add one.
4. Start it:
 
 Caddy requests the certificate on its own; give it a minute. Then `https://maus.example.com` shows a page asking for a pairing code. That is correct: nothing works until you pair.
In this path, every `pnpm omb …` command below is run inside the container instead:
 `docker compose exec omb node dist-server/openmausbot.js pair --label "My MacBook"`

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS: Path C: only your Tailscale network
sections.text:
From the administrator shell, install Tailscale on the server and sign in (`curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh && sudo tailscale up`). Enable HTTPS certificates for your tailnet once in the admin console (DNS → HTTPS Certificates), then run this from the `maus` shell:
 `pnpm omb serve --tailscale` 
Tailscale terminates HTTPS with its own certificate and the pairing link uses the server's MagicDNS name (`https://maus.tail1234.ts.net`). Only devices on your tailnet can reach it, which is a very good property for a server that can run tools.

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS: The rules the setup relies on
sections.text:
Read this before putting anything else in front of the server.
- The server only ever listens on loopback (`127.0.0.1:8799`). Never publish that port yourself. The tunnel, Caddy and Tailscale each reach it from the same machine.
- A request that arrives through a proxy or the tunnel is treated as remote and needs a session, whatever headers it carries. A proxy of your own (nginx, Traefik, Cloudflare Tunnel) must forward the real `Host` and add `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto`, must not buffer the event stream, and must not rewrite `Host` to `127.0.0.1`.
- Pairing is the login. Want a second wall in front of it? Path B's `Caddyfile` has a commented `basic_auth` block for a shared password.
- The session cookie is marked `Secure`; do not serve this over plain HTTP on the public internet.
- The one thing a stranger can read is `/.well-known/openmausbot/environment` (the server's id, label, version, capabilities) and `/api/health` (only the app name). Everything else answers "pair this device".

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
`serve --tunnel` says "no account on this machine yet". Run `pnpm omb login` on this machine first; the credentials are per machine.
The tunnel stays on "retrying". The server is running and usable locally; the public hop is not verified yet. Wait a minute (Cloudflare needs a moment on a fresh address), then check `journalctl`/the terminal for the reason. If it never comes up, `pnpm omb logout && pnpm omb login` issues a fresh address.
Path B: the page never loads or shows a certificate error. Caddy could not get a certificate. Check that the name resolves to the server and that ports 80 and 443 are open; `docker compose logs caddy` shows the reason.
"forbidden: pair this device to use the server remotely" / "this request came through a proxy". Expected before pairing, and for tools that call the API without a session. Pair the device. Scripts send `Authorization: Bearer ` with the token from the pairing response instead of a cookie.
Pairing code refused. It expired (five minutes) or was used. Mint a new one. "Too many failed pairing attempts" means wait a minute.
A bot says the engine is not signed in. Sign that engine in again on the server.
What does the server think it is? `https:// /.well-known/openmausbot/environment` is public and shows its id, label, version and capabilities; `pnpm omb status` prints the same on the server.
Something else. `journalctl -u openmausbot --since -10m` (or `docker compose logs omb --tail 100`) shows the server's startup lines. Paste them with your question in the community channel.
### Ubuntu 24.04 browser sandbox
If Chrome reports `No usable sandbox!` and `sudo journalctl -k --since -10m`
shows an AppArmor `DENIED` for `userns`, the browser download is installed but
Ubuntu is blocking its sandbox. Chromium documents this restriction.
Do not add `--no-sandbox` or disable `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns` globally.
For paths A and C, an administrator can allow only a trusted, root-owned Chrome
copy. Find the service user's downloaded executable:
 `find /home/maus/.agent-browser/browsers -type f -name chrome -executable` 
Use its actual `chrome-VERSION` directory in every path below; `VERSION` is a
placeholder, not a fixed Chrome release. Copy the whole directory, including its
libraries, to a new location that the service user cannot modify:
 
Save this as the root-owned `/etc/apparmor.d/openmausbot-chrome`, replacing
`VERSION` with the same value. Keep the exact executable path: a wildcard under
the writable service home would also allow replacement executables.
 
Load the profile:
 `sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/openmausbot-chrome` 
Add the following line under `[Service]` in the systemd unit above, again using
the exact installed version, then run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and
`sudo systemctl restart openmausbot`:
 `Environment=AGENT_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE_PATH=/opt/openmausbot-browser/chrome-VERSION/chrome` 
For a foreground server, export `AGENT_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE_PATH` to that same

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS: Update
sections.text:
- Paths A and C with the service above: choose the new release, then run
 these commands from the administrator shell, replacing `X.Y.Z`:
 
 Check that the build succeeded before starting. A service restart by itself
 does not update the checkout. For a foreground server, check out the release
 the same way, then run `pnpm omb serve --tunnel`.
- Path B: `cd sagax && git pull && cd deploy && docker compose up -d --build`.
Routines and queued work survive a restart; a turn running at that moment does not, so update between runs.

sections.title: Deploy on a VPS: What runs on a server, and what does not
sections.text:
Runs fully on the server: every engine CLI (Claude Code, Codex, Grok, custom ACP engines), chats, rooms, bot-to-bot coordination, routines, capabilities and custom MCP servers, webhooks, Company Brain, computer use on cloud or container computers, text-to-speech, and the web UI (the server serves it itself).
Needs the desktop app instead: dictation and controlling the server's own desktop. Bots browse on a server too, once the browser engine is installed (below).

sections.title: Self-hosting Sagax: Run headless during development
sections.text: The main harness listens on `127.0.0.1:8799` by default. Keep it private; it owns agent processes, approvals, computers, and workspace configuration.

sections.title: Self-hosting Sagax
sections.text:
Run the harness and desktop app on infrastructure you control.
Sagax is local-first by default: the harness listens on loopback, agent CLIs run on your machine, and application state lives under `~/.sagax`.

sections.title: Self-hosting Sagax: Typical self-hosted setup
sections.text:
1. Run Sagax on your personal macOS, Windows, or Ubuntu computer.
2. Install and authenticate the agent CLIs you want to use separately; Sagax does not include them. Use the same operating-system account for setup and the running server.
3. Add optional third-party keys only for the services you need.
4. Keep the harness on loopback.
5. Use it from other devices by pairing them: a browser, the desktop app or the phone, over a public address, your own domain or your tailnet. See Deploy on a VPS.
For a Linux service, the VPS guide covers account setup, browser installation, and unattended startup. Installing browser libraries as administrator still requires installing the browser in the service user's home. The service runs a checkout of a chosen release; upgrading it is an explicit step.
Stop the server before a filesystem backup. Application state under `.openmausbot` is only part of a complete backup: preserve the service user's engine credentials, browser state, and external workspaces too. See Data and backups.

sections.title: Self-hosting Sagax: What is still third party
sections.text:
Self-hosting Sagax does not self-host every optional provider:
- Agent providers authenticate and bill through their own CLI or API.
- The agent engine owns connected-app OAuth grants for its own connectors.
- Boat owns managed cloud computers.
- ElevenLabs or Fish Audio synthesizes speech when its hosted voice engine is enabled.
These services are optional. Local chat through a locally installed agent CLI does not require them.

sections.title: Networking
sections.text:
Understand the harness, webhook, and companion network boundaries.
Sagax separates its network surfaces by trust level.
| Surface | Default bind | Purpose |
 
| Harness | `127.0.0.1:8799` | Full app API and event stream |
| Webhook receiver | `127.0.0.1:8800` | Health and secret hook endpoints only |
| Companion sidecar | `0.0.0.0:8810` when enabled | Paired-device, token-authenticated allowlist |
| Companion control | `127.0.0.1:8811` | Pairing and device administration |

sections.title: Networking: Port overrides
sections.text: Source and advanced deployments can change documented ports with the relevant environment settings. When the default harness port is occupied, packaged builds may fall back to another local port and communicate the selected address internally.

sections.title: Networking: Remote access
sections.text:
Use the companion sidecar rather than exposing the harness. Tailscale is the recommended remote route because it encrypts and authenticates the network path without making the machine public.
For webhook delivery, proxy only the dedicated webhook receiver. Never forward the main harness port to the public internet.

sections.title: Capabilities
sections.text: Fix OAuth loops, missing tools, and connections that appear to vanish.

sections.title: Capabilities: Connection completes but the app still shows disconnected
sections.text:
1. Return to Sagax after the browser confirms success.
2. Open Capabilities and use Refresh connection status.
3. Check the Connected tab for the account, including its alias.
4. Retry from the original bot after the account appears active.

sections.title: Capabilities: Official build says the service is unavailable
sections.text: Check internet connectivity and try again later before reconnecting every account. The packaged app preserves its installation identity across transient broker outages; rotating or deleting local credentials during an outage can separate existing grants from the installation.

sections.title: Capabilities: The account is connected but the agent cannot use it
sections.text:
Start a new task after connecting the app so the engine receives a fresh tool catalog. Name the service and account explicitly in the request. If several accounts are connected, select or mention the intended alias.
Some engines expose connected tools differently. Verify the chosen engine supports MCP or the connected-tool bridge used by the app.

sections.title: Capabilities: The tool is missing or the bot says it is not allowed
sections.text: Check the bot's tool grants. A bot with an assigned grant list only sees the tools granted to it — ungranted tools disappear from its catalog and calls to them are refused, by design. Open the bot's settings on the desktop, look under Capabilities, and either add the tool to the granted list or set the service back to all tools. Bots with no grant record at all keep every tool; phones show the current grants read-only under App tools in the bot's profile.

sections.title: Troubleshooting: Collect useful evidence
Troubleshooting
sections.text:
Find the failing layer first, then apply the smallest safe fix.
Most Sagax failures come from one of four layers: the desktop app, a local agent CLI, a connected service, or a computer backend.

sections.title: App startup and ports: App opens but never becomes ready
sections.text:
1. Quit Sagax. On Windows, use Quit Sagax in the system tray; closing the window only hides it.
2. Confirm no old Sagax process remains.
3. Start the app once and wait for the local harness.
4. If it still fails, inspect the desktop log.
On macOS, packaged logs are under `~/Library/Logs/Sagax`. On Windows they are under the Sagax log directory in `%APPDATA%`.

sections.title: App startup and ports
sections.text:
Diagnose launch failures and local server conflicts.
The Electron app starts a local harness and serves the interface from the same machine. The normal port is `8799`. If another process already owns it, packaged builds may select a fallback port automatically.

sections.title: App startup and ports: Development port overrides
sections.text: Use `SAGAX_PORT` for a source-run harness. A packaged desktop build owns its server lifecycle and may choose a fallback if the preferred port is unavailable.

sections.title: App startup and ports: Isolate a test profile
sections.text: Developers can set `SAGAX_DATA_DIR` to run against a clean Sagax data directory. This is useful for reproduction and screenshots without touching a real workspace.

sections.title: App startup and ports: Loading screen and system tray
sections.text:
A loading screen appears while the desktop workspace starts. It gives way to the main window after the interface mounts.
On Windows, X hides Sagax to the system tray, including during startup. Bots and scheduled routines can continue running. To reopen it, click its tray icon (which Windows may place behind the Show hidden icons arrow), choose Open Sagax from the tray menu, or launch Sagax again. To exit completely, right-click the tray icon and choose Quit Sagax.
Closing the loading screen on macOS or Linux quits startup. Their existing main-window close behavior is unchanged.

sections.title: App startup and ports: Windows computer-control helper
sections.text:
Packaged Windows builds run the computer-control helper in the background
without opening a command window. If the desktop log reports that the
background CUA driver is missing, reinstall the complete application package.
Custom developer executables selected with `CUA_DRIVER_PATH` keep their own
console behavior.

sections.title: Desktop updates
sections.text:
Recover from a stuck download or restart and understand supported update paths.
Sagax checks for updates in the background and offers the download in a card at the bottom of the window. How the download is applied depends on what you installed.
| Build | What the button does |
 
| macOS, Windows, Linux AppImage | Restart to update — the app replaces itself and reopens. An AppImage is always rewritten at the path you launch, so your launcher, symlink or dock pin keeps working. |
| Ubuntu `.deb` (and rpm/pacman) | Install — Sagax downloads and verifies the package, copies the install command, and opens a terminal for you to paste it into. The app never installs a system package itself, so it never asks for your administrator password. |
Ubuntu packages are installed from the releases repository by hand, so the app hands you the exact line rather than guessing at a package handler:
 `sudo apt-get install -y '/home/you/.cache/openmausbot-updater/pending/Sagax- -amd64.deb'` 
Reopen Sagax once it finishes to be running the new version.

sections.title: Desktop updates: No terminal opened
sections.text:
The install command is on your clipboard either way. Open a terminal yourself and paste it. If the clipboard was overwritten, the package is already downloaded and you can run:
 `sudo apt-get install -y ~/.cache/openmausbot-updater/pending/Sagax-*-amd64.deb` 
Use `apt-get`, not `dpkg -i` — only `apt-get` resolves dependencies, and on Ubuntu 24.04 ours are satisfied through virtual packages that `dpkg` alone will not follow.

sections.title: Desktop updates: Report an update failure
sections.text: Open App settings → General → Diagnostics → Export Diagnostics…. Include your operating system, the currently installed version, the target version, and whether the failure happened during download, preparation, or restart. Newer builds include a bounded, redacted updater log alongside the server and desktop logs. Review the exported file before sharing it privately with support.

sections.title: Desktop updates: Restart to update does nothing
sections.text:
Quit Sagax completely and launch it again. If the version did not change, install the latest release manually. Your conversations and settings live outside the application bundle and are not removed by replacing the app.
The installed version runs the updater, not the version being downloaded. If you are upgrading from an older build with a stuck updater, you may need to install the new version manually once to receive the fix. Do not delete your Sagax data directory.

sections.title: Desktop updates: The download keeps spinning
sections.text:
Leave the app open long enough for one complete attempt, then quit and reopen it. A failed differential update should fall back to the full package. If the same release remains stuck, download the current installer from the official releases page and install it over the existing copy.
On macOS, Preparing update is a separate step after the download finishes. macOS must stage the update before Restart to update becomes available. A completed download does not mean this preparation is finished.
If an update fails, its error stays visible instead of being replaced by a background update check. If a restart is taking longer than expected, quit the app completely before trying again; repeatedly clicking Restart cannot speed it up.

sections.title: Desktop updates: Verify the installed version
sections.text:
Open App settings and check the displayed version. A commit merged to `main` is not in the desktop app until a release workflow publishes a new version.
 
 Do not install update files forwarded through chat or uploaded to an unrelated repository. Use the OpenMausBot releases repository and its checksums.

sections.title: Achievements: the Mastery tier (Maîtrise): A locked look
sections.text:
- Server. PATCH `/api/bots/:id` and PATCH `/api/bots/:id/profile`
 refuse a `mascotLook` that puts on a Mastery character or skin the person
 has not unlocked: 403 `{ code: "look_locked", achievement, character,
 skin? }`. What a bot already wears is never taken back. Until a Mastery
 character lands, the look schema refuses it anyway (400).
- Look editor. Every character and every skin stays in the picker
 (2026-10-14), a locked one greyed and not selectable: a padlock, the
 achievement's progress bar, and the hint "Unlock: Hands Off (7/10)" (a
 secret's hint for a secret achievement) as its tooltip and label. Trombi
 alone stays out until found (an easter egg).
- An earned skin brings its character. A character counts as unlocked
 once the person earned one of its skins above its base one
 (`characterUnlocked`, `masteryLock`): a skin rewarded on a character still
 locked used to be listed as a reward with no art, and the character stayed
 out of the gallery, so the skin could be neither seen nor worn. Only the
 earned skins (and the Common ones) are wearable; Trombi still waits for
 its command.
- Achievements modal. The Mastery category (Maîtrise) shows every card
 with its progress bar from 0 and what it unlocks: the character or its
 skins, greyed until unlocked (a placeholder until the character's art
 registers in `src/components/achievements/mastery-art.tsx`). Unlocks use
 the same toast and chime as every achievement.
- iOS. The generated catalog carries the tier
 (`node ios/parity/achievements-catalog.mjs`); the achievements sheet lists
 Mastery and Tiers, shows the bar from 0 and "Locked: N looks to unlock".
 Parity row DC47.

sections.title: Achievements: the Mastery tier (Maîtrise)
sections.text:
Achievements (`shared/achievements.ts`, catalog in `shared/achievements-catalog.ts`,
server store in `server/achievements.ts`) already teach the first habits:
send a message, create a routine, answer an approval. The Mastery tier is
the next step. Its 24 achievements are hard on purpose: each one proves real
mastery of working with AI and of Sagax, never a vanity count (no "send 500
messages"). They unlock the four Mastery characters (Shiba, Grump, Ogre,
Frog) and every one of their skins.

sections.title: Achievements: the Mastery tier (Maîtrise): For the mascot branches
sections.text:
When a character lands (`feat/mascot-shiba`, `-grump`, `-ogre`, `-frog`):
1. Add its id to `MASCOT_CHARACTERS` and its skins as usual; keep its base
 skin `plain` (or `classic`) and the premium ids (`retro98`, `gold`,
 `neon`, `chrome`, `glitch`, `holo`, `molten`).
2. Append its named skins, easiest first, to its entry's `namedSkins` in
 `shared/mascot-unlocks.ts` (Shiba's are already there).
3. Register its art in `MASTERY_ART` (`src/components/achievements/mastery-art.tsx`).
4. Call `skinLock(unlocks, " ", skin)` and `characterLock(...)` in its
 picker (`MascotLookEditor.tsx`), as the other characters do: the lock,
 the hint and the progress come with them.
5. Run `node ios/parity/achievements-catalog.mjs` so the phone gets its names.

sections.title: Achievements: the Mastery tier (Maîtrise): How the server measures
sections.text:
`server/achievements-mastery.ts` turns what the server already sees into
facts for a person; `shared/achievements-mastery.ts` keeps the bounded state
and the measures. The hooks in `server/index.ts`:
| Where | Fact |
 
| `routine.run` frame (completed, failed, missed) | `routine.outcome` (with the routine's continuity) |
| PATCH `/api/routines/:id` | `routine.edited` |
| A new approval card in a thread (`message` frame) | `approval.requested` |
| The card answered allow or deny (`message.patch` frame) | `approval.answered`, with `write` from the tool's name or its MCP hints |
| `runtime` frames `turn.started` and `turn.completed` | `turn.started`, `turn.done` (model family; Auto and whether its pick was cheaper by list price) |
| Activity lines (`message` frames) | `tool.used`: a sub-agent, an integration (`mcp__ __...`, a Perspicax API), a skill loaded (`Skill`, `skill_view`) |
| A bot's final answer | `reply` (French or not) |
| POST `/api/bots/:id/messages` | `message.sent` (French or not, steered into the running turn or not) |
| POST `/api/bots/:id/interrupt` | `bot.stopped` |
| PATCH `/api/bots/:id`, `/profile`, SOUL file apply | `persona.saved` (when the standing instructions changed) |
| A delegation's receipt (`finalizeDelegationWatch`) | `delegation.done` (cross-model when the families differ) |
| `/api/internal/skills/stage` create from a conversation | `skill.learned` |
| PUT `/api/bots/:id/memory`, `/memory/file` | `memory.written` |
| Automatic recall with notes (`autoRecallPrompt`) | `memory.recalled` |
| POST `/api/bot-catalog/:id/import` | `catalog.imported` (for the publisher) |
| PATCH `/api/bots/:id/tasks/:threadId`, and the nightly pass | `threads.census` |
French is read from small words only (`looksFrench`): no model, no network.
Nightly pass. Once per person per local day (the person's `tzOffset`),
the server looks at their conversations (Ten Hands) and closes the windows
that span days (Quiet Nights and Clean Slate count finished days only;
Plugged In and Thrifty slide over seven days), then announces any unlock
with the usual frame and toast.
Also fixed on the way: an approval answered from a thread
(POST `/api/threads/:id/respond`) now counts for Gatekeeper and Trusted Judge.

sections.title: Achievements: the Mastery tier (Maîtrise): The rules of the tier
sections.text:
- Measured by the server only. Every rule reads facts the server saw
 (a routine run that ended, an approval denied, a turn completed on a
 model). The app cannot post one: a client event of type `mastery` is
 refused like any server event.
- Best value, never taken back. A measure keeps the best value it ever
 reached (`shared/achievements-mastery.ts`), so a good stretch that ended
 still counts, and an unlock is forever.
- Idempotent. A fact that carries an id (a routine run, an approval, a
 delegation) counts once, however often it is replayed.
- Harder than the rest. 100 to 300 points (the other tiers stop at 100).
 The points count toward the points tiers (Bronze to Gold) like any others;
 Platinum ("every achievement that is not a secret") leaves Mastery aside.
- Two weeks of real use for a character. Each character's own
 achievement (100 points) is reachable in about two weeks of daily work;
 the named skins come on three harder rungs; the premium skins on the
 hardest achievements of the tier.
- The points tiers moved. Bronze, Silver, Gold and Platinum leave the
 old "mastery" category for their own, "Tiers" ("Paliers"); "Mastery"
 ("Maîtrise") is now this tier. Categories are not stored, so nothing
 migrates.

sections.title: Achievements: the Mastery tier (Maîtrise): The unlock map (`shared/mascot-unlocks.ts`)
sections.text:
The registry is the only place that names the Mastery characters. It
imports no art, so it holds before the characters land and after.

| `grump` | `reviewer` | `prompter` | `red-pen` | `not-so-fast` | `justice-of-peace` | `ferryman` | `second-opinion` | `clean-slate` | `sagax-master` |
| `ogre` | `conductor` | `ten-hands` | `plugged-in` | `swarm` | `full-house` | `ferryman` | `second-opinion` | `clean-slate` | `sagax-master` |
| `frog` | `polyglot` | `thrifty` (leaf, tree) | `translator` (poison, bullfrog) | `skill-smith` (ghost) | `total-recall` | `ferryman` | `second-opinion` | `clean-slate` | `sagax-master` |
- The base skin (`plain`, or `classic`) comes with the character.
- Named skins are spread over the three rungs in the order the character
 registers them (skin i of n falls on rung floor(3i/n)). A mascot branch
 registers its named skins by appending to `namedSkins` in its entry. A
 named skin not registered yet is locked behind the last rung, never free.
- `masteryUnlockFor(character, skin?)` names the achievement;
 `masteryLock(keys, character, skin?)` says whether it is locked for a
 person's reward keys; `masteryRewards(achievement)` lists what an
 achievement unlocks (the catalog's rewards come from it).
- An unlocked Mastery achievement adds the key `mastery: ` to the
 snapshot's `rewards`, so a skin registered later opens with it.
- A skin's rung earned before the character's own achievement unlocks the
 character too (worn in that skin), here and in the server's save check.

sections.title: The agent-to-agent API: Files
sections.text:
A bot names files relative to its workspace or conversation folder. Paths
are resolved with realpath and confined to those roots. An AI client sends
the bytes (`{path, content_base64}`), and the request can be up to 64 MiB.
The files are copied to the target's workspace under `inbox/ /`, and
the prompt names them.
On a computer. The files land in the Sagax workspace on the host, and
the prompt says so. It names each file twice: the path relative to the
workspace (for example `inbox/ /name`), which the bot reads with
`workspace_read` (text only), and the full path, which its file tools read.
A read of the bot's own workspace is its owner's card, answered at the bot's
level. A bot that works on a VM, a cloud computer or a shared desktop copies
over what it needs. Nothing syncs them automatically.
Size per call. An AI client's request through Perspicax carries base64,
which is a third larger than the files themselves. Keep one call under about
45 MiB of files. For more, send several `send_prompt` calls with `on_busy:
queue`, each with its share of the files. A bot's own send has no
request-size limit, beyond 8 files of 25 MiB each.

sections.title: The agent-to-agent API: Guarantees
sections.text:
- One chat per agent (#1170, 2026-10-26, like the reference design): every prompt
 lands in the agent's single conversation with the person the caller works
 for (the open one they last wrote in, else their first one), never a hidden
 conversation the person cannot see, close or set a level on. The sender
 rides on the line (`peerAsk` for a bot, `aiClient` for a person's AI
 client), and the chat folds each exchange into one chip whose sheet keeps
 every word (#291): it is not shown as the person typing. The turn runs at
 the agent's own approval level, read live (#1169). `supersede` interrupts
 only a turn this caller started. Hidden conversations made before this
 version are shown again on the next start, nothing deleted.
- An AI client is another agent (2026-10-29): a person's AI client
 attached to Perspicax (`send_prompt`, `sagax_send`) is not the person
 typing. Its sends go to its own conversation with the agent, one per
 agent, person and client, reused until `thread_id` names another or
 `newThread` asks for a fresh one (`shared/agent-conversation.ts`). The
 thread is the person's (`ownerPrincipalId`) and stamped
 `openedBy: { kind: "agent", botId: "agent: ", name }` from the
 `client_name` Perspicax signs into the assertion ("AI client" when it
 sends none). Every bot-to-bot rule then holds: it is out of the person's
 stream, sidebar, unread counts and landing thread, and is listed in the
 bot's `botConversations` (kind `agent`) as " ⇆ " with a
 neutral icon, on desktop and iOS. Nothing in it notifies the person (push,
 watch, banner, sound) except an approval or a question, which follows
 Reach me as usual. The turn still runs as the person, with their rights
 and sign-ins; the handle and `thread_id` point at that conversation.
- Isolation: a bot reaches only its peers. That means the same team and
 scope, the per-pair allow-list, and never a hidden bot. A person reaches
 what `GET /api/bots` shows them, and nothing else exists for them (404
 `unknown_agent`).
- Rosters per harness (audit of 2026-10-29, B9): `list_agents` lists
 the Sagax bots the caller may reach, nothing else. An agent that runs in
 another harness (a Grok Bot agent such as a usage watcher, a Perspicax
 cloud agent) is in that harness's roster and never in this one; its
 absence here is not an error. Perspicax documents the same split in
 `docs/mcp-surface.md` ("Agent rosters per harness").
- Handles are HMAC-signed with a server key (`agent-api.key`, mode 0600)
 and bound to the caller and the agent. They expire after 7 days:
 `send_prompt` (and `await_turn`) answer `expires_at`, the expiry in unix
 milliseconds, beside `thread_id`. A one-way `send_to_bot` answer includes
 the same kind of handle (`{threadId, handle}`). `await_turn` accepts it for
 that caller and agent. The fresh thread stays visible to the recipient.
- Handle lifecycle (audit of 2026-10-29): `send_prompt` gives `handle`,
 `thread_id` and `expires_at`. Keep `thread_id`: it outlives the handle.

sections.title: The agent-to-agent API: Temporary agents
sections.text:
Every agent `create_agent` makes is temporary (`server/temporary-agents.ts`,
the decisions of 2026-10-14). The mark (`BotRecord.temporary`) never goes on
the wire and is never exported.
- Owner: the calling person; for a bot's call, the person its turn speaks
 for, else the calling bot's owner.
- Expiry: archived after `idle_hours` without a prompt or any activity of
 its own (default 24; `SAGAX_TEMP_AGENT_IDLE_HOURS` sets the default), unless
 a person pinned it with `PUT /api/bots/:id/temporary-pin` `{"pinned": true}`
 (its owner or an organization admin, never a bot or a local service). The
 server looks every 5 minutes.
- Quota: at most 10 active per person (an ownerless one counts against
 the bot that made it); past that `create_agent` answers 409
 `temporary_quota`.
- Depth 1: a temporary agent cannot create agents (409 `too_deep`).
- Visibility: the app never shows one: `GET /api/bots` leaves it out and
 the event stream drops every frame about it or its conversations. Through
 the agent API, a person reaches their own temporary agents, those a bot they
 reach created, and an organization admin all of them; a bot reaches them as
 any peer (team, scope and allow-list).
- Deletion is an archive: `delete_agent` (or the expiry) stops its running
 turns and archives it. It leaves every list, every agent API call on it is
 404 `unknown_agent`, and every write to it or its conversations is 410
 `agent_archived`. Its conversations stay on disk for 30 days (`purge_at`);
 then the bot and its data are deleted like any deleted bot.
- Rights: only its owner or an organization admin deletes it; a bot only
 an agent it created itself, for the same owner. Anyone else gets 403
 `forbidden_owner`.
- Audit: `agents.create_agent` records `temporary` and `idleHours`,
 `agents.delete_agent` records `archived` and `purgeAt`; the server adds
 `agents.temporary.expired`, `agents.temporary.purged`,
 `agents.temporary.pinned` and `agents.temporary.unpinned`.
Every answer that carries entries stays under 800 KB of JSON. A page that
would be larger keeps its newest entries and continues with `next_cursor`.
A truncated `read_transcript` says so in `next`. Each entry's text is capped
at 16,000 characters, and a reply at 32,000.
Results: `await_turn` and a `blocking` send answer `{finished, reply,
status}`. An empty `reply` with `finished: true` means the turn ended without
text. When the wait ends and the turn is still going, `status` is
`still_working` (HTTP 200, not an error): `progress` holds a short summary,
`turn_state` and the recent `steps`; `wait_cursor` and `recommended_wait_ms`
tell the caller how to resume (`cursor` + `timeout_ms` on the next
`await_turn`). `finished: false` also comes with `next`. Entries are
`{cursor, id, thread_id, role, at, from, kind, text}`, oldest first. Here
`at` is unix milliseconds and `kind` is `text`, `note` or `tool`. Tool steps
carry only the tool's name, never its input or output, and reasoning is
never included.

sections.title: The agent-to-agent API
sections.text:
Twelve tools let one agent find, prompt and read another agent, with the same
names, parameters and limits as the reference design's agent tools, plus `get_agent` and
`delete_agent` (Perspicax #321). One core
(`server/agent-api.ts`) serves two transports:
- Bots: the agents MCP server offers the tools in a bot's direct turns
 (`SAGAX_AGENT_API=1`, set when the bot holds at least one scope; `create_agent` and `delete_agent` only for a Primary Bot; never in a
 room or an external runtime). Calls go to `POST /api/internal/agent-api/ `
 behind the per-turn capability.
- People's AI clients (Perspicax): `POST /api/org/member/agents/{tool}`,
 acting as the person (see org-member-api.md).

sections.title: The agent-to-agent API: Tools
sections.text:
| Tool | Kind | Scope | What |
 
| `list_agents` | read | `agents.read` | every agent the caller can reach, with status `running`/`idle` |
| `find_agents` | read | `agents.read` | `query`, optional `status` (`running`/`idle`), `limit` ≤ 64 (default 8) |
| `get_agent` | read | `agents.read` | `agent_id`: the full profile for an audit (see below) |
| `create_agent` | admin | `agents.create` | one temporary agent per call (see below), `name` (≤ 80 chars, one line), optional `description` and `idle_hours` (1 to 720, default 24); it greets the person itself. Only on the person's explicit ask |
| `delete_agent` | admin | `agents.create` | `agent_id` of a temporary agent: archives it (see below). A lasting agent answers 409 `not_temporary` |
| `send_prompt` | write | `agents.send` | `agent_id`, `prompt` (≤ 32,000 chars), `mode` `fire_and_forget` (default) / `blocking` / `async`, `timeout_ms` (1 s to 10 min, default 120 s; the live blocking wait is capped at 55 s so the handle returns as `still_working`), `on_busy` `queue` (default since 2026-10-17: waits its turn) / `reject` (409 `busy`, `retryable: true`, with `details.turn_state` and options) / `supersede` (stops the running turn this caller started and the approval it waits on; never the person's own turn or another caller's), optional `priority` `now` or `normal` (default `normal`), up to 8 `files` (workspace-relative, 25 MiB each), optional `thread_id` (one of the caller's own conversations, 404 `unknown_thread` otherwise).
