or one chosen when it was opened) is not converted (409
`confidential_shared_folder`): its files and checkpoints already live with
that folder. The person opens a new confidential thread instead. On an
OMB Cloud home only its owner opens confidential threads: the owner holds
the disk and every conversation on it, so a guest's could never be kept
from them.
It is permanent. The server refuses any change back
(`confidential: false` on a confidential thread is 409
`confidential_permanent`, confirmed or not). To work normally the person
opens a new thread; deleting the thread is the only way to end it.
The clients show it everywhere the thread appears: a classification banner
(solid band, « CONFIDENTIEL », lock icon, `role="note"`, read as « Fil
confidentiel : ce fil n'est ni mémorisé, ni exporté, ni partagé ») at the top
of the conversation and above the composer, not dismissible, with its height
reserved; a lock and « Confidentiel » on the sidebar row and in the window
title; a stamp on a Markdown export the person makes of their own thread.

sections.title: Confidential threads (Fil confidentiel): What the server does while a thread is confidential
sections.text:
| Path | Ordinary thread | Confidential thread |
 
| Automatic memory capture (upkeep) | queued after each turn | never queued; turns already waiting are dropped when the thread turns confidential |
| Daily log line (`memory/log/ .md`) | one per turn | none |
| `memory_update`, `memory_log`, group and team memory, rules, docs, skill staging | allowed | refused (403 `confidential_thread`) |
| Perspicax `memory_write` to a team or `org`, `memory_propose`, `memory_promote` | allowed | refused |
| Perspicax `memory_write` to the person's own tier (`me`) | allowed | `scope: "me"` is written in (an omitted scope never falls to Perspicax's own default); then it waits for the owner's Allow on a card; on Allow the bot is asked to repeat that exact write (scope, topic, title, body, tags, directory title, searchable), which a one-shot pass lets through |
| Any other Perspicax call | allowed | fail closed: only known reads pass (`api_list`, `api_search`, `api_describe`, `api_lookup`, `identity`, `memory_recall`, `memory_search`, `work_search`, `claim_list`, Perspicax's own unprefixed `find_*`, `get_*`, `read_*`, `list_*`; of a profile's tools only ` __query` and `read_action`; `api_plan` only when every step passes); every other call waits for the owner's card showing the server, the tool and every argument, whole (a call too long to show whole is refused); a JSON-RPC batch is refused. The file-style `memory` tool reads freely and changes only plain paths under `/memories/me/`, with the card |
| Other MCP servers (connected apps, personal servers, the workplace, the bot's data tools) | by approval mode | a read verb with something after it passes; a read verb followed by a write verb is refused; a bare verb and anything else waits for the owner's card, whatever the approval mode (Full and always-allow included); the one-time Allow is bound to the server, the tool and the arguments |
| A bot acting as its person (`act`) from an ordinary thread | the person's routes | a request naming a confidential thread is refused (any method, Full included); lists and search hits come back without confidential threads; screen commands never open one |
| Routine results, the bot's main thread, Retry thread, pages (`propose_page`) | allowed | never into or from a confidential thread |
| Peers, rooms and channels (`ask_bot`, `delegate_bot`, `coordinate_bots`, `post_to_room`, `create_room`, `manage_room`, `act`, `start_thread` on another bot, the agent API) | allowed | refused |
| Turns that name no thread (peer asks, asides, delegations, automation) | the bot's selected thread | never a confidential thread, even its owner's selected one: the bot owner's newest ordinary conversation, else a new one |
| Threads it opens (`start_thread` on itself, parallel tasks) | ordinary | confidential, same owner |

sections.title: Content encryption at rest: Backups
sections.text:
The workspace backup (`server/workspace-backup.ts`) exports the message
database in the clear, inside the archive it already encrypts with the
backup password, as before this change: the server hands its unwrapped keys
to the backup worker in memory (`contentKeysForExport`), the snapshot copy
is opened (`unsealDatabaseCopy`), and keys, bindings and blind index are
dropped from the copy. A key the server cannot open at that moment fails the
backup instead of leaving conversations out. A restore brings plain rows,
which the destination's own migration seals under its own keys, so an
archive restores on any machine. A raw copy of `messages.db` made outside
Sagax is sealed, and opens only with that installation's KEK.

sections.title: Content encryption at rest
sections.text:
Conversations are encrypted in the message database (`DATA_DIR/messages.db`)
with a content key per person, and a key of its own for each confidential
thread. Deleting a person or a confidential thread destroys its key, so what
was sealed under it never opens again (cryptographic erasure). Search and
recall keep working through a blind index: keyed tokens, never text. The
bots' memory, the attachments and the event logs are sealed with the same
keys ("Files and logs" below).
Code: `server/content-crypto.ts` (sealing, blind tokens),
`server/content-keys.ts` (keys and their wrapping),
`server/content-key-azure.ts` (Azure Key Vault),
`server/content-encryption-env.ts` (settings), `server/message-sealing.ts`
(row shape, recall terms, snippets), `server/message-db.ts` (reads, writes,
migration, erasure), `server/message-search-query.ts` and the search worker,
`server/content-export.ts` (backups), `server/content-file-crypto.ts` and
`server/content-at-rest.ts` (files and logs). Tests:
`server/content-encryption.test.ts`, `server/content-at-rest.test.ts`.
Benchmarks: `node --experimental-strip-types scripts/bench-content-encryption.ts`
(transcripts) and `scripts/bench-content-at-rest.ts` (files and logs).

sections.title: Content encryption at rest: Erasure
sections.text:
- A person (`DELETE /api/me`, the provider's purge, `erasePersonDataNow`
 in `server/index.ts`): after their threads go, `eraseContentOwner`
 re-seals any thread still bound to their key that now belongs to someone
 else (a bot that changed hands), then deletes the rows still sealed under
 their keys and destroys their owner key and every confidential-thread key
 under it.
- A confidential thread (`deleteThread`): its rows go, and its own key
 is destroyed with them.
- Any thread: its rows, receipts and key binding go (`deleteThread`).
A key is destroyed by deleting its row with `secure_delete` on, then
truncating the write-ahead log. This erases within the live database: a
copy made before (a disk snapshot, a copy of the data folder) still holds
the wrapped key of that time and opens with the key-encryption key, which an
erasure does not change. The workspace backup is in the clear by design
(above) and follows its own retention.

sections.title: Content encryption at rest: Files and logs
sections.text:
What the server keeps outside `messages.db` is sealed with the same content
keys (`content_keys`, the same KEK, no second key store), reversibly, by the
same setting (`SAGAX_CONTENT_ENCRYPTION`).
| What | Where | Key | Read by |
 
| bot memory | `workspaces/ /` `MEMORY.md`, `memory/` (topics, daily logs, archive), `docs/` | the bot's owner on an organization server, else the workspace | the prompt, the Memory editor and journal, search; the engine's own file tools |
| memory index | `memory_files` in `messages.db` | the same | `session_search`, automatic recall, `workspace_search` |
| memory journal | `memory-journal/ .ndjson` (each row keeps the full prior text) | the same | Memory panel, revert |
| group memory | `group-memory/ /MEMORY.md` | the workspace | the room's prompt and editor |
| attachments | everything under `attachments/`: uploads, generated files, scaled pictures (`.model/`), an Office document's pictures (`.office/`), archive manifests (`.archives/`) and unpacked archives (solo) | the uploader on an organization server (known at upload), else the workspace | downloads and previews (streamed), copies to a person's computer or server environment, the Office, picture and archive readers, the drivers; the engine by path |
| event logs | `events/ .ndjson`, `native/ .ndjson` | the thread's key, as its messages | inspector, Activity, session ids |
| decision log | `decisions/YYYY-MM.ndjson` | the row's thread, else the workspace | Activity, Journal, History |
| admin activity | `admin-activity/YYYY-MM.ndjson` | the workspace | Activity, the organization audit |
| video jobs | `video-jobs/ .json` | the job's thread | video generation resume and status |
| held steers | `held-steers/ .json` | the thread's key | restart recovery of messages accepted into a running turn |
File format (`server/content-file-crypto.ts`): a header (`SGXF`, version,
chunk size, key id, context) then AES-256-GCM chunks of 64 KiB, each with its
own nonce and tag. The additional data of a chunk is the key, its owner, the
file's context (an attachment's stored path, `memory/ `), the chunk's
index and whether it is the last one: a chunk moved, dropped or cut off, or a
file copied to another place or another bot, does not open. A file is sealed
and opened as a stream, never whole in memory, and a byte range (the audio
route's `Range`, a download) opens only the chunks it covers.
Log lines are sealed in blocks, one physical line per record kept (so
counts, line numbers, the organization audit's ids and a rotation that cuts
on a line boundary stay as they are): every line of a block but the last is
`{"sb":" "}`, and the last one is
`{"sb":" ","n": ,"l": ,"sealed":" : ","p":[ ]}`,
the AES-256-GCM of the block's original lines, byte for byte (additional
data: key, owner, folder and file name, block id, count and the projection
text: a block moved, cut or with a projection edited does not open). A
reader opens a block once for all its lines (`LogReader`), reading the line

sections.title: Content encryption at rest: Keys
sections.text:
| Key | Owner | Wrapped by |
 
| owner key | a person (`principals.json` id); the workspace (`@workspace`) for rooms, unowned threads and receipts | the KEK |
| thread key | one confidential thread | its owner's key (AES-256-GCM) |
A thread's owner is its recorded person (`ownerPrincipalId`), else on an
organization server the bot's owner, else the workspace (a solo or desktop
install has one person, so one key in practice). A thread keeps the key its
rows were sealed with (`thread_keys`); turning it confidential or giving it
an owner (`assignTaskOwners`) gives it its new key at once, and the migration
re-seals its older rows. Keys live wrapped in `content_keys` in
`messages.db`; unwrapped, they stay in the server's memory only.

sections.title: Content encryption at rest: Migration
sections.text:
A background loop on timers, about 4 ms of work then a 20 ms pause (a
sixth of one core while it runs). `on`: plain rows are sealed (each batch
checks that the sealed copy opens to the same message before it replaces
it) and rows under an older key are re-sealed under their thread's key.
`off`: sealed rows are opened back to plain. Receipts and follow-ups follow.
A pass runs at start and after any key change; reads accept both states
throughout. While rows are sealed, `PRAGMA secure_delete` is on, so the
plain cells they replace are zeroed.
After a pass that sealed plain rows, the next start (before the server
serves anything) rebuilds the plain full-text index (`messages_fts`, whose
segments could still hold words of the rows just sealed) and runs one
`VACUUM` (free pages written before the pass can still hold old text), then
checkpoints the write-ahead log (`vacuumAfterSealing`; skipped above 1 GB,
retried at the next start).

sections.title: Content encryption at rest: Performance
sections.text:
`scripts/bench-content-encryption.ts`, synthetic text (about 1 KB a message,
25,000 rows), medians, macOS arm64, Node 26 (2026-10-26, on a shared host:
compare columns, not absolute values):
| Measure | Off | On |
 
| append (row + branch head), p50 / p95 | 0.11-0.16 / 0.40-0.50 ms | 0.09-0.10 / 0.12-0.17 ms |
| blind index, background, per row | none | about 0.2 ms, in 6 ms slices |
| streamed patch, p50 | 0.30-0.38 ms | 0.20-0.21 ms |
| read a 5,000-message thread (cold) | 15-20 ms | 29-30 ms |
| read the newest 100 | 0.3-0.5 ms | 0.6-0.7 ms |
| substring search, word present / absent | 54-71 / 49-57 ms | 57-77 / 35-42 ms |
| substring search, two characters | 88-102 ms | 38-40 ms |
| search through the worker | 49-56 ms | 37-46 ms |
| recall (any terms) | 4-5 ms | 7-9 ms |
Writes are faster sealed: the plain full-text index tokenizes every write in
the transaction, the blind index runs just after it. Opening costs about
2.5 µs a message, seen only on a cold read of a whole long thread (the
store keeps it in memory after). Migrating 15,000 rows took 6-13 s on a quiet
host (40 s on a saturated one) in steps of 6-11 ms (p95 about 20 ms; a WAL
checkpoint or FTS5 merge now and then makes a step of 100-300 ms), and the
next start's rebuild and VACUUM took 0.2-0.5 s (0.8 s saturated). `off`
took 6-12 s, with steps up to a few hundred milliseconds (1.3 s once on a saturated host) when FTS5 merges
the plain index it refills.

sections.title: Content encryption at rest: Row format
sections.text:
A sealed row keeps its columns (`thread_id`, `id`, `at`, `role`, `kind`)
and adds:
- `sealed`: version byte `0x01`, 12-byte IV, 16-byte tag, then AES-256-GCM
 of the whole message JSON (text included). The additional data is
 `sagax-content:v1 \0 key id \0 owner \0 thread id \0 message id`: a
 blob copied to another row, thread or person does not open (the row reads
 as absent, and one line, without content, says so);
- `key_id`: the content key;
- `text`: empty;
- `json`: a cleartext projection with only what the server's own SQL filters
 on: `id`, `at`, `role`, `kind`, `sealed: 1`, `hasText`, `from.name` and
 `from.botId`, `peerAsk.name`, `relayed`, `sendId`, `webhookPost`,
 `goalRun.status`, the open-card flags (`card.requestType`, `requestId`,
 `answered`, `dismissed`, `expired`) and `refs` (stored attachment names
 the message points at, for `threadsReferencing`).
A plain row has `sealed` and `key_id` empty: a database never encrypted
reads exactly as before, and every read accepts both. Receipts
(`command_receipts.result`) and queued follow-ups (`chat_followups.payload`)
are sealed as text fields (`sagax-sealed:v1: : `, additional
data naming the field, its key and its id).
A row whose key was destroyed is skipped by every read (erased, never
wrong). A key that exists but cannot be unwrapped on this launch (the
keychain unreadable, Key Vault unreachable) makes a read fail
(`ContentKeyUnavailable`) rather than show an empty or partial transcript,
and new rows are written plain until the key is back.

sections.title: Content encryption at rest: Search and recall
sections.text:
Nothing is reduced: substring search (`/api/search`, the sidebar), ranked
recall (`session_search`, automatic recall, `recentMessages`,
`readMessageText`, `latestSaidByBot`) and the attachment checks work on
sealed and plain rows alike, mixed during a migration.
- Substring search: every sealed text row (and activity chip, by its
 tool name) has a keyed Bloom filter of its three-character windows
 (`message_index.bloom`: one bit per window, AES-256 of the window under
 the key's index key, twice as many bits as windows, 256 at least). The
 search worker, given the unwrapped keys in memory, keeps the rows whose
 filter holds every window of the needle, opens them newest first and
 confirms the substring on the text (same snippet and highlight). A
 needle under three characters opens the sealed rows newest first until
 it has its hits.
- Recall: the keyed words of text and digest rows (and their first four
 letters, for a prefix stem) are in a contentless FTS5 table
 (`messages_sealed_fts`, `detail=column`), so bm25 ranks them as before;
 the candidates are opened, checked against the query and snippeted
 (matched words in brackets) from the text.
- Tokens are written just after the row, in slices of a few milliseconds
 (a streamed reply is indexed once, not per patch), and always before a
 search, a recall or a backup reads them.
- Deleting a row (or re-sealing it) removes its index rows (triggers);
 destroying its key leaves any token that remains in an FTS segment
 meaningless.
What the index still reveals to someone holding the database file
without the keys: per row, which keyed words recur and how often, which
rows share a word or a four-letter prefix (with one owner's key), and how
long a row's text is (its filter size). Not the words themselves, and
nothing across two people's keys.

sections.title: Content encryption at rest: Settings
sections.text:
All by environment, read at start. Nothing here names a vault, tenant or
organization; the operator supplies their own.
| Variable | Values | Default |
 
| `SAGAX_CONTENT_ENCRYPTION` | `on`, `off` | `on` |
| `SAGAX_CONTENT_KEY_PROVIDER` | `local`, `azure-keyvault` | `local` |
| `SAGAX_CONTENT_KEY_AZURE_KEY_URL` | `https:// .vault.azure.net/keys/ [/ ]` | none |
| `SAGAX_CONTENT_KEY_AZURE_ALG` | `RSA-OAEP-256`, `RSA-OAEP`, `A256KW` | `RSA-OAEP-256` |
| `SAGAX_CONTENT_KEY_AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET` | a client secret (or `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET`) | none |
| `SAGAX_CONTENT_AT_REST_GRACE_MS` | idle time before a file written plain is sealed (files and logs, below) | `600000` (10 minutes) |
On by default. A new installation writes sealed rows from the first
message. An existing one migrates in the background (below), reversibly.
`SAGAX_CONTENT_ENCRYPTION=off` is the way back: the migration opens every
sealed row back to plain, a little at a time, and new rows are written plain.
Key-encryption key (KEK).
- `local`: the vault key the encrypted MCP sign-in store already uses
 (`resolveVaultKey` in `server/mcp-oauth.ts`): on the desktop the OS
 keychain through Electron safeStorage (`SAGAX_MCP_OAUTH_KEY`), on a
 headless server a 0600 key file in the data folder. A derivation of its
 own (HKDF, `sagax content kek v1`) wraps the content keys (AES-256-GCM).
- `azure-keyvault`: each person's content key is wrapped and opened by Key
 Vault (`wrapKey` / `unwrapKey`, REST API 7.4), so the key that opens the
 transcripts never sits on the server's disk. Credentials, first match
 wins: a client secret (`AZURE_TENANT_ID`, `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`, the secret
 above); workload identity (`AZURE_TENANT_ID`, `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`,
 `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE`, `AZURE_AUTHORITY_HOST`, as AKS sets them);
 a managed identity (`IDENTITY_ENDPOINT` + `IDENTITY_HEADER`, else the
 instance metadata service; `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` picks a user-assigned one).
 The identity needs the key permissions `wrapKey` and `unwrapKey` only.
 Keys are unwrapped once at start, before the store reads a transcript; a
 key created later is wrapped asynchronously and the rows written meanwhile
 stay plain until the migration seals them. Switching from `local` to
 `azure-keyvault` (or back) re-wraps the existing keys at the next start;
 the local key keeps opening rows it wrapped until then. A wrapped key
 records the Key Vault key version that wrapped it, so a rotated key keeps
 opening older content keys; a row naming another vault is refused. The
 access token stays in memory; no token, secret or key is ever logged.
A misconfigured provider (an unknown name, Key Vault without a key URL)
stops the server at start with the variable to fix.

sections.title: Cursor Agent CLI: Autonomy
sections.text:
For compatibility with direct driver embedders, an instance `fullAuto: true`
adds `--force` (the CLI's documented auto-approve switch) only when a turn
does not provide a bot approval level. Sagax app turns always provide
one: both Ask for approval and Approve for me launch Cursor without
`--force`, then Sagax handles its permission requests according to the
bot's current level.

sections.title: Cursor Agent CLI
sections.text:
Cursor is an optional Sagax engine. Sagax runs the official
`cursor-agent` CLI in ACP stdio mode (`cursor-agent acp`), so
sessions, streaming, coding tools, permission requests, MCP integrations,
resume, and cancellation use the same runtime as the other ACP engines.
Bots on this engine consume the user's Cursor subscription (or a
`CURSOR_API_KEY` / `CURSOR_AUTH_TOKEN`), not a separate Anthropic/OpenAI/xAI
key.

sections.title: Cursor Agent CLI: Models
sections.text:
The picker starts from a small static catalog and refreshes from plain
`cursor-agent models` output (`slug - Label`, with `(default)` / `(current)` markers).
Live ids are merged into the main cloud rail (not the local-models pane). A
failed listing keeps the last usable catalog (then the static fallback) rather
than emptying the rail.
`--model ` is passed as a global CLI flag before `acp`. Current CLIs
(checked with 2026.09.28) ignore that flag in ACP sessions: every session
starts on `default[]` (Auto). The pick only lands through ACP
`session/set_model`, which accepts only the parameterised ids the session
advertises, such as `grok-4.7[context=256k,reasoning_effort=high,fast=true]`.
Sagax maps the picker slug onto that list: `auto` to `default[]`, a
plain slug to its Standard variant, `-fast` to `fast=true`, and an effort
slug such as `grok-4.7-high-fast` to the variant with that effort. The
session advertises one variant per base, so a slug with another effort
(`grok-4.7-medium-fast`) gets that variant and a notice in the conversation.
If `session/set_model` is missing (`-32601`), the argv pin is left to stand
and the turn continues. If Cursor refuses the id (`-32602`), the turn also
continues, on the model the session started with, and the conversation shows
a notice that names it.

sections.title: Cursor Agent CLI: Setup
sections.text:
1. Install Cursor CLI:
 `curl https://cursor.com/install -fsS | bash # macOS / Linux` 
 Windows (native): `irm 'https://cursor.com/install?win32=true' | iex`
2. Sign in from the provider card. Sagax runs `cursor-agent login` and opens
 Cursor's page; you finish there. Or paste an access key on that same card.
 The command `cursor-agent login` stays under "Prefer a terminal?" for
 anyone who still wants to type it. `CURSOR_API_KEY` or `CURSOR_AUTH_TOKEN`
 in the instance environment still works.
3. Confirm `cursor-agent --version` works. Cursor's docs call the command `agent`;
 the installer adds `cursor-agent` beside it, and Sagax runs that name,
 because other tools also install an `agent`. The binary installs to
 `~/.local/bin` by default (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\cursor-agent` on Windows);
 Sagax already looks in both, so a CLI installed while the app is open
 is found without restarting.
The engine stays unavailable until the `cursor-agent` executable is found. A
missing login shows as unauthenticated rather than crashing the fleet.

sections.title: Cursor Agent CLI: Testing
sections.text:
Normal unit and ACP protocol tests use the scripted fake CLI and do not
require a Cursor subscription. Do not print credentials or upload native
protocol logs from a credentialed live run.

sections.title: Cursor Agent CLI: What this driver does not do yet
sections.text:
- Cursor ACP extension methods (`cursor/ask_question`, `cursor/create_plan`,
 todos/tasks/images) are not given a dedicated UI. Unknown JSON-RPC requests
 are rejected with method-not-found so the CLI is not left blocked.
- MCP servers passed in `session/new` follow Cursor's ACP limitations; prefer
 project or user `.cursor/mcp.json` where needed.
- Live smoke (`cursor-agent login`, `cursor-agent models`, one real turn) should be run on
 a machine with the CLI installed and signed in before relying on this in
 production.

sections.title: Bring your own engine: Any ACP agent (a CLI you spawn)
sections.text:
If an agent CLI speaks ACP over stdio —
`fx acp`, a Zed-style agent server, your own wrapper — point a `customAcp`
instance at it:
- `config.cli` is the whole command, args included (`"npx -y some-agent acp"`
 works). You can also set it from the app: Settings → Engines → *Set CLI…* on
 the instance's row. An instance without a command shows up with exactly that
 hint instead of failing at first message.
- Sign in first. The driver has no auth flow of its own — run the CLI once
 in a terminal and log in there; Sagax spawns it with your login intact.
- Model choice stays inside the agent. The picker shows a single
 "Agent default" entry; whatever the CLI is configured to run is what runs.
- `environment` is passed to the CLI child. Foreign provider keys
 (XAI_API_KEY, OPENAI_COMPAT_API_KEY, …) are deliberately stripped so a
 custom CLI can never bill against another engine's login.
- Permissions ride ACP's own `session/request_permission` — if your agent
 asks, the request becomes a normal approval card in chat.
- Multiple instances are fine — one per agent.

sections.title: Bring your own engine: Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (no process at all)
sections.text:
The built-in `openai-compat` driver supports multiple instances, so a local
vLLM/LM Studio/Ollama-openai endpoint or any hosted compatible API is one
entry:
- `apiKeyEnv` names which `environment` value carries the key, so several
 instances can hold different keys without colliding.
- The driver lists the endpoint's `/models` when it can and keeps your
 `model` as a custom option either way.
- OpenAI-compatible instances support structured tools and image input. With a
 model that accepts both, the harness can mount the approved host, Local VM,
 VPS, Boat cloud or built-in browser tools and return their screenshots to the model.
 The existing platform, computer-selection and approval checks still apply.
 Boat turns retain the selected API model in direct chats, rooms and cloud
 routines, as they do for every engine with computer tools.
- Set `config.tools` to `false` for a model without tool support. Image support
 also depends on the chosen model; the driver cannot add vision to a text-only
 model. See tool verification for scope and tests.

sections.title: Bring your own engine
sections.text:
Two zero-code ways to run Sagax bots on an engine the app doesn't ship.
Both live in `~/.sagax/config.json` under `"instances"`; restart the app
after editing (instance entries are read at boot).

sections.title: Bring your own engine: Engines baked into a server image
sections.text:
A server image can carry every engine CLI Sagax drives, so the people of an
organization server only sign in or add a key. The pins live in ONE file,
`engines.lock.json`. The
`Dockerfile` installs them with
`scripts/install-engines.mjs`.
The image default is that full set. On 2026-10-12 a build that left
`ENGINE_SET` unset shipped `engineSet none` and no CLIs
(`pulsa-bot-server:main-example1`). `SAGAX_REQUIRE_ENGINES=1` (also the
default) fails a build that is not the full lock, including an explicit
empty `--build-arg ENGINE_SET=`.
 
The legacy `ENGINES` (npm specs) and `NATIVE_ENGINES` (native ids such as
`grok`) arguments still replace the lock's npm or native set; `none` drops
that kind. Each installed CLI must answer `--version` or the build fails.
| Engine | Driver | Installed as | Pinned | Licence |
 
| Claude Code | `claudeAgent` | npm `@anthropic-ai/claude-code` | 2.1.288 | Anthropic Commercial Terms |
| Codex (and the ChatGPT plan instance) | `codex` | npm `@openai/codex` | 0.160.0 | Apache-2.0 |
| pi | `piAgent` | npm `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` | 1.0.1 | MIT |
| Gemini CLI | `geminiAgent` | npm `@google/gemini-cli` | 0.62.0 | Apache-2.0 |
| Kimi Code | `kimiAgent` | npm `@moonshot-ai/kimi-code` | 2.1.1 | MIT |
| Qwen Code | `qwenAgent` | npm `@qwen-code/qwen-code` | 0.24.7 | Apache-2.0 |
| OpenCode | `opencodeGo` | npm `opencode-ai` | 1.18.34 | MIT |
| Droid | `droidAgent` | npm `@factory/cli` | 0.230.0 | Factory proprietary |
| Grok Build | `grokAgent` | x.ai release binary, SHA-256 per architecture | 1.0.46 | Apache-2.0 |
| Cursor Agent | `cursorAgent` | downloads.cursor.com package, SHA-256 per architecture | 2026.10.01-e373342 | Cursor proprietary |
| Hermes Agent | `hermesAgent` | Python venv, editable install of the v2026.9.24 source archive (SHA-256) | 0.21.5 | MIT |
Not preinstalled, and why (the card then reads "Not available on this
server" instead of "Not installed"):
- Antigravity (`antigravityAgent`): Google's runtime is about 2 GB
 unpacked under Google's own terms; Sagax already downloads and verifies it
 itself (Settings) where it can run. On an organization server it would run
 its own tools on the Sagax host, so organization turns are refused anyway.
- mmx-cli: the MiniMax engine calls the API with a key; the CLI is only
 a sign-in helper and publishes no licence.
No install needed: Grok (API), OpenAI, OpenRouter and other
OpenAI-compatible endpoints, Mistral, Cerebras, MiniMax (a key each), the
Boat agent (runs on its cloud computer) and custom ACP agents (your own
command, above).
Proprietary CLIs (Claude Code, Droid, Cursor Agent) are part of the
production image (`ENGINE_SET=all`, the default). The image with none of
them is the explicit opt-out `ENGINE_SET=none` and
`SAGAX_REQUIRE_ENGINES=0`. At startup the server runs each baked CLI's
`--version` once, logs
it (`[engines] claude: 2.1.288 (Claude Code) (pinned 2.1.288, ...)`), and a

sections.title: Bring your own engine: Notes
sections.text:
- `config.json` is written with mode 0600; values in `environment` are stored
 as plaintext in that file. Prefer keys scoped to the one engine.
- A typo'd `driver` or invalid `config` never breaks the app: the instance
 shows as unavailable with the reason, and the rest of the fleet loads.

sections.title: Bring your own engine: Provider icons
sections.text:
Settings does not offer a provider icon on each provider. The card uses the driver's own mark.
An `icon` already stored on an instance still shows until that field is removed from `config.json`.

sections.title: Bring your own MCP servers: Advanced: edit the file
sections.text:
The same registry lives in `~/.sagax/config.json`:
 
`type` is `http` (Streamable HTTP, the default) or `sse`. If you edit the file
by hand, restart Sagax. Every bot whose engine can mount custom MCP
servers gets the enabled tools on its next task.

sections.title: Bring your own MCP servers
sections.text:
Open Plugins → MCP servers → Add server to give your bots tools from an
MCP server you trust. A server is one of two things:
- Run a command — a local stdio server. Add the executable, put each
 argument on its own line, and add any environment variables as `KEY=value`.
- Connect to a URL — a remote server. Paste its address and, if it needs
 a token, add it as a header (`Authorization: Bearer …`, one header per
 line). Most servers speak Streamable HTTP; pick SSE only for an
 older server that documents the `/sse` endpoint.
Sagax saves a new server switched off. Use Test to start the command
(or connect to the address), complete the MCP handshake, and see the tools it
advertises. Then turn it on. It becomes available to compatible bots on their
next task; no app restart is needed.
Tokens for URL servers go in headers, never in the address.
### Whop
In Plugins, find Whop alongside Gmail, Slack and the other apps and click Connect. The built-in card
uses Whop's official hosted MCP endpoint and opens Whop's browser sign-in;
no API key or local CLI is needed. After successful
sign-in and tool discovery it enables the connection. A cancelled or failed
first setup remains off and can be retried without adding another server.
Open Bot access on the Whop card to reach each bot's existing Access
settings. Bots set to use every enabled MCP server inherit the connection;
bots with an explicit selection must include its server name. The next task
uses the selection. Whop also appears in the Connected filter. Disconnect disables the connection and signs out;
the saved entry remains available to reconnect. Existing custom Whop entries
at the official HTTP endpoint are recognized rather than replaced.
Whop currently requests admin access across businesses your Whop account can
manage, and its own consequential-action confirmations still apply. See the
official Whop MCP documentation.
This is an optional connected tool.
### Servers that need a sign-in (OAuth)
Many hosted servers (Linear, Notion, Sentry, GitHub and others) answer
`401` until you sign in. When you add a URL server, or open the list,
Sagax asks the server whether it needs a sign-in and shows the answer on
its row: Sign-in required, Connected, Sign-in expired, or
Sign-in unavailable with the reason.
Click Sign in. Sagax opens the provider's page in your browser; after
you approve, the browser comes back to this app at
`http://127.0.0.1: /api/mcp-oauth/callback`, shows "Sign-in complete. You
can close this tab.", and the row flips to Connected within a few seconds.
Disconnect revokes the tokens at the provider (when it offers revocation)
and forgets them here. Then turn the server on as usual.
How it works, following the MCP authorization spec (2025-06-18 and
2025-11-25):
- Discovery. The server's `401` names its Protected Resource Metadata
 (RFC 9728) in `WWW-Authenticate`; otherwise Sagax tries
 `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` on the server's origin. The

sections.title: Bring your own MCP servers: Rules that keep this safe
sections.text:
- Permission cards by default. Custom servers are never pre-approved:
 on Claude their tools route through the permission broker into Allow/Deny
 cards; on Codex they keep the on-request approval policy; ACP engines
 relay the agent's own permission asks. Built-ins stay pre-quieted — only
 *your* servers ask.
- Reserved names are refused (`computer`, `agents`,
 `browser`, `phone`, `dweb`, `ogb`, …) so a custom entry can never shadow
 a built-in tool surface. Names are lowercase letters/digits/`_`/`-`, max
 32 chars, starting with a letter.
- Environment names are checked. `SAGAX_*` and `OGB_*` are refused:
 Codex hands MCP children their variables from one shared environment,
 and those names carry Sagax's own routing and bearers.
 `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE` is accepted as `1` only, the value Sagax's own
 proxies use, so a server bundled inside an Electron app (its binary as the
 command) can run as node; any other value is refused (port de
 OpenMausBot #2865).
- One bad entry never takes the fleet down. Invalid entries are skipped
 with a logged reason; the rest still mount.
- Credentials are write-only in the UI. The API returns environment and
 header names, never their values. Leaving an existing value blank keeps it
 saved; removing its line deletes it.
- Credentials stay off argv. `env` values travel in the child
 environment (Codex argv carries env *names* only; Claude uses the private
 0600 mcp-config file; ACP passes them in the session payload with the
 wire log redacted). Header values do the same: Sagax's connector
 reads them from a private environment record (Codex names only the
 record's variable on argv; ACP gets it in the session payload), Claude
 Code from the 0600 file. They do persist as plaintext in the 0600 config file — prefer
 tokens scoped to the one server. Codex gives its MCP servers their
 variables from the same environment it runs the bot's shell commands in,
 so each variable a server needs there is excluded from that shell; a value
 you already had in your own environment, like a proxy setting, stays.
- Proxies. Where Sagax's own remote proxy connects to a URL
 server, an `https://` server goes through your `HTTPS_PROXY` /
 `HTTP_PROXY` (CONNECT), with this computer's loopback names always added
 to `NO_PROXY` (`[::1]` included). An `http://` server goes through your
 `http_proxy` / `HTTP_PROXY`, sent by the connector itself in absolute form
 (Node's own env-proxy switch stays off, `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=0`, since
 Node 24's fetch hangs on a plain http request sent through it); loopback
 and `NO_PROXY` hosts are reached directly. Proxies set only in macOS
 System Settings are not read.
- Testing is bounded. A command is stopped after the handshake (or eight
 seconds), its output is capped, and its stderr is never sent to the UI. It
 inherits none of Sagax's workspace or provider credentials; only the
 environment variables configured for that MCP server are added. A test

sections.title: Bring your own MCP servers: What a Claude bot sees, and the "Also use my Claude Code MCP servers" switch
sections.text:
A bot on the Claude engine gets the tools and instructions its owner gave it:
the servers above, its integrations (computer, browser, agents, phone), and
its own project's ` /.mcp.json`. It does not inherit your skills and
agents, your hooks, or your personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` from this
machine's Claude Code setup. The MCP servers and claude.ai connectors of your
user or local Claude config come in only through the switch below (one
measured desktop added 407 tools, ~10k tokens per model call). Codex bots, by contrast, have always read the
MCP servers in `~/.codex/config.toml`, which is why the two engines looked
different.
The switch Also use my Claude Code MCP servers at the top of Plugins → MCP
servers lets Claude bots see your own Claude Code MCP servers too. Since
2026-10-27 (#1098) it is on by default on your own computer (a solo
server) and off by default on an organization's shared server, whose
Claude Code setup belongs to no one person; turning it on or off is kept
either way. With it on, every Claude bot also loads the servers and
connectors from your Claude Code config on every message; skills, hooks and
the personal `CLAUDE.md` still stay out. More tools means more tokens per
message: turn it off if you do not need those servers.
Those servers cost less with tool search. Outside a compact prompt, Sagax
starts Claude Code with `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true` (unless you set the variable
yourself): a server Sagax does not load up front, yours included, shows only
its tool names, and a tool's schema loads when the bot searches for it. The
CLI's own default sent every schema on a model with a 1M-token window. Codex
bots, and Claude bots outside a compact prompt, also see Sagax's own tools by
family: one tool per family (`cloud_agents`, `artifacts`, `routines`, …) whose
`tool` argument names the tool to run, approved as that tool.
The switch drops the CLI flag `--strict-mcp-config` (Claude Code 1.0.60+)
while keeping `--setting-sources project` (1.0.122+). The environment variable
`SAGAX_CLAUDE_INHERIT_USER_CONFIG=1` on the Sagax process remains the full
escape hatch back to the old launch: it restores everything, for every Claude
bot, until you remove it. The harness also picks the session's compaction
window with `--autocompact` (2.1.122+). Sagax reads `claude --version`
whenever it lists engines (app load, the Engines page, after an update) and
only passes each flag to a CLI that accepts it, so an older CLI keeps working
— without the controls it predates — and the Engines page shows an update
notice with the exact command. `claude update` clears it.

sections.title: Bring your own MCP servers: When your organization manages MCP servers
sections.text:
If this computer is connected to an organization (Settings → Organization)
and its Admin turns off custom MCP servers, only servers whose name or address
is on the organization's approved list reach bots. Other configured servers
stay in your list, marked Managed by your organization, but bots do not
get them, and the "Also use my Claude Code MCP servers" switch has no effect.
Paste config is off, and Add server accepts only approved servers.
Nothing is written to `config.json`; disconnecting the organization restores
the list as you configured it. With no organization connection, none of this
applies.
Address entries are HTTPS only. The host is compared label by label, where
`*` stands for one or more whole labels (`https://*.example.com/mcp` matches
`https://a.example.com/mcp`, never `https://evil.test/x.example.com/mcp`),
and the path separately, where `*` matches anything.
Limits: a personal Codex engine also loads MCP servers from your own
`~/.codex/config.toml`, which Sagax does not filter. An organization that
must block those can allow only company models, or leave personal Codex off
its engine list. Company Codex uses its own separate home, without your
`config.toml`.

sections.title: Decision model: Configuration reference
sections.text:
`baseUrl` points at a Jev-compatible server instead of TypeSafe's. It has no
Settings UI. It must be https, or http to this machine only. Requests go to
`{baseUrl}/v1/systemone` with model `jev-latest`.

sections.title: Decision model
sections.text:
Sagax can use a fast decision model to pick things for your bots. It
answers in a few hundred milliseconds for a fraction of a cent. It never does
the work: the chosen bot still runs its own turn on its own engine. The first
supported model is TypeSafe's Jev.
Everything is in Settings → Decision model: one master switch, the Jev key
with Save and Test, and one switch per job it can do.

sections.title: Decision model: It fails open
sections.text:
The decision model never blocks or delays a turn beyond its short budget.
With no key, the switch off, the job off, a timeout, a network error, an HTTP
error (401, 429, 529, 5xx), or an answer that does not check out (a choice
that was not offered, a probability that is not a number), the room does
exactly what it would have done without it. Every answer is validated before
it is used.

sections.title: Decision model: Measuring it
sections.text:
`server/decider/room-routing.eval.test.ts` replays 53 labelled room messages
(`server/decider/fixtures/room-routing.json`) against the live model. It is
skipped unless `SAGAX_JEV_LIVE_EVAL=1` is set with a key, and costs about
$0.002 per run.

sections.title: Decision model: Turning it off
sections.text:
Switch off Use Jev for fast decisions, or clear the key. To keep Jev on but stop room routing, switch off Who answers in
rooms. To stop one room asking, set its responder to a lead, Everyone
responds or Only when mentioned.

sections.title: Decision model: What is logged
sections.text:
Each call that reaches the model adds one row to
`~/.sagax/decider-log/YYYY-MM.ndjson` (mode 0600). This is separate
from the approvals log in `decisions/`.
 `{"at":"…","seam":"roomRouting","provider":"jev","ok":true,"choice":" ","pTop":0.94,"margin":0.9,"latencyMs":341,"inputTokens":712,"stateHash":"3f1c…"}` 
A row never holds the message text, the bots' descriptions or the key; a
16-character hash of the state is enough to spot repeats. Failed calls record
the reason (`timeout`, `overloaded`, …) and the HTTP status. Month files are
kept for the approvals log's retention window (180 days by default).
The log stays on this machine: workspace backups leave it out.

sections.title: Decision model: What it decides today
sections.text:
Who answers in rooms. A room whose responder is set to Auto (Jev) asks
Jev who should answer each message that @mentions nobody. The question offers
the room's active bots, each described by name, title and description, plus
"several members". The state it reads is the room's name, its people, the last
room lines (the same window room turns use, clipped in size) and the new
message.
- If one bot comes back with a probability of at least 0.6, only that bot
 answers.
- If "several members" comes back at 0.6 or above, every member answers.
- Anything less sure goes to the room's fallback: the lead it had before it
 became Auto, or else its first member. That is what a lead-mode room does
 today.
@mentions, `@everyone`, team goals and the other responder modes never ask
Jev. The message is appended and the send returns straight away; the answer
is awaited only when the room's turn starts, within 1.5 seconds.
A reply whose speaker Jev picked shows a small line under it: *Picked by
Jev · 94%*.
New rooms start on Auto while the decider and its room job are on. Existing
rooms keep their mode. With Jev off, an Auto room shows a one-line hint and
answers like lead mode.
Browser clicks, tool selection and where work runs are listed as "Coming
soon" and have no switch yet.

sections.title: Decision model: Where the key lives
sections.text:
- Desktop app: in the operating system's encrypted store
 (`credentials.bin`), like the other workspace keys. The server receives it
 as `SAGAX_JEV_API_KEY` at start-up; `config.json` keeps only an empty
 placeholder.
- Server or browser use: in the server's own `config.json` (mode 0600),
 under `decider.key`. `SAGAX_JEV_API_KEY` overrides it.
The key is write-only: `GET /api/config` reports only whether one is saved
and which switches are on. Engines never inherit it, and diagnostics exports
mask it. Saving a key makes one tiny test call; a key Jev rejects is not
saved. The Test button makes the same call on demand. A room decision
costs about $0.00003; the test call costs less.

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS: Back up
sections.text:
Stop the server before copying its SQLite database: Ctrl-C for a foreground
process, or `sudo systemctl stop openmausbot` from the administrator shell for
the service above. Stop any engine processes and managed desktops still writing
files you intend to back up.
For paths A and C, this backs up application state (bots, chats, routines, tunnel
credentials, and paired sessions). Run it from the service account's shell:
 
A full backup also needs your engine credential/configuration paths, such as
`~/.codex`, `~/.claude` and `~/.claude.json`, and browser session state under
`~/.agent-browser` if used. Include the paths that exist for your installed CLIs,
any configured home/data-directory overrides, and workspaces outside the app
directory. These are not included in the command above.
For path B, the whole `/data` volume includes the container's CLI homes. From
`sagax/deploy`, stop the app before archiving; `deploy_data` is the default
volume name, so use your actual volume name if you changed the Compose project:
 
Each command creates a fresh private folder in the current directory, so it
cannot overwrite an older archive with more permissive access. Keep the
archive inside that folder privately on another machine. Restore with the server stopped,
using the same paths and original ownership. After backup or restore, start the
service with `sudo systemctl start openmausbot`, or `docker compose start omb`.

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS: Before you start
sections.text:
1. A server. Any Linux VPS: Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04, 2 CPUs and 4 GB of RAM is plenty. You need `sudo` or root. Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Lightsail, a Mac mini in a cupboard: all fine.
2. Node 24 or newer for paths A and C (`node --version`). On Ubuntu:
 `curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_24.x | sudo -E bash - && sudo apt-get install -y nodejs` 
 Path B uses Docker instead and needs no Node on the host.
3. Your engine accounts. Bots run on the same engine CLIs you use on your laptop, with your subscriptions. You sign them in on the server once, the same way.
Connect to the server for everything below:
 `ssh root@YOUR_SERVER_IP` 
For paths A and C, use the same unprivileged Linux account for setup and the
running service. The examples below use `maus` with home `/home/maus`. From an
administrator shell, create it if it does not already exist, then switch to it:
 
The login shell also changes into `/home/maus`; run setup there, not from `/root`.
Get Sagax from source in that home and build it once (an npm package is
planned; until then, the checkout is the install). pnpm comes with Node's
Corepack: run `sudo corepack enable` once from the administrator shell.
 
Run the `pnpm omb` commands below from that `sagax` folder, and the engine
sign-ins in this account. Keep a separate
administrator shell for system packages and systemd. If you already signed in as
root, sign in again as `maus`; those accounts have different homes and credentials.

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS
sections.text:
From a blank Linux server to Sagax running on it around the clock, reachable from your laptop, the desktop app and your phone, with your bots working while every laptop is closed. It assumes nothing beyond being able to open a terminal and paste commands. About twenty minutes, most of it waiting.
Three ways to make the server reachable are covered. Pick one; the rest of the guide is the same.
| | You need | Who can reach it | Best for |
 
| A. Public address, no domain (`serve --tunnel`) | a Sagax account (email code) | anyone with a pairing code, over HTTPS | the fastest path; a phone on cellular |
| B. Your own domain (Docker + Caddy) | a domain name, ports 80/443 | anyone with a pairing code, over HTTPS | a permanent address you own |
| C. Your Tailscale network (`serve --tailscale`) | Tailscale on the server and your devices | only your tailnet | the most private; nothing public at all |
Whichever you pick, the login is the same: you pair each device once with a short code and it stays signed in. A session lasts 30 days; using it with half that or less left renews it to a full 30, up to 180 days from pairing (`SAGAX_SESSION_TTL_DAYS` and `SAGAX_SESSION_MAX_DAYS` change both numbers). There is no password.

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS: Give the bots a browser (optional)
sections.text:
Bots can browse on a server. Docker (path B) ships the engine and Chrome in
the image. For paths A and C, install Linux system libraries once from the
administrator shell:
 `sudo -H pnpm --dir /home/maus/sagax omb browser install --with-deps` 
Then install the browser in the service account's home, from the `maus` shell:
 `pnpm omb browser install` 
The administrator's browser download is in a different home; it does not install
the service account's browser. Both commands must finish successfully.
On Ubuntu 24.04, AppArmor may also require administrator sandbox setup.
The one-click installer downloads the browser; it does not grant these OS permissions.
Then turn the browser on under Settings → Computers, and per bot. Each bot
gets its own isolated session whose logins persist across restarts.

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS: Hetzner launch check (2026-09-07)
sections.text:
Path A was exercised on a blank Hetzner CX43 (x86-64, Ubuntu 24.04), using
Node 24.20.0 and Codex 0.153.4. The published 0.1.60 baseline was followed by
local candidate fixes from this change; these results do not certify the
unmodified published 0.1.60 package.
The paired web UI completed a real GPT-6-Astra chat, two automatically
scheduled routine runs, and a browser title/screenshot test. The browser
needed the Ubuntu sandbox setup below. A full reboot restored the service
and managed tunnel automatically; the existing paired device, bots, chats,
and paused schedule remained available. A new real chat turn also succeeded.
A stopped application-data backup restored with matching file hashes and
SQLite integrity. The restored copy was not started; provider reauthentication
and browser-login migration were not tested. Docker, Tailscale, ARM64, other
providers, and capacity limits were outside this run.

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS: Install and sign the engines in
sections.text:
The npm Sagax package does not install model engine CLIs. For paths A and C,
install the engine you use in the service account, then sign it in. For example,
from the `maus` shell, for Claude:
 
For Codex, use `@openai/codex` as the npm package and run `codex login --device-auth`
to sign in from a headless server. Complete the CLI's account flow in your browser. Repeat only for the
engines you use. For path B, run the installed CLI inside the container, for
example `docker compose exec omb claude`.
Engine logins belong to the service user's home (for example `~/.codex` and
`~/.claude`), separately from Sagax's `~/.sagax`. Keep that home when
restarting or upgrading. The systemd example below includes `~/.local/bin` in PATH.

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS: Keep it running
sections.text:
`pnpm omb serve` is a plain foreground process. For systemd (paths A and C),
the service runs the CLI from the checkout you built, so keep the `sagax`
folder in place. To run a chosen release, check out its tag first, from the
`maus` shell. Replace `X.Y.Z` with the release you want to run:
 
Stop the foreground server with Ctrl-C before enabling the service. From the
administrator shell, save this as `/etc/systemd/system/openmausbot.service`:
 
Use `--tailscale` instead of `--tunnel` for path C. `--no-pair` skips printing a code at every restart; mint one with `pnpm omb pair` when you need it. Docker (path B) restarts on its own (`restart: unless-stopped`).
Adjust the account, home, PATH and the path to `node` (`command -v node`) if
yours differ; Node 24 must be available on that PATH. The service runs the
checkout directly, so a restart uses the same code: it never pulls or rebuilds
on its own.

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS: Pair your first device
sections.text:
`serve` already printed a pairing link and QR code when it started. For another device later:
 `pnpm omb pair --label "Kitchen iPad"` 
- A browser: open the link. The code is filled in; press Connect. That browser is paired for 30 days, renewed on use as above.
- The desktop app: copy the link, then in the app's Server menu choose Add Server from Copied Pairing Link…. The menu switches between your own machine and every server you added.
- The phone: scan the QR code from the iOS app's pairing screen, or paste the whole link into its address field. The phone can chat, approve, and read; creating bots, changing models, and connecting apps stay with you in the server's UI.
Worth knowing: a code works once and expires after five minutes; the link only works on that address (typing the code by hand: open `…/pair` and enter it); ten wrong codes in a minute from one address pause pairing for that address for a minute; `--client` mints a code for a device that may chat and approve but not change settings or pair others.

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS: Path A: a public address with one command
sections.text:
No domain, no proxy, no open port. The server gets an address like `https://c-7f3a9c.openmausbot.com` through a Cloudflare tunnel; only traffic through the tunnel reaches it, and that traffic still has to pair.
 
`setup` connects an AI provider; it is separate from the Sagax account.
Use Codex's device-code option over SSH, or enter a hidden API key for a
chat-only connection. More engines can be added later. See CLI setup.
`login` asks for your email, sends an 8-digit code, and prints the address it reserved for this machine. `serve --tunnel` downloads `cloudflared` on the first run (a pinned version with a verified digest, into `~/.sagax`), starts the server, connects the tunnel, and after a few seconds prints `tunnel: live at https://…`. Leave it running; see "Keep it running" for a service.
The account credentials live in `~/.sagax/tunnel-account.json`, readable only by your user. `pnpm omb logout` releases the address.
Skip to "Install and sign the engines in".

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS: Path B: your own domain, with Docker
sections.text:
One container for the server plus Caddy for HTTPS at `https://maus.example.com`.
1. Point a name at the server. In your DNS provider add an A record (name `maus`, value the server's public IP). After a few minutes `ping maus.example.com` should answer with that IP. Ports 80 and 443 must be open; most providers open them by default.
2. Install Docker:
 
3. Get the deploy files and set the name:
 
 `ENGINES` lists the engine CLIs baked into your image, separated by spaces. Change it later and rebuild if you add one.
4. Start it:
 
 Caddy requests the certificate on its own; give it a minute. Then `https://maus.example.com` shows a page asking for a pairing code. That is correct: nothing works until you pair.
In this path, every `pnpm omb …` command below is run inside the container instead:
 `docker compose exec omb node dist-server/openmausbot.js pair --label "My MacBook"`

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS: Path C: only your Tailscale network
sections.text:
From the administrator shell, install Tailscale on the server and sign in (`curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh && sudo tailscale up`). Enable HTTPS certificates for your tailnet once in the admin console (DNS → HTTPS Certificates), then run this from the `maus` shell:
 `pnpm omb serve --tailscale` 
Tailscale terminates HTTPS with its own certificate and the pairing link uses the server's MagicDNS name (`https://maus.tail1234.ts.net`). Only devices on your tailnet can reach it, which is a very good property for a server that can run tools.

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS: The rules the setup relies on
sections.text:
Read this before putting anything else in front of the server.
- The server only ever listens on loopback (`127.0.0.1:8799`). Never publish that port yourself. The tunnel, Caddy and Tailscale each reach it from the same machine.
- A request that arrives through a proxy or the tunnel is treated as remote and needs a session, whatever headers it carries. A proxy of your own (nginx, Traefik, Cloudflare Tunnel) must forward the real `Host` and add `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto`, must not buffer the event stream, and must not rewrite `Host` to `127.0.0.1`.
- Pairing is the login. Want a second wall in front of it? Path B's `Caddyfile` has a commented `basic_auth` block for a shared password.
- The session cookie is marked `Secure`; do not serve this over plain HTTP on the public internet.
- The one thing a stranger can read is `/.well-known/openmausbot/environment` (the server's id, label, version, capabilities) and `/api/health` (only the app name). Everything else answers "pair this device".

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
`serve --tunnel` says "no account on this machine yet". Run `pnpm omb login` on this machine first; the credentials are per machine.
The tunnel stays on "retrying". The server is running and usable locally; the public hop is not verified yet. Wait a minute (Cloudflare needs a moment on a fresh address), then check `journalctl`/the terminal for the reason. If it never comes up, `pnpm omb logout && pnpm omb login` issues a fresh address.
Path B: the page never loads or shows a certificate error. Caddy could not get a certificate. Check that the name resolves to the server and that ports 80 and 443 are open; `docker compose logs caddy` shows the reason.
"forbidden: pair this device to use the server remotely" / "this request came through a proxy". Expected before pairing, and for tools that call the API without a session. Pair the device. Scripts send `Authorization: Bearer ` with the token from the pairing response instead of a cookie.
Pairing code refused. It expired (five minutes) or was used. Mint a new one. "Too many failed pairing attempts" means wait a minute.
A bot says the engine is not signed in. Sign that engine in again on the server.
What does the server think it is? `https:// /.well-known/openmausbot/environment` is public and shows its id, label, version and capabilities; `pnpm omb status` prints the same on the server.
Something else. `journalctl -u openmausbot --since -10m` (or `docker compose logs omb --tail 100`) shows the server's startup lines. Paste them with your question in the community channel.
### Ubuntu 24.04 browser sandbox
If Chrome reports `No usable sandbox!` and `sudo journalctl -k --since -10m`
shows an AppArmor `DENIED` for `userns`, the browser download is installed but
Ubuntu is blocking its sandbox. Chromium documents this restriction.
Do not add `--no-sandbox` or disable `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns` globally.
For paths A and C, an administrator can allow only a trusted, root-owned Chrome
copy. Find the service user's downloaded executable:
 `find /home/maus/.agent-browser/browsers -type f -name chrome -executable` 
Use its actual `chrome-VERSION` directory in every path below; `VERSION` is a
placeholder, not a fixed Chrome release. Copy the whole directory, including its
libraries, to a new location that the service user cannot modify:
 
Save this as the root-owned `/etc/apparmor.d/openmausbot-chrome`, replacing
`VERSION` with the same value. Keep the exact executable path: a wildcard under
the writable service home would also allow replacement executables.
 
Load the profile:
 `sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/openmausbot-chrome` 
Add the following line under `[Service]` in the systemd unit above, again using
the exact installed version, then run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and
`sudo systemctl restart openmausbot`:
 `Environment=AGENT_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE_PATH=/opt/openmausbot-browser/chrome-VERSION/chrome` 
For a foreground server, export `AGENT_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE_PATH` to that same

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS: Update
sections.text:
People should not see errors during a short restart: Caddy holds requests while
the process drains, and clients show Reconnecting and resume the stream
(Invisible deploys).
- Paths A and C with the service above: choose the new release, then run
 these commands from the administrator shell, replacing `X.Y.Z`:
 
 Check that the build succeeded before starting. A service restart by itself
 does not update the checkout. For a foreground server, check out the release
 the same way, then run `pnpm omb serve --tunnel`. Prefer `systemctl restart`
 (SIGTERM) over a hard kill so the drain and Caddy hold can run.
- Path B: `cd sagax && git pull && cd deploy && docker compose up -d --build`.
Routines and queued work survive a restart. A teammate turn running at that moment runs again once at the next start, told to check what it already did, and the bot that asked for it is told. A person's own turn and a running routine are not run again: the conversation says it was interrupted. Update between runs where you can.

sections.title: Deploy Sagax on a VPS: What runs on a server, and what does not
sections.text:
Runs fully on the server: every engine CLI (Claude Code, Codex, Grok, custom ACP engines), chats, rooms, bot-to-bot coordination, routines, connected apps and custom MCP servers, webhooks, Company Brain, computer use on cloud or container computers, text-to-speech, and the web UI (the server serves it itself).
Needs the desktop app instead: dictation and controlling the server's own desktop. Bots browse on a server too, once the browser engine is installed (below).

sections.title: Open a chat from outside the app
sections.text:
Open a chat row's ··· menu in the sidebar and choose Copy link (a bot
conversation, a room, or a channel). It copies a `sagax://` link that
opens that chat in the desktop app, so an external dashboard, a browser
bookmark, or a script can bring the person straight to the right conversation:
 `sagax://thread/ ?bot= ` 
A dashboard that only knows a bot (or a room) also has a link, which opens
its current conversation:
 `sagax://bot/ `

sections.title: Open a chat from outside the app: The link
sections.text:
- `sagax://thread/ ?bot= ` — one exact chat. The
 `?bot=` part names who owns it (a bot id or a room id). It is optional when
 opening (a bare `sagax://thread/ ` resolves against the chats
 on this computer the same way a pasted in-app reference does), but Copy
 link always writes it, and the app checks it strictly: if the thread is not
 that bot's, nothing opens.
- `sagax://bot/ ` — the bot's current conversation, exactly
 as clicking the bot in the sidebar opens it: with threads hidden, its main
 thread, the conversation the person last wrote in. Handy for a team map
 whose Chat button only knows the bot's id. A room's id works here too.

sections.title: Open a chat from outside the app: What opening one does
sections.text:
- Brings the window to the front. If it is showing a connected server (Server
 menu), it switches back to Local first — the chats live on this computer —
 and opens the link when that page is up.
- Opens the named chat and reveals its row in the sidebar. Nothing else: it
 never sends a message, interrupts a running turn, or starts a new
 conversation.
- Works at launch too: the link is held until the app has loaded its bots, so
 it can start a closed app and still find its chat. On macOS, where the app
 keeps running with its window closed, the link opens a new window.
- Works from any page — the team map, Routines, a room — and leaves it for
 the chat. Settings and the keyboard shortcuts list close so the chat is not
 hidden behind them; a dialog with unsaved input, such as New Bot, stays.
- Unknown or mismatched ids show a short notice in the chat instead of
 opening anything: "That bot is no longer here." for an unknown bot link;
 "That thread is no longer here." for an unknown thread, or, when the link
 names a bot that exists, "That thread is no longer here. Showing 
 instead." — the window moves to that bot, the same way a dead in-app thread
 reference behaves.
Like the `sagax://cloud` and `sagax://organization` links, these are
local-shell actions: a page loaded from a remote server never receives them, and
the browser build has no such links at all. An app connected to another
computer as its companion (Settings → Remote access → Connect to another
computer) opens them against that computer's chats, the ones it shows.

sections.title: Desktop-to-desktop companion mode: Control a VPS desktop remotely
sections.text:
A desktop client can open an agent's self-hosted VPS display through either paired transport. On the host, enable Cloud desktop access for that paired desktop in Settings → Remote access. On the client, open the bot's Computer panel and choose Take control.
The Computer panel also shows a periodically refreshed VPS screenshot. Preview and live control share the same per-device permission, which defaults off. The VPS still publishes no VNC port. The host opens its existing loopback-only SSH tunnel, the companion creates a random device-scoped viewer path, and the client relays noVNC HTTP and WebSocket traffic through its loopback Electron service. Closing the viewer removes the companion session, closes the SSH tunnel, and hands control back to the agent.
Remote clients can preview, open, and close the viewer only. VPS provisioning, replacement, sleep, removal, SSH aliases, Local VM controls, and host browser surfaces remain available only on the host.
The client Calendar supports scheduled routines end to end: create, edit, move, resize, pause, delete, run now, cancel an active run, and acknowledge failures. Scheduled calls and webhooks remain host-only and are omitted from client mode.
The remote Computer panel includes the host panel's per-agent Scheduled tasks card. It lists that agent's next routines and active run, opens the full schedule view, and creates a new schedule already assigned to the agent.
A Mac remote client supports dictation and live calls against any host: Apple Speech runs locally on the Mac, and only the transcript crosses the paired connection. When a Mac client selects a built-in system voice, reply speech is synthesized and played locally on that Mac; ElevenLabs and Fish Audio reply audio is synthesized by the host and relayed byte for byte. A Windows remote client still needs a future Windows speech-to-text implementation for microphone input.
Voice-note attachments stream through the same relay: the mp3 serving route is on the companion allowlist, the audio crosses byte for byte, and `Range` requests are forwarded so a player can seek inside a clip without re-downloading it.
The host must be running and awake. Cleartext HTTP is accepted only for a `.ts.net` MagicDNS hostname because that connection is encrypted inside Tailscale's WireGuard tunnel. Raw IP addresses, LAN hostnames, URL credentials, paths, queries, and fragments are rejected.

sections.title: Desktop-to-desktop companion mode
sections.text:
Every Sagax desktop build can play either role:
- Host mode is the normal app. It owns the agents, conversations, credentials, routines, and computers.
- Client mode controls a paired host through the same authenticated, default-deny companion API used by the phone app.
The roles are platform-independent. A Windows, macOS, or Ubuntu build can host, and any other desktop build can be its client. One app installation uses one role at a time; disconnecting a client returns that installation to host mode without deleting its local host data.
This mode is separate from Self-hosted server in Settings → Remote
access → Connect to another computer (also available through the Server
menu). Self-hosted server connections load the remote server's web UI directly
using that server's browser session. Use that option for a custom HTTPS domain
or Cloudflare tunnel to a self-hosted server and its 12-character pairing link.
Desktop companion mode instead keeps the bundled UI and native integrations on
the client, sends API traffic through the default-deny companion boundary, and
provides the per-device VPS viewer and client-local Mac voice behavior described
below. The two connection types intentionally do not share credentials.

sections.title: Desktop-to-desktop companion mode: Pair over secure HTTPS
sections.text:
1. On the host, open Settings → Remote access and finish Secure HTTPS pairing.
2. Open a pairing window so the host displays a six-digit code.
3. On the client, open Settings → Remote access → Connect to another computer
 and choose Desktop companion.
4. Enter the host's managed `https://…openmausbot.com` companion address and the six-digit code.
5. Choose Pair and switch to client mode. The client restarts and opens the host's bot UI.
The HTTPS address uses the host's managed outbound tunnel. TLS is verified by the operating system, and the client does not need Tailscale. HTTPS is intentionally restricted to Sagax-managed companion names so a typo cannot redirect a paired-device token to an unrelated site.

sections.title: Desktop-to-desktop companion mode: Pair over Tailscale
sections.text:
1. Install Tailscale on both computers, sign into the same tailnet, and leave MagicDNS enabled.
2. On the host, open Settings → Remote access, turn on Remote access, and open Pair over Tailscale to display a six-digit code.
3. On the client, open Settings → Remote access → Connect to another computer
 and choose Desktop companion.
4. Enter the host's full `.ts.net` MagicDNS name and the six-digit code.
5. Choose Pair and switch to client mode. The client restarts and opens the host's bot UI.
To switch that installation back, open Settings → Remote access and choose Disconnect and use this computer.

sections.title: Desktop-to-desktop companion mode: Runtime shape
sections.text: While client mode is active, Electron does not start its local harness, companion sidecar, computer-use daemon, or browser engine host. The renderer still uses ordinary same-origin API calls and `EventSource`, so the existing UI and streaming store do not learn or handle a second transport.

sections.title: Desktop-to-desktop companion mode: Security model
The organization library on the desktop: Compatibility
sections.text:
| Desktop \ Admin | Admin without `capabilities.library` | Admin with it |
 
| Sagax before this channel | as before | ignores the pointer, stays connected |
| Sagax with it | no library request, no shelf; file import and export work | the shelf |
| No organization account | as before | — |
This channel and the runtime's handler for `openmausbot:managed-library`
(`server/org-library.ts`) ship in the same release. A runtime without that
handler never acknowledges, so main would relay again on every sync and wait
out the 15 s timeout each time.
How this is tested: verification/desktop-library.md.

sections.title: The organization library on the desktop: Files
sections.text:
| Where | What | Written by |
 
| ` /company-library.bin` | which catalog was applied, for which Admin, Organization and device, OS-encrypted | Electron main |
| ` /org-library/catalog.json` | the exact catalog bytes last applied (owner-only) | Electron main |
| ` /org-library/blobs/ .json` | release files, owner-only, written atomically | Electron main |
| ` /org-library/state.json`, `presets.json` | what this installation added | the runtime |
` ` is `~/.sagax` unless `SAGAX_DATA_DIR` says otherwise.
Workspace and company backups leave out `catalog.json` and `blobs/`, because
main downloads them again and sign-out deletes them. They keep the runtime's
`state.json` and `presets.json`.

sections.title: The organization library on the desktop: Install reports
The organization library on the desktop: Messages with the local runtime
sections.text:
Electron main → runtime, over the private utility-process port (never HTTP,
never a remote server):
 
The runtime swaps its in-memory catalog and answers at once, before any
install work, with `{ "type": "openmausbot:managed-desktop-result", "requestId", "ok": true }`
(the relay gives up after 15 s). It reads release files from `blobs/` itself
and checks their SHA-256 on every read.
Runtime → Electron main, unsolicited, after it processed a relayed catalog and
after any change to what it added:
 
Main checks each entry on its own (a bad one is dropped, at most 100) and
ignores a snapshot whose digest it did not relay for this enrollment.

sections.title: The organization library on the desktop: Start, sign-out and restarts
sections.text:
- At start, before any request to Admin, main reads `company-library.bin`.
 It uses the saved catalog only for the same Admin, Organization and device,
 only while the sign-in has not expired, and only if `catalog.json` still
 hashes to the recorded digest. Otherwise the file is ignored and the first
 sync fetches again.
- A lapsed Admin licence or an unreachable Admin changes nothing: the last
 catalog stays.
- Sign-out, expiry or revocation relays `library: null` (the shelf
 disappears) and deletes `company-library.bin`, `catalog.json` and the cached
 release files. Bots, rooms, routines and skills that were added stay.
- An Admin that stops advertising the library is treated the same way.
- A restarted runtime is sent the applied catalog again when it is ready.
 A runtime that did not acknowledge a catalog gets it on the next sync. The
 log says so once per runtime and catalog, not on every sync.

sections.title: The organization library on the desktop
sections.text:
When an Organization shares packages with its members, or a partner shares
them with its Customers, Admin builds a catalog for each receiving
Organization. A connected Sagax desktop keeps a verified copy of that
catalog and of each package's release file, so Templates → From
{Organization} can show and add them. This page describes the desktop's half
of that channel: Electron main. The runtime's shelf, the Add button and the
provenance lines are described with the runtime (`server/org-library.ts`).
Nothing on this channel asks anyone anything. What an Organization offers is
decided in Admin; adding a package is a person's own click. There are no
update controls: the catalog always names the newest release.

sections.title: The organization library on the desktop: What main does with a new pointer
sections.text:
1. `GET /api/desktop/library` (at most 256 KiB, 20 s). The catalog must be an
 `openmaus.org-library` version 1 envelope for this Organization. A
 malformed envelope or another Organization's catalog is refused whole and
 the last good catalog stays. A malformed entry is dropped on its own;
 unknown fields are ignored.
2. For every entry that is not Off, has a release, and whose format this
 app reads (version 2 or lower), and whose file is missing:
 `GET /api/desktop/library/blobs/ ` (at most 4 MiB, 60 s, and never
 more than the catalog's `sizeBytes`). The bytes must hash to the catalog's
 `sha256`, or they are never written. A failure leaves that package
 unavailable and is retried on a later sync with a growing delay (a `429`
 pauses downloads for its `retry-after`). Files already cached are re-hashed
 after each new catalog; a file that no longer matches is fetched again.
 Downloads stop at 64 MiB per catalog.
3. The raw catalog bytes are saved as `catalog.json`, then
 `{portalOrigin, organizationId, deviceId, libraryVersion, digest}` is saved
 OS-encrypted in `company-library.bin`.
4. Main relays the catalog to the local runtime (below).
5. The applied digest is the SHA-256 of the bytes actually received, not the
 pointer's, so a catalog rebuilt between the two requests converges on the
 next sync.
6. Release files the catalog no longer names are removed 7 days later.
Every library request uses the device's `omd_` token (never the model
token), refuses redirects, sends no cookies, and is checked against the same
connection generation as company backups: signing out aborts it.

sections.title: The organization library on the desktop: When it is used
sections.text:
- No organization account: nothing. No request, no file and no message.
- An Admin without the library: nothing either. The desktop reads
 `capabilities.library` from `GET /api/public/config`, the same answer it
 already reads once per start for renewal, and calls no library route unless
 it is `1` or higher. A desktop that could not read the config at start (it
 was offline) asks again at most every 10 minutes after a successful sync.
- An Admin with the library: every successful session sync
 (`GET /api/desktop/session`, about once a minute) carries a small
 `library: { version, digest }` pointer. When the digest differs from the
 catalog this desktop last applied, main fetches the catalog. Nothing large
 rides on the session itself, which keeps its 512 KiB cap.

sections.title: Grok approval gate (Sagax gates MCP calls; Grok runs in default mode): Grok bug: allow rules do not skip the auto classifier over ACP
sections.text:
xAI has no public issue tracker (`xai-org/grok-build` has issues disabled), so the repro lives here.
Docs claim (user guide 22-permissions-and-safety, "How a tool call is authorized"): rules (`--allow`, `[permission] allow`) are evaluated before the mode's prompt policy, where the auto classifier runs.
Observed with grok 1.0.46 (server) and 1.0.50 (Mac), `grok --permission-mode auto [rules] agent stdio`:
1. The client is `initialize` with `clientInfo: {name: "openmausbot"}`.
2. `session/new` passes one stdio MCP server `clock` with one tool, `query_time`.
3. The prompt is "call clock__query_time once".
The classifier gap is the time between `pending_interaction kind=permission` and `interaction_resolved`:
| Mode / rule | Gap | Card |
 
| auto, no rule | 4.5 s | none |
| auto, `--allow 'MCPTool(clock__query_time)'` | 7.9 s | none |
| auto, project `.grok/config.toml` `[permission] allow = ["MCPTool(clock__query_time)"]` | 6.7 s | none |
| auto, `--allow MCPTool` | 7.3 s | none |
| auto, `--allow mcp__clock__query_time` | 6.1 s | none |
| auto, `--allow '*'` | 6.8 s | none |
| default, any rule or none | 0 s | none (the tool runs) |
On production, the live ACP wire log shows `pending_interaction` for `agents__list_bots` from 00:25:43.001 to 00:25:51.474 UTC, with `--allow MCPTool(agents__list_bots)` on argv.
PreToolUse hooks cannot pre-approve: per the docs, a hook "allow" only means "not blocked".

sections.title: Grok approval gate (Sagax gates MCP calls; Grok runs in default mode): How it works
sections.text:
