- Default: on for every bot since 2026-10-19 (engine parity: Approve for me decides through Sagax on Grok as on Claude since #797, so the owner's setup #820 and the member rules apply the same way).
- Opt-out: `DATA_DIR/grok-approval-gate.json`, either `{"off": [" "]}` or `{"bots": "none"}`. Those bots' Auto turns run Grok's own auto mode. A missing, empty or invalid file means on; the earlier opt-in list `{"bots": [...]}` no longer narrows anything. The file is read on every turn; the next turn of each bot respawns Grok in the new mode.
- Scope: only Auto turns (`approvalMode: "auto"`, not Full access). Ask, Edits and Full access are unchanged.
- When the flag is on:
- Grok starts with `--permission-mode default`. Its built-in tools prompt through ACP and each prompt is a card (the classifier no longer answers them); on an organization server they are withheld anyway.
- A solo turn whose Grok config (`$GROK_HOME/config.toml` or the project's `.grok/config.toml`) declares `[mcp_servers.*]` keeps Grok's own auto mode: Sagax does not mount those servers, so the gate could not hold their calls.
- The xAI account's cloud connectors load only when host tools are withheld (an organization turn): Grok reaches them through `use_tool`, and a server Sagax did not mount keeps its card. A solo turn forces `GROK_MANAGED_MCPS_ENABLED=false`, because `default` mode can call those servers with no prompt. Gateway tools stay off. A tool selection turns the connectors off too.
- Every MCP server, built-in or not, is mounted through `mcp-gate` with an approval socket (`server/mcp-gate-approval.ts`).
- Only reviewed read-only tools run unasked:
- agents: `READ_ONLY_AGENT_TOOL_NAMES`
- harness-spawned Perspicax bridges: `PERSPICAX_READ_ONLY_TOOLS`
- Every other call, including unknown, new and third-party tools, waits for a canonical approval card. A server's own `readOnlyHint` is ignored.
- Fail closed: a decline, the 15 min timeout, a stopped turn, no running turn, a closed or unreachable socket, an answer other than an explicit allow, a corrupt config, and JSON-RPC batches or unreadable frames all mean the call never reaches the server.
- No replay: each call is its own card. An "always" answer is not reused.

sections.title: Grok approval gate (Sagax gates MCP calls; Grok runs in default mode): Production finding: Grok's `use_tool` ask (2026-10-11)
sections.text:
The first live gated turn (Nova, thread 84c81700…, 2026-10-12T01:04Z)
showed that with many MCP tools mounted (158 in production) Grok defers them
behind its `use_tool` meta tool, whose `_meta["x.ai/tool"].read_only` is
false. In `default` mode Grok therefore sends `session/request_permission`
for every MCP call, reads included:
 
The local repro had a handful of tools, so Grok called them directly and never
asked. On a gated turn the driver now answers that ask allow once (never
always) only when every name in it resolves to one of the turn's gated mounts
(`server/drivers/acp/gated-mcp-ask.ts`): the call then reaches the MCP gate,
which runs it only if it is a reviewed read and otherwise holds it for the
person's card. Built-in tools, commands, file changes, unmounted servers and a
`use_tool` without a target keep their card.

sections.title: Grok approval gate (Sagax gates MCP calls; Grok runs in default mode): Rollback
sections.text: Add the bot to `"off"` in the flag file (or write `{"bots": "none"}`). That needs no deploy.

sections.title: Grok approval gate (Sagax gates MCP calls; Grok runs in default mode): Why
sections.text: In `--permission-mode auto`, Grok runs its safety classifier before every MCP tool call. On production this measured 4–9 s (up to 17 s, and once an approval card for the read-only `agents__list_bots`) for tools that answer in under 0.5 s. Allow rules do not skip it over ACP (repro below). In `default` mode Grok runs MCP tools supplied by the ACP client with no prompt at all, so Sagax gates them itself.

sections.title: Health scan
sections.text:
A separate process reads the local logs and databases and writes a report.
It does not modify those files. It does not call a model. It does not open
a ticket. If the app is not running, the scan still reads whatever files
are on disk.
 `node --experimental-strip-types server/health-scan.ts --data ` 
Or `pnpm health-scan` with `SAGAX_DATA_DIR` set. The report is
`health-reports/latest.md` inside that directory. Message text is not
copied. Failures are grouped by a short code.
 `GET /api/me/health-report` 
The answer is `{ report: null }` until a scan has written one, then the
markdown. Any signed-in person can read it. No admin right.

sections.title: Import an agent you already use: Code
sections.text:
- `shared/grok-import.ts`: the Grok Bot export, the share link, the package.
- `shared/claude-code-import.ts`: the Claude Code folder to a package.
- `src/lib/claude-code-folder.ts`: which picked files are read.
- `src/components/AgentImport.tsx`: the dialog (New bot, guided first run).
 It reuses `GrokImportBox` and the bot import panel (`BotZipImport.tsx`).
- Settings > Import (`ImportSettings.tsx`) keeps its Grok Bot import too.
- Tests: `shared/claude-code-import.test.ts`, `shared/grok-import.test.ts`,
 `src/components/AgentImport.test.ts`, `src/components/BotZipImport.test.ts`,
 `src/components/onboarding/GuidedFirstRun.test.ts`,
 `server/routes/team-library-grok.test.ts`.

sections.title: Import an agent you already use: From Claude Code
sections.text:
Choose the project folder (or your `~/.claude` folder). The app opens only
these files, from the public Claude Code layout (code.claude.com/docs):
| File | Becomes |
 
| `CLAUDE.md` or `.claude/CLAUDE.md` (else `AGENTS.md`) | The bot's standing instructions. A whole-line `@path` import of one of these files is inlined; an `AGENTS.md` next to a `CLAUDE.md` that does not import it is added under its own heading. |
| `CLAUDE.local.md` | Added under "Personal notes". |
| `.claude/skills/ /SKILL.md` | A skill (off). |
| `.claude/commands/ .md` | A skill (off): Claude Code treats commands as skills. |
| `.claude/agents/ .md` | One more bot per subagent: its `name`, `description` and body as instructions, plus the imported skills it names. Its `tools`, `model` and `permissionMode` are not carried: the new bot follows the person's own settings. |
| `.mcp.json` | Each `http` or `sse` server with a plain `https://` address becomes a connection slot, with the names of its headers only. A server that runs a command (`command`, `args`) is listed under Left out with its program and the names of the values it needs, never their values. |
A file that may hold a secret (`.env*`, `.envrc`, `.netrc`, `*.pem`, `*.key`,
`*.p8`, `credentials*`, `auth.json`, `.credentials.json`,
`settings.local.json`, SSH keys) is never opened. When it sits at the top
of the folder or under `.claude/`, it is named under Left out. Everything else
in the folder (source code, `node_modules`, ...) is not read.

sections.title: Import an agent you already use: From Grok Bot
sections.text:
What the public documentation says (docs.x.ai/grok-bot, read 2026-10-26):
| Fact | Status | Source |
 
| Grok Bot is xAI's hosted product for persistent bots ("AI teammates with names, jobs, and context"). | Confirmed | docs.x.ai/grok-bot/overview |
| There is no documented export, download or backup of a bot, its memory or its skills. | Confirmed (absence) | docs.x.ai/grok-bot (overview, bots, skills, computer) |
| A bot can be shared as a template; its public link "shows the Bot's shared configuration, including its identity, description, skills, and routines". Adding it copies it to the recipient's account. | Confirmed | docs.x.ai/grok-bot/bots |
| The format behind a template is not documented. | Confirmed (absence) | docs.x.ai/grok-bot/bots |
| A routine has an Instruction and a When to run. | Confirmed | docs.x.ai/grok-bot/skills-routines-and-automations |
| Private skills are one library shared by all of a person's bots; no file format is given. | Confirmed | same page |
| Instructions are set through the conversation; there is no separate field. | Confirmed | docs.x.ai/grok-bot/bots |
| Connector sign-ins live on the vendor's backend, not on the bot's computer. | Confirmed | docs.x.ai/grok-bot/computer-and-apps |
| A template carries instructions, selected memories, skills, routines and first-party integrations, not custom MCP servers or scripts. | Secondary source, not official | a third-party guide (2026-10-21) |
So Sagax does not parse an undocumented file. The person's own Grok Bot writes
its setup out:
1. Copy export prompt (`GROK_EXPORT_PROMPT`, `shared/grok-import.ts`) and
 send it to the bot on x.ai. It answers with one JSON block
 (`openmaus.grok/1`): name, description, instructions, skills, routines
 (the "When to run" in plain words plus a cron when it has a clock), the
 apps it uses, and memories only if the person says yes. It is told to
 write `[removed]` in place of any key or personal data.
2. Paste the reply, or choose it saved as a `.json` file. The format
 `grokbot-bundle/v1` of the community tool pi-grokbot-import is also read.
3. Alternatively, paste the bot's public link (`https://x.ai/bot/ `): Sagax
 reads only the public card (name, creator, description) and offers
 Start from the description.
Routines with a cron or a plain time ("weekdays at 9am") come over paused.
Routines that start on an event, and schedules that cannot be read, are
listed under Left out with their original text. Text that looks like a key is
replaced.

sections.title: Import an agent you already use
sections.text:
New bot > Start from > Grok Bot or Claude Code…, or Import an agent on
the "create your first bot" step of the guided first run, brings an existing
agent into Sagax as a new bot. Anyone who may create bots can do it. No admin
is needed, and in an organization the bot is the person's own.
The imported bot arrives inert:
- its skills are switched off until the person turns them on;
- its routines are paused until the person starts them;
- an app it used becomes an empty connection slot, which keeps only the
 address and the names of the values it needs;
- no key, token, password or sign-in comes over;
- it uses the person's own engines and approval level, not the source's
 model or permissions.
Nothing existing is changed: every bot it creates is new. A preview lists
what will be created and what was left out (with the original text, to
redo it by hand) before anything is created.
Under the hood both sources become an ordinary Sagax package
(`openmaus.package` v2) in the app. It is then staged and imported through the
same bot import as New bot > Zip file… (`POST /api/bots/import/upload`,
member scope), so the rules of `server/package-import.ts` apply unchanged.

sections.title: Import an agent you already use: Left out, in the person's language
sections.text:
Every left-out line carries `nameKey`, `reasonKey` and `params` (catalog keys
`leftOut.*` in `src/locales`, and the same English templates in the iOS
`Localizable.xcstrings`), so the app shows it translated; the English text
stays as the fallback.

sections.title: Import an agent you already use: On iPhone and iPad
sections.text:
Create New Bot > Import from Grok Bot does the Grok Bot import: Copy export
prompt, send it to the bot on x.ai, paste its reply, Preview, Import. The phone
has no copy of the converter, so it sends the reply to
`POST /api/bots/import/agent` (`{ text, timeZone }`; `GET` gives the prompt):
the server makes the same package with `shared/grok-import.ts` and stages it
like an uploaded zip, for this person only, then the zip import's own
`/api/bots/import/:id` finishes. Same rights as the upload: anyone who may
create bots. The Claude Code folder import is desktop only.

sections.title: Install the Sagax server in one line: After the install
sections.text:
- Open the link, then Settings > Engines to install and sign in the AI
 engines from the browser, with no terminal
 (details).
- Pair your other devices with `sagax pair` (or from Settings in a signed-in
 browser).
- Back up the `sagax_data` volume and `.env`. See
 Back up for the scope; the volume holds the engine
 logins too.

sections.title: Install the Sagax server in one line
sections.text:
For a server you run yourself (a VPS, a home server, a Mac or a Linux box
with Docker). One command checks Docker, writes a small install folder,
generates the server's secrets on that machine, starts the public image and
prints the address with a one-time sign-in link.
 `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pulsatrixtechnologies/Sagax/main/install.sh | bash` 
On your own domain, with an automatic HTTPS certificate (DNS pointing at the
machine, ports 80 and 443 open):
 `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pulsatrixtechnologies/Sagax/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --domain bots.example.com` 
Read the script first if you like: it is `install.sh` at the
root of this repository. `--dry-run` prints what it would do and touches
nothing.
The desktop app needs none of this: it runs its own server. This page is for
a server that stays on when your computer is off, or that several devices
share. The guides behind it are Self-hosting (reference)
and Deploy Sagax on a VPS (step by step).

sections.title: Install the Sagax server in one line: Options
sections.text:
| Option | Default | Meaning |
 
| `--dir DIR` | `$SAGAX_DIR` or `~/sagax` | The install folder. |
| `--domain HOST` | none | Serve `https://HOST` with an automatic certificate. |
| `--port N` | `8080` | Without `--domain`: the HTTP port on this machine. |
| `--bind ADDR` | `127.0.0.1` | Without `--domain`: the address that port listens on. `0.0.0.0` opens it to your network; a remote browser still signs in with a pairing link. |
| `--version X.Y.Z` | latest release | The release to run. |
| `--image REF` | `ghcr.io/pulsatrixtechnologies/sagax` | Another image repository (a mirror, your own build). |
| `--no-start` | | Write the files, do not pull or start. |
| `--no-link` | | Do not put `sagax` on the PATH. |
| `--dry-run` | | Print the plan; write and start nothing. |
For private access over Tailscale without a public domain, keep the default
`127.0.0.1:8080` and point Tailscale Serve at it, or use the
local Compose setup, which maps the Tailscale
host name for HTTPS.

sections.title: Install the Sagax server in one line: Other ways in
sections.text:
Nothing here replaces the existing paths:
- From a checkout, building the image yourself:
 Docker (with HTTPS on your own domain),
 updated with `git pull && docker compose up -d --build`.
- Without Docker: From source or the npm CLI
 (`sagax service install`).
- Many client workspaces on one server: `sagax fleet`.
An AI coding agent can run the install for you: give it
`SETUP_PROMPT.md`.

sections.title: Install the Sagax server in one line: The image
sections.text:
`ghcr.io/pulsatrixtechnologies/sagax` is built by `release.yml` once per
published release (job `server-image`), from the tagged commit and this
repository's `Dockerfile`, with no deployment's configuration in it: no
domain, no keys, no organization. Tags: `X.Y.Z`, `X.Y`, `sha- ` and
`latest` (the latest full release only). Each digest is scanned on both
platforms with zero critical and high findings required, signed keyless and
given a vulnerability attestation. To check a tag yourself:

sections.title: Install the Sagax server in one line: The `sagax` helper
sections.text:
| Command | What it does |
 
| `sagax update [X.Y.Z]` | Moves to that release (default: the latest): pulls the image, restarts, waits until the server answers. The server applies its data migrations itself when it starts, so there is nothing else to run. On a failed pull it stays on the current release; after a failed start it prints the command that goes back. `--dry-run` only prints. |
| `sagax pair` | A new one-time sign-in link for another browser, phone or the desktop app. |
| `sagax status` | The containers and what the server says about itself. |
| `sagax logs` | The last 200 lines (`sagax logs -f omb` follows the server). |
| `sagax start`, `stop`, `restart` | The stack. |
| `sagax version` | The release in `.env`. |
| `sagax ` | Any other command runs the server CLI inside the container: `sagax sessions`, `sagax access add you@example.com`, ... |
Going back is the same command with the older number: `sagax update 0.8.3`.

sections.title: Install the Sagax server in one line: What it does
sections.text:
1. Finds `docker compose` (or `docker-compose`) and checks that Docker answers.
2. Reads the latest release (`pulsa-vX.Y.Z`) from GitHub, unless you pass
 `--version X.Y.Z`. The install always runs one exact release, never a
 floating tag.
3. Writes the install folder (`~/sagax`, or `--dir DIR`, mode 0700):
 | File | What it is |
 
 | `.env` | Your settings and the vault key. Created once, mode 0600, never overwritten. |
 | `compose.yaml` | The server and Caddy, from `ghcr.io/pulsatrixtechnologies/sagax: `. Rewritten on each run. |
 | `Caddyfile` | The edge: plain HTTP on `localhost:8080` by default, HTTPS with `--domain`. Rewritten on each run. |
 | `sagax` | The helper (below). Linked into `/usr/local/bin` or `~/.local/bin` when one is writable and no other `sagax` is on your PATH. |
4. Generates the vault key (`SAGAX_MCP_OAUTH_KEY`, 32 random bytes from
 `openssl` or `/dev/urandom`) straight into `.env`. It is never printed. It
 encrypts the sign-ins and the credentials the server keeps for your bots.
 Because it sits outside the data volume, a copy of the volume alone does
 not open them. Back `.env` up apart from the volume. An existing data
 volume keeps the key it already has, and no new key is written for it.
5. Pulls the image, starts it, waits until `/api/health` answers, then prints
 the address and a one-time sign-in link (the same as `sagax pair`). The
 link works once and expires; it is not a stored password.
Run the script again at any time: it keeps `.env` and the data volume, moves
the install to the release you name (the latest by default) and refreshes the
generated files. Options you pass on a re-run (`--domain`, `--port`,
`--bind`, `--image`) are written to `.env`; the others stay as they were.
Your own changes to the stack go in `compose.override.yaml` next to
`compose.yaml`: Compose reads both, and the script never touches it.

sections.title: Install the Sagax server in one line: What you need
sections.text:
- Docker with Compose (Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows, Docker Engine on
 Linux), running, usable by the user who runs the script.
- About 4 GB of disk for the image (it carries every engine CLI and the bots'
 browser), plus your data.
- amd64 or arm64. The same image tag serves both.

sections.title: Sagax in the car (Siri, CallKit, CarPlay): Not done
sections.text:
- A bot calling the person (an incoming call) needs PushKit VoIP pushes
 from the server; the call is always placed from the phone today.

sections.title: Sagax in the car (Siri, CallKit, CarPlay)
sections.text:
What the phone app does in a car, within Apple's CarPlay rules (CarPlay
Developer Guide, October 2026), and what still waits for Apple.

sections.title: Sagax in the car (Siri, CallKit, CarPlay): Testing
sections.text:
- `swift test --filter CarAssistTests`: names, replies, handles, the car's
 list, the driving rules, the voice screen states.
- CarPlay screen: CarPlay Simulator (Xcode 27 Device Hub, an iPhone on USB)
 or a car, with a build from `project-carplay.yml` and a CarPlay profile.
 The iOS Simulator's CarPlay window needs Simulator's I/O menu: there is no
 headless `simctl` path to it.
- Siri: on a device, "Call with Sagax", "Send a message to with
 Sagax", then a reply to an announced message (Settings > Notifications >
 Announce Notifications).

sections.title: Sagax in the car (Siri, CallKit, CarPlay): With the CarPlay entitlement (build flag)
sections.text:
Sagax fits Apple's voice-based conversational category
(`com.apple.developer.carplay-voice-based-conversation`, iOS 26.4): apps
that "enable conversations with voice assistants". One category per app.
The communication category (messaging and VoIP) is for conversations
between people and requires the three SiriKit messaging intents; it is not
the one for bots.
The CarPlay screen (`ios/App/CarAssist/CarPlaySceneDelegate.swift`):
1. the recent bots (a list: name and mascot, never a message), at most
 twelve;
2. choosing a bot calls it; CarPlay's voice screen shows the call
 (calling, listening, thinking, speaking, microphone off) with two action
 buttons, mute and hang up (iOS 26.4). A call started from Siri or the
 phone shows the same screen while it runs, as the category requires.
Depth two, Apple allows three. The audio session is the call's only (no
recording outside the voice screen). An approval is answered by voice or
waits; a call that cannot start shows its title, never "pick up the phone".
The code is in every build and never runs without the entitlement. The
build flag is a second XcodeGen spec:
 `cd ios && xcodegen generate --spec project-carplay.yml` 
It adds the entitlement, the CarPlay scene (`UIApplicationSceneManifest`)
and the `SAGAX_CARPLAY` Swift condition to `project.yml`. Use it only once
Apple has granted the entitlement and the App ID has the CarPlay
capability: signing without a CarPlay profile fails, so it cannot ship by
accident. Plain `xcodegen generate` stays the usual build.

sections.title: Sagax in the car (Siri, CallKit, CarPlay): Without any CarPlay entitlement (every build)
sections.text:
| Feature | How | Where |
 
| A call with a bot is a phone call | CallKit (`CallKitBridge`): the car shows it with mute and end, its audio goes to the car, the steering wheel button ends it | `ios/App/Call/CallKitBridge.swift` |
| The call names the bot | The CallKit handle is `sagax-bot: ` (`CarCallHandle`), the caller name is the bot's name: calling again from the call screen, the car or Siri reaches the same bot | `ios/Sources/CompanionCore/CarAssist.swift` |
| "Call Scout with Sagax" | `INStartCallIntent`, handled in the app's process (`application(_:handlerFor:)`), places the CallKit call even with the phone locked | `ios/App/CarAssist/SiriIntentHandlers.swift` |
| "Send a message to Scout with Sagax", a reply to an announced message | `INSendMessageIntent`: the reply goes back to the conversation the banner donated (`CommunicationNotification`), a new message to the bot Siri heard (`CarDirectory.route`) | same |
| Messages announced by Siri | Communication notifications already donate `INSendMessageIntent` with the bot as sender, which is what Announce Notifications reads | `ios/NotificationService/CommunicationNotification.swift` |
| Driving-safe call | When CarPlay is connected or the audio goes to a car (`CarRoute`), an approval is asked aloud and shorter, a learned skill waits until the person has stopped (a no is still heard), and nothing says to look at the screen (`DrivingSafety`) | `ios/App/Call/CallController.swift` |
Siri needs its permission: the app asks once, the first time the person
calls a bot (`SiriAccess.askOnce`). The Siri capability of the App ID is
turned on by automatic signing (`com.apple.developer.siri`); it is not a
request to Apple.
The main app includes `AppIntentVocabulary.plist` under
`ios/App/{Base,en,fr,pt-BR}.lproj/`. Each file supplies example phrases for
both `INSendMessageIntent` and `INStartCallIntent`. `en`, `fr` and `pt-BR`
are the app's supported catalog locales; Base supplies the development
language fallback. XcodeGen includes these localized resources through
the app's `App` source path, without adding them to an extension.
Apple requires examples for every supported intent and locale
(QA1950,
Intent Phrases);
omitting them produces ITMS-90626 after a successful upload.
Who a name is (`CarDirectory.resolve`): the same name first, then a name
that starts with what was said, then one that contains it; case, accents and
a leading article do not count. Two bots for one name make Siri ask which
one. Hidden bots and conversations with people are never reached.

sections.title: iOS companion architecture: Connectivity
sections.text:
### Same Wi-Fi
The QR code is still the primary path on the same Wi-Fi. If it is unavailable,
the user can open Other ways to connect and choose a nearby computer or
enter the address shown in desktop Settings → Remote access. Nearby discovery does not
run until the user opens that fallback.
Nearby discovery uses Bonjour and direct LAN traffic. Use it only on a network
you trust.
Choosing a nearby computer or manually entering a LAN address is therefore an
explicit fallback. Once the app is using a hosted or Tailscale route,
automatic reconnection stays within those protected transports. Moving back to
direct LAN requires choosing that computer or address again.
### Tailscale
Tailscale is an optional route away from home and on Wi-Fi networks that
isolate clients. In desktop Settings → Remote access, the primary card remains
Secure HTTPS pairing — Recommended. The separate Tailscale pairing
card is only for people who already use Tailscale. Install or open Tailscale
on both devices, sign in to the same tailnet, leave MagicDNS enabled, and
choose Turn on device access & check followed by Pair over Tailscale.
That first action explicitly starts Remote access so the phone has a listener
to reach. Sagax then places the computer's MagicDNS name in that
dedicated QR; it never silently replaces the default hosted HTTPS route.
Manual entry remains available as a fallback.
The URL is still `http`, but the path is encrypted and authenticated by
WireGuard inside the tailnet. Use the MagicDNS name rather than the
`100.64.0.0/10` address: App Transport Security exceptions are domain-based,
and `ios/project.yml` narrowly allows insecure HTTP for `ts.net` subdomains.
Tailscale is optional. The direct path does not use a Sagax-operated
relay or create a cloud copy of local transcript data.
### Optional hosted HTTPS
In desktop Settings → Remote access, Use your phone anywhere accepts a
passwordless email code and provisions one HTTPS address for that computer.
This desktop sign-in is only for hosted HTTPS. The iPhone never signs in; it
trusts the computer through the same pairing QR. Nearby, manual, and Tailscale
connections continue to work without an account.
The desktop runs an outbound connector to Cloudflare, so no inbound router
configuration or Tailscale installation is required. The hosted address is
included in a pairing invitation only after it is ready. The default setup
waits for that HTTPS address instead of silently substituting Tailscale;
Tailscale pairing remains an explicit choice in its own optional card.
Cloudflare terminates and proxies the encrypted connection to the connector.
The Sagax control plane stores account and installation metadata plus
opaque tunnel/DNS identifiers in D1, but not bots, transcripts, approvals,
screen frames, pairing tokens, or connector tokens. See `docs/ios-privacy.md`
for data and deletion details.
The connector does not point at the reusable LAN port. Electron launches one

sections.title: iOS companion architecture: Current status
sections.text:
The first version includes:
- QR-first pairing from desktop Settings → Remote access, with the computer name
 confirmed on the iPhone before it connects.
- Hosted HTTPS for the default QR after the desktop owner enables it, with
 dedicated Tailscale and trusted-local QR routes only after an explicit
 choice.
- Nearby computers, a manual address, and a six-digit code under Other ways
 to connect when the QR path is unavailable.
- Secure per-device trust, device listing, and revocation.
- Multiple saved computers with a one-tap switcher. Each pairing has its own
 Keychain credential, and only the selected computer is connected at a time.
- Bot and room lists, paged transcripts, sending, interruption, and unread
 state.
- Approvals and questions, including narrow “always allow” grants.
- Resumable SSE, streamed reply text, reconnect hydration, and an opt-in live
 Boat computer view. The loopback-only VPS SSH viewer remains desktop-only.
- On-demand stills of a bot's Local VM, idle or working, for a phone the
 computer owner has allowed computer access.
- Markdown rendering and Keychain storage for the phone's pairing trust.
- Secure completion of supported credential-request cards using iOS Password
 AutoFill and QR-pinned HPKE encryption. Apple Passwords/iCloud Keychain is
 sufficient; 1Password, Bitwarden, and other AutoFill providers are optional.
Alerts work while the app is open or for the short period it remains connected
after moving to the background. Once iOS suspends or closes the app, new alerts
cannot arrive. Closed-app push delivery, voice, and App Store release
automation are not part of this version. The optional hosted transport connects
to the user's own computer; it is not a cloud transcript store and cannot wake
a terminated iOS app.
The Mac must be running Sagax and must not be asleep. Desktop
Settings → Remote access offers an off-by-default Keep this computer awake
switch that prevents system sleep while device access is on; the display may
still turn off. A sleeping or powered-off computer cannot receive phone
requests or run its local routines, including through the optional hosted
transport.

sections.title: iOS companion architecture: Follow-on releases
sections.text:
Keep the foundational merge separate from capabilities that widen security or
distribution scope:
1. Foundation: sidecar, desktop controls, Swift core/app, pairing, chat,
 approvals, reconnect, simulator and contract CI.
2. Desktop conversation parity: task create/switch/rename/delete, SQLite
 search with exact-message landing, transcript export/share, reactions, and
 edit/version controls. Archived or hidden chat management remains desktop-only.
3. Notifications: native permission, live/replayed alerts, time-sensitive
 approvals, badges, and a brief background grace period are in the app.
 Closed-app delivery still requires project-owned APNs credentials and a
 hosted relay; Tailscale cannot wake a terminated iOS process.
4. Distribution: signing, bundle ownership, privacy declarations,
 TestFlight, and App Store review material. Swift tests and an unsigned
 simulator build already run in the repository CI.
5. Optional expansion: voice/call mode or Local VM/host-computer
 interaction. Each requires its own threat-model review.

sections.title: iOS companion architecture
sections.text:
The iOS app is a thin, native client for the Sagax instance running on
your Mac. The Mac remains the only machine that persists agent processes,
credentials, SQLite data, transcripts, and computers. The iPhone trusts a Mac
by scanning the QR code shown in desktop Settings → Remote access; it does not need
a Sagax account of its own.

sections.title: iOS companion architecture: iOS feature parity routes (2026-10-03)
sections.text:
From the feature parity matrix
(`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-03-ios-feature-parity-matrix.md`, packages S1,
S2 and S3, with the decisions D1 yes, D3 yes, D4 keep).
Through the companion (S1, D1, D3). A companion request is the computer's
owner to the harness, so these get the owner checks the desktop's own renderer
has. Added to `ALLOWED` in `companion/src/routes.ts`:
| Route | Why |
 
| `GET /api/bots/:id/harness-commands` | the engine's own slash commands (names, descriptions, hints) |
| `POST /api/bots/:id/parallel/:threadId/stop` | Stop on a parallel task card |
| `GET /api/bots/:id/activity`, `GET /api/bots/:id/activity/item` | what the bot is doing, its history and one item |
| `POST /api/bots/:id/primary` | Make primary bot (the harness checks the owner) |
| `GET /api/me/harness-connectors` | the owner's own claude.ai connectors (names, statuses) |
| `GET /api/bots/:id/computer` | the bot computer's status and phase (read-only) |
| `GET/PUT /api/groups/:id/memory` | a room's shared memory (D3): its people read, its owner edits or switches it off |
| `PUT /api/tts/provider` | the voice engine alone (`{ provider }`, nothing else); `PUT /api/config` stays refused |
| `GET /api/bots/:id/system-prompt` | prompt preview (D1) |
| `GET /api/bots/:id/history`, `POST /api/bots/:id/history/rollback` | history of changes, restore instructions (D1) |
| `GET/POST /api/bots/:id/skills`, `GET/PATCH/DELETE /api/bots/:id/skills/:name` | skills: list, read, import (lands disabled), enable, remove (D1) |
| `GET /api/bots/:id/memory`, `GET/PUT/DELETE /api/bots/:id/memory/file`, `GET /api/bots/:id/memory/journal`, `POST /api/bots/:id/memory/journal/:changeId/revert`, `GET /api/bots/:id/memory/upkeep`, `POST /api/bots/:id/memory/tidy` | memory: overview, files (saved with their hash), journal and revert, upkeep (D1) |
| `GET /api/bot-presets` | New bot's starting roles (D1) |
| `GET /api/me/achievements`, `POST /api/me/achievements/events`, `PUT /api/me/achievements/settings`, `GET /api/achievements/public` | achievements (D1) |
The companion's bot `PATCH` also takes `memoryEnabled` and `memoryUpkeep`
(`companionBotFieldViolation`): the advanced panel's memory switches. Approval
mode, folder, computer, MCP servers and access stay refused, as does
`POST /api/bots/:id/memory/open` (it opens a window on the host's screen).
Client sessions on a server (S2). Added to `CLIENT_ALLOW` in
`server/request-auth.ts`, each held by its handler:
| Route | Who |
 
| `GET /api/bots/:id/command-allowlist`, `DELETE /api/bots/:id/command-allowlist/:ruleId` | the bot's owner, or this computer's own person; adding a rule stays admin |
| `POST /api/plugins/install` | an admin, or this computer's own person |
| `GET /api/bots/:id/overview` | the bot's owner (or edit grant on an organization server), or an admin |
"This computer's own person" (`clientSessionIsComputerOwner`) is the loopback
owner, an admin session, or on a personal server (not an organization server,

sections.title: iOS companion architecture: Markdown
sections.text:
Bot and room replies are rendered. Messages the person typed stay literal.
Rendered blocks are paragraphs, headings, lists, task lists, quotes, thematic
rules, fenced code, and top-level tables indented by at most three spaces. A
table inside a list item, a blockquote, or a fence stays text or code, as
does a row indented by four spaces or a tab. Inline emphasis, code,
strikethrough, and links use Foundation attributed text. A table scrolls
horizontally inside the bubble. A task item shows a checkbox, and an ordered
task keeps its number beside that checkbox.
The in-app spoken form reads each table row and each task's words. It skips a
delimiter-only paragraph and the checkbox token. Closed-app voice is not part
of this version.

sections.title: iOS companion architecture: Pairing and device security
sections.text:
1. On the Mac, open Settings → Remote access and choose Pair a phone. The app
 starts device access as part of setup.
2. On the iPhone, choose Connect my computer and scan the QR.
3. Confirm the computer name and the displayed transport — HTTPS connection,
 Tailscale connection, or Trusted local connection. The phone stores
 its trust securely in Keychain; no iPhone account is required. A camera QR
 also pins that computer's public credential-encryption key. Manual and old
 pairings can still chat, but must scan a fresh QR before entering a key on
 the phone.
4. If scanning is unavailable, open Other ways to connect for a nearby
 computer, manual address, or six-digit code.
5. Revoking the phone on the Mac removes its access and lets it pair again.
To add another Mac, open Settings → Computers → Connect another computer
on the iPhone and scan that Mac's QR. The existing computer stays usable if
the new pairing fails or is cancelled. Switching computers replaces the live
event stream and in-memory chat state, but keeps every saved pairing; removing
one computer deletes only that computer's Keychain credential from the phone.
An app upgrade migrates the previous single saved pairing automatically.
The Mac must remain awake with Sagax running for chats, approvals, and
routines to work, including through hosted HTTPS or Tailscale.
After pairing, the phone periodically reads the authenticated, sidecar-owned
`GET /api/companion/endpoints` snapshot. This lets an existing phone learn a
new hosted address—or its withdrawal—without another pairing ceremony. The
route never reaches the harness and returns only the computer name plus a
bounded list of connection origins.
A Sagax account is not required for nearby, manual, or Tailscale
connections. Only the desktop owner signs in when enabling the optional hosted
HTTPS route; the iPhone always uses the same QR trust flow.
### Secure credential entry
This is Password AutoFill, not a password-vault integration. A native
`SecureField` marked as a password lets the user explicitly choose Apple
Passwords or any enabled third-party AutoFill provider. SagaxMobile does
not enumerate a vault, receive a provider token, or save the entered value in
its own Keychain.
The packaged desktop creates one stable P-256 recipient key pair and keeps the
private JWK inside its operating-system-encrypted credential document. Only the
65-byte uncompressed public point is added to a camera QR. The phone validates
and pins that point with the connection; manual and older pairings remain fully
usable for chat but cannot submit a credential until they scan a fresh QR.
Credential submission is enabled only while the phone is using hosted HTTPS or
a Tailscale route. Local and Bonjour chat pairing still work as before, but
their cleartext HTTP transport would expose the reusable device token to anyone
who could observe that Wi-Fi network, so the app directs the user to finish the
credential request on the computer instead.

sections.title: iOS companion architecture: Phone tools (2026-10-21, the reference design parity row 81)
sections.text:
A bot can ask the person's own iPhone for something only the phone knows:
its position once, a contact by name (only the fields asked for), reminders
and calendar events (read, or add one), the home (list scenes and
accessories, or run one scene) and alarms (list, or add one), photos the person picks, one of
their Shortcuts by name, the clipboard text, and battery, network and Focus.
Health is not offered.
- Only over a protected transport (2026-10-21): hosted HTTPS or
 Tailscale, read from the connection, never from what the phone says
 (`shared/phone-transport.ts`; through the sidecar, `companion/src/transport.ts`
 sends `x-openmausbot-companion-transport`: the guardian's socket or a
 tailnet address is protected). On plain local Wi-Fi the server offers
 nothing from that phone and says why; the phone also refuses with the
 reason, and Settings > Approval rules says the tools are off there.
- Only native clients answer: a phone the companion vouched for, or the
 native app's bearer session; never a browser cookie, a bot's session or
 an ephemeral one. The routes are `admin` rows in the tool policy
 (`defaultEnabled: false`): a bot's `act` never reaches them.
- Never in a turn another bot's words joined (an aside folded into the
 owner's live turn), nor in one `ownEnvironmentOrigin` does not call the
 owner's (internal turn, routine lineage, automation, unattended run).
 Parallel tasks the owner opens in their own turn inherit the owner's
 access; the card on the phone still asks.
- The bot sees one tool, `phone_tool` (`server/drivers/agents-phone-tools.ts`),
 only in a 1:1 turn the person speaking started with their own words (on
 their own bot, or since 2026-10-28 on a bot shared with them: it is the
 speaker's phone, never the owner's), and only while a phone of
 theirs offers tools (it registered in the last 15 minutes, or in the last
 day when the server can push to it). Its `tool` enum lists exactly what
 the phone offers. Never in a room, a routine, a webhook turn or a turn
 another bot started; never another member's phone.
- Each request shows a card on the phone (Refuser / Toujours permettre /
 Permettre une fois, `Features/PhoneTools`), never on the lock screen: the
 push uses the question category, without Allow. Toujours permettre is
 saved for exactly what was allowed (` /phone-tools/grants.json`):
 status, the approximate position, contacts with that very set of fields,
 reading reminders, the calendar, the home or alarms. Running one home
 scene and adding one alarm each have their own key. Never for a precise position,
 creating a reminder or an event, a shortcut, the clipboard or photos. It
 runs only while the app is open on screen, and a banner says which bot
 used which tool each time. After a refusal the same bot cannot show the
 same tool's card again for a minute. Settings > Approval rules lists the tools this
 phone offers (a switch each) and the grants (Remove).

sections.title: iOS companion architecture: Runtime architecture
sections.text:
There are three deliberately separate trust surfaces:
| Surface | Bind | Purpose |
 
| Harness | `127.0.0.1:8799` | Existing app API; remains loopback-only |
| Companion | `0.0.0.0:8810` | Paired native devices; authenticated and allowlisted |
| Companion control | `127.0.0.1:8811` | Start pairing, cancel pairing, list devices, revoke |
| Hosted gateway | `127.0.0.1:8812` | Guardian-owned route to one exact sidecar generation |
The desktop app owns the sidecar lifecycle through
`electron/companion.mjs`. The renderer only receives narrow IPC operations; it
does not fetch the control port directly. Every control route needs a token
the app makes for each sidecar launch and hands over Electron's private port
(port of OpenMausBot #2930), so a page served from `127.0.0.1:8811` itself, as
a bot's browser could open it, cannot start pairing or change a device's
access. A standalone sidecar prints its pairing page link with that token
(`http://127.0.0.1:8811/#token=…`); the page reads it from the fragment,
which never leaves the browser.

sections.title: iOS companion architecture: SQLite compatibility
sections.text:
SQLite does not move onto the phone. It is an implementation detail behind the
harness API:
- `server/message-db.ts` and `server/store.ts` persist and page transcripts.
- The phone asks for `GET /api/bots?messages=50` and
 `GET /api/threads/:threadId/messages?before=…&limit=50`.
- SQLite ordering and cursors are therefore tested at the server boundary,
 while the Swift package tests decoding and prepend/deduplication using
 responses captured through the real sidecar.
- A storage migration may change the bytes on disk without changing the app.
 If an API payload changes, regenerate the fixtures with
 `node scripts/capture-companion-fixtures.mjs` and review the diff.
The sidecar keeps its device registry in `~/.sagax/devices.json`. That is
security state owned by the network boundary, not transcript data, so it does
not belong in the message database.

sections.title: iOS companion architecture: Stream and state model
sections.text:
`CompanionCore` contains the wire models, client, raw-byte SSE parser, and pure
state fold. The SwiftUI target owns lifecycle and presentation only.
On connection, the server sends a `hello` frame containing a cursor and whether
the requested gap was replayed. The client:
1. resumes from its last ` : ` cursor;
2. folds replayed and live frames when the gap is available;
3. hydrates the newest page of each visible conversation when it is not; and
4. paginates older transcript pages on demand.
Unknown message and frame kinds degrade safely instead of failing an entire
response, and one malformed fleet record does not hide every healthy chat.
Screen frames are off by default and enabled only while a computer view is
visible. Backgrounding keeps the stream for only the short grace period iOS
allows, then closes it; foregrounding reconnects from the saved cursor. A hello
cursor is committed only after a cold hydration succeeds; replayed streams
advance it one folded frame at a time, so a disconnect during recovery cannot
skip the remaining gap.

sections.title: iOS companion architecture: Use My Cloud on your phone
sections.text:
With MausBot Cloud, pair the phone with your Cloud instead of your computer, and
it keeps working while the computer is off.
1. In the desktop app, open the menu under your name and choose Get the
 phone app: the App Store for iPhone, or the APK for Android. Scan its code
 with the phone's camera.
2. In the same menu, choose Connect your phone · to your Cloud (always on).
 (Settings → Sagax Cloud → Use My Cloud on your phone does the same.) The
 app opens your Cloud in its window, at the Cloud's phone pairing.
3. Choose Create pairing code and scan the QR code with the phone app.
On your computer, Connect your phone offers your Cloud first and this
computer second, once your plan is paid and your Cloud is Ready. Until the Cloud
is Ready it offers only *to this computer*, with a note that the Cloud will show
there. With the Cloud open in the app window, the entry reads *to your Cloud*
and pairs with it directly. On another server it pairs with that server, and it
is shown only to a session allowed to make pairing codes there.

sections.title: iOS companion architecture: Verification contract
sections.text:
The merge gate for this feature is:
 
The simulator validates compilation, launch, layout, manual address parsing,
and failure states. Bonjour, Local Network permission, Tailscale routing,
Keychain behavior across a reboot, and approval delivery still require a real
iPhone pass.

sections.title: iOS companion architecture: Visual parity routes (2026-10)
sections.text:
The parity screens (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-01-ios-visual-parity-design.md`)
use the routes below. Each one is reachable both through the companion
sidecar (a personal computer: the phone acts as its owner) and for a phone
paired with a server (`request-auth.ts` `CLIENT_ALLOW` for member reads and
owner actions, admin scope otherwise). The harness applies the same owner or
admin rule to both: a companion request is a loopback owner, but the harness
holds its bot and room `PATCH` to the member fields (`memberBotFieldViolation`,
`clientGroupPatchViolation`). Tests: `companion/test/routes.test.ts`
("iOS parity routes"), `server/ios-parity.e2e.test.ts` and each route
module's own test under `server/routes/`.
| Route | Payload / answer | Who |
 
| `POST /api/bots` | `{ name, settings: { color }, mascotLook, mascotSkin, ... }` | as before (member's own bot on an organization server) |
| `PATCH /api/bots/:id` | look and framing (`color`, `mascot*`, `avatarCrop`, `avatarZoom`, `avatarFocusX/Y`, `pinned`); owner adds `name`, `soul`, `notifications`, `avatarUrl`, `modelSelection` | any member for look; owner or admin for the rest |
| `GET /api/bots` | each bot carries `instructionsLead` (first non-empty line of `soul`, no heading marks, at most 140 characters) | member |
| `GET /api/bots/:id/soul`, `POST /api/bots/:id/avatar/generate`, `DELETE /api/bots/:id` | as before | owner or admin |
| `GET /api/bots/:id/links?cursor=&limit=` | `{ links: [{ url, domain, title?, messageId, threadId, at }], nextCursor, total }`, newest first, one per URL, the viewer's threads only | member |
| `GET /api/bots/:id/files?kind=media\|file&cursor=&limit=` | `{ files: [{ id, threadId, messageId, name, mime?, size, available, source, at, kind, url, previewUrl? }], nextCursor, total }`; `url` and `previewUrl` are the existing `/api/threads/:id/files/:fileId[?preview=1]` | member |
| `POST /api/bots/:id/export` | `{ document, filename, redacted, skipped, summary }`: the bot as a team package v2, without chats, header values or keys | owner or admin |
| `POST /api/bots/:id/computer/input` | `{ events: [{ type: "move", dx, dy } \| { type: "moveTo", x, y } \| { type: "button", button, action, count? } \| { type: "scroll", dx, dy } \| { type: "key", key, modifiers? } \| { type: "text", text }], controlLeaseId? }` (at most 64) -> `{ ok, applied }` | owner or admin holding control |
| `GET/PUT /api/bots/:id/computer/clipboard` | `{ text }` (16 KiB) | owner or admin holding control |
| `GET/PUT /api/settings/bot` | `{ settings: { autoReviewDefault, timeZone, timeZoneAuto }, scope, hostTimeZone, effectiveTimeZone }` | read: member; change: the person (organization) or the owner (personal) |
| `GET /api/auto-review/rules`, `DELETE /api/auto-review/rules/:id` | `{ rules: [{ id, scope, botId, botName, command, cwd, providerInstanceId }], global: [], total }` | owner or admin |

sections.title: Sagax for iPhone and iPad: privacy: Children
sections.text: The app is a work tool and is not directed to children under 13.

sections.title: Sagax for iPhone and iPad: privacy: Connecting
sections.text:
- Computer pairing. The camera is used only to scan the pairing QR code;
 no image is kept. On the same Wi-Fi the app finds your computer with
 Bonjour (local network permission) and talks to it directly. Away from
 home it can reach the computer through Tailscale, a separate service with
 its own privacy terms. Pulsatrix does not operate a relay for computer
 pairing in this version.
- Organization sign-in. The app opens your organization server's sign-in
 page in the iOS authentication sheet. You sign in with Pulsatrix Perspicax
 (OpenID Connect; passkeys and Safari's saved sign-ins work). The server, not
 the phone, receives your identity from Perspicax: an identifier, your email
 address, your name, your username and, when set, your profile photo. The
 phone receives only a short lived pairing link, exchanges it for a session
 bound to you, and never receives a Perspicax token.
- At pairing the app sends the phone's name as iOS reports it (on current
 iOS, a generic name such as "iPhone"), so you can recognize and revoke the
 device later.

sections.title: Sagax for iPhone and iPad: privacy: Diagnostics and feedback
sections.text:
The app has no crash reporting or analytics SDK and sends no diagnostics to
Pulsatrix. If you share crash data or TestFlight feedback with developers in
iOS settings, Apple provides it to Pulsatrix under Apple's terms. Send
feedback in Settings opens an email to hello@pulsatrix.ca with the app
version and iOS version filled in; you see and send it yourself.

sections.title: Sagax for iPhone and iPad: privacy: Messages, files and sharing
sections.text:
- What you type, the files and photos you pick, and what you send from
 another app's Share sheet go to the bot or room you choose, on your
 computer or your organization server. The app does not keep a copy after
 sending; the Share extension deletes its temporary copy after sending or
 cancelling.
- Images are limited to 10 MiB each and documents to 25 MiB, at most four
 items and 50 MiB per message.
- Opening a file a bot sent downloads it from your computer or server and
 keeps a temporary preview only while it is open.
- Voice notes a bot sends are audio files stored with the conversation on
 your computer or server; the app plays them and does not record voice
 notes itself.
- When a bot asks for a password or API key, the value you enter is
 encrypted on the phone (HPKE with Apple CryptoKit) for the paired computer
 or server and sent only over an encrypted connection. The app clears the
 field right away and never stores the value.

sections.title: Sagax for iPhone and iPad: privacy: Microphone, speech recognition and voice calls
sections.text:
The microphone is used only while you dictate a message or are on a voice
call with a bot, and the app shows when it is listening.
- Dictation (the microphone in the message field) uses Apple's speech
 recognition. When iOS supports on-device recognition for your language,
 the app requires it, so the audio stays on the phone. Otherwise Apple
 processes the audio under Apple's own privacy terms. The words appear in
 the message field and are sent only when you tap Send.
- Voice calls with a bot keep the microphone open for the whole call,
 like a phone call. iOS shows the call through CallKit; Sagax keeps bot
 calls out of the Phone app's Recents.
- Your speech is recognized on the phone with Apple's speech recognition
 (on device whenever iOS allows; on iOS 26 and later with Apple's on-device
 transcriber once the language model is installed).
- Only when the phone cannot recognize speech itself (no recognizer for
 your language, or speech recognition access turned off for Sagax) and
 voice mode is available does the app upload each spoken turn (a short
 audio clip) to your computer or organization server, which sends it to
 xAI speech to text and returns the words. The clip is not stored.
- The recognized text of each turn goes to the bot as an ordinary
 message and is stored in the conversation, marked as said on a call.
- The bot's reply is read aloud. Depending on what your computer or server
 has set up, the reply text is turned into speech by: xAI text to
 speech through your computer or organization server (voice mode); the
 voice provider configured on your computer; ElevenLabs, called directly
 from the phone with your own key if you added one; or the phone's built-in
 voice, which stays on the phone.
- The xAI key is never on the phone. On an organization server the key is
 your own xAI key registered in Perspicax if you have one, otherwise the
 organization's key; on your own computer it is the key you configured
 there. xAI receives the audio or text it converts, under the terms of that
 key's account. xAI is used only to convert speech and text, never to
 write the bot's answers.
- The server records how much speech was converted (characters or audio
 length) for usage reporting, not the audio itself.

sections.title: Sagax for iPhone and iPad: privacy: Notifications
sections.text:
When you allow notifications, the app gives the active computer or server
the phone's Apple Push Notification service (APNs) token, the phone's name,
the app version and your notification sound settings
(`POST /api/push/devices`). A server set up to send pushes (organization
servers are) then sends notifications through Apple when the app is closed: a message (its text, cut to 240 characters), a nudge, an approval, a
failed routine or an achievement, with the sender's name and a link to their
avatar. Notification content travels through Apple like any messaging app.
The Sagax notification extension runs on the phone when such a notification
arrives. It reads only that notification, downloads the sender's avatar from
the same server (other addresses are ignored), and shows the bot or person as
the sender. Signing out removes the token from the server. While a voice
call is live, notifications for that conversation stay silent.

sections.title: Sagax for iPhone and iPad: privacy: Other services the app may contact
sections.text:
Only in response to what you open:
- A YouTube link in a conversation plays in an embedded player from
 youtube-nocookie.com.
- Connected app icons may be loaded from the address your server gives or
 from Google's favicon service (which then receives that app's web domain).
- Web links open in Safari or an in-app Safari view.

sections.title: Sagax for iPhone and iPad: privacy
sections.text:
Last updated: 2026-10-16. Applies to Sagax for iOS and iPadOS 0.5.8 and later.
Sagax for iPhone and iPad ("the app") is published by Pulsatrix Technologies
Inc. ("Pulsatrix"). It is the phone app of Sagax: it shows and controls AI
assistants ("bots") that run somewhere the person chose:
- on their own computer, in the Sagax desktop app, paired by scanning a
 QR code; or
- on their organization's Sagax server, after signing in with the
 organization's Pulsatrix account (Pulsatrix Perspicax).
The app also has a demo with made-up data that never leaves the phone.
The app contains no advertising, no analytics SDK and no third-party
tracking SDK. It does not track people across other companies' apps or
websites, and Pulsatrix does not sell personal information.

sections.title: Sagax for iPhone and iPad: privacy: What the phone keeps
sections.text:
- The address of each paired computer or organization server, and which one
 is active (iOS preferences and the private Sagax App Group).
- The session credential for each of them, in the iOS Keychain (shared only
 with the Sagax Share, widget and notification extensions through a private
 Keychain group).
- The last organization server address typed, so it is prefilled next time.
- Your profile photo for each connection, as served by that connection, in
 the app's cache.
- A small summary for the Home Screen widgets and Live Activities (bot names,
 status, the question a bot is asking you), in the private App Group.
- Settings such as theme, language, notification sounds and voice call
 preferences.
- If you turn on Only my voice for calls: a record of your usual speaking
 level, kept in the app's preferences on this phone. It is not a voice
 recording and not a biometric template, it is never sent anywhere, and
 Forget my voice deletes it.
- If you add your own ElevenLabs key under Settings > Call voice: that
 key, in this phone's Keychain only. It is never sent to your computer or
 organization server.
Removing a connection (or signing out) deletes its address and credential
from the phone and ends the session on that server. Deleting the app removes
everything the app keeps on the phone, except Keychain items, which iOS may
keep until the device is erased.

sections.title: Sagax for iPhone and iPad: privacy: Who handles your data
sections.text:
- Your computer (computer pairing): the Sagax desktop app on your own
 computer stores your bots, conversations, approvals, files and settings.
 Pulsatrix does not receive a copy.
- Your organization's server (organization sign-in): the organization
 that runs the server, or the provider that runs it for them, stores your
 conversations, files, settings and account. That organization decides how
 long they are kept. Ask its administrator for access or deletion. When
 Pulsatrix operates a server for an organization, Pulsatrix processes that
 data on the organization's behalf and under its instructions.
- The phone keeps only what is listed below.

sections.title: Sagax for iPhone and iPad: privacy: Widgets and Live Activities
sections.text:
Widgets and Live Activities show the summary listed above. The Needs You
widget can answer a bot's question from the Home Screen: the widget sends
that one answer to your computer or server using the stored session.

sections.title: Sagax for iPhone and iPad: privacy: Your choices and rights
sections.text:
- Turn off camera, microphone, speech recognition, local network or
 notifications at any time in iOS Settings > Sagax.
- Remove a connection or sign out in Sagax Settings.
- For conversations and account data held by your organization, contact its
 administrator. For data on your own computer, use the Sagax desktop app.
- For any privacy question or request to Pulsatrix, including requests under
 Quebec's privacy law (Law 25), write to hello@pulsatrix.ca. Never include a
 password, code or token in the message.

sections.title: Push notifications for the phone app (APNs): Checking it end to end
sections.text:
Nothing can be checked end to end without the real key. With the key on the
VM and a TestFlight build:
1. Open the app signed in to production once (it registers: `GET /api/push/devices`
 lists the phone, token masked).
2. Close the app (swipe it away), then from another account send a direct
 message, then a nudge. The phone shows both; the nudge plays the nudge
 sound. A tap opens the conversation.
3. Close the app, then have a bot finish a turn in a thread of yours. The
 banner must show that bot's name as the sender and, when the bot has a
 stored picture, that picture as the icon. Without a picture, the name is
 still the sender and the icon may stay empty or fall back to initials.
 A tap opens that thread.
4. Keep the desktop app open on that conversation while a message arrives:
 no push.
5. Keep the phone app in front, on that bot's conversation (or any screen):
 no banner and no sound. A second phone of yours that is locked still
 gets the push.
6. The server log shows no `InvalidProviderToken`. If it does, the `.p8` is
 the App Store Connect key, or the Key ID or Team ID is wrong.

sections.title: Push notifications for the phone app (APNs): Code
sections.text:
- `server/push/config.ts`: the `SAGAX_APNS_*` settings.
- `server/push/jwt.ts`: the provider token (JWT ES256 signed with the `.p8`,
 renewed every 40 minutes).
- `server/push/payload.ts`: the APNs body and headers.
- `server/push/activity-payload.ts`, `activity-content.ts`,
 `activity-devices.ts`, `activity-hub.ts`, `activity-frames.ts`: Live
 Activity push payload, content-state, token store, send hub and frame
 mapping.
- `server/push/apns.ts`: HTTP/2 to APNs with Node's `http2`, no dependency.
- `server/push/devices.ts`: each person's devices in
 ` /push-devices/ .json` (mode 0600). A device APNs answers
 410 Unregistered, or 400 BadDeviceToken / DeviceTokenNotForTopic, is
 removed.
- `server/push/frames.ts`, `server/push/hub.ts`: which live frames become
 pushes, the decision, the sends.
- `server/routes/push-devices.ts`: `POST`, `GET`, `DELETE /api/push/devices`
 (the signed-in person's own devices only; tokens are masked in every
 answer and every log line).
- `server/routes/push-activities.ts`: `POST`, `GET`, `DELETE
 /api/push/activities` (Live Activity tokens for the signed-in person).
- `ios/Sources/CompanionCore/Push.swift`, `ios/App/PushRegistrar.swift`: the
 phone registers its token with the server it is signed in to at every
 launch, when the token changes, when another server becomes active and
 when Settings > Notifications changes; it removes it on sign-out. A tap
 opens the conversation; a nudge received in front shakes and rings like
 the in-app nudge, once; a push wakes the app for a moment
 (`content-available`) to recount the icon badge.
- `ios/Sources/CompanionCore/LiveActivityPush.swift`,
 `ios/App/LiveActivities.swift`: ActivityKit `pushType: .token`, token
 registration for update and push-to-start.
- `ios/NotificationService`: Notification Service Extension. A
 `mutable-content` push downloads the avatar and attaches
 `INSendMessageIntent` so the banner uses the bot's name and face.
The APNs hosts appear only in the server bundle: `check:no-phone-home`
refuses `api.push.apple.com` and `api.sandbox.push.apple.com` everywhere
except the server's host table in `dist-server/`.

sections.title: Push notifications for the phone app (APNs): Creating the APNs key (once, Apple Developer portal)
sections.text:
1. Sign in to https://developer.apple.com/account with the Apple Developer
 team (Team ID ` `).
2. Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles > Keys > +.
3. Name it (for example `Sagax APNs`), check Apple Push Notifications
 service (APNs), Configure: environment Sandbox & Production, then
 Continue and Register.
4. Download the `AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8` file. Apple lets you download it
 only once: keep it in the password vault.
5. Note the Key ID (10 characters, shown on the key's page and in the
 file name).
6. Identifiers > `ca.pulsatrix.sagax`: check that Push Notifications is
 enabled (Xcode's automatic signing usually turns it on with the
 `aps-environment` entitlement; check after the next archive).
7. On the same App ID, enable Communication Notifications. Create (or
 let Xcode create) the extension App ID `ca.pulsatrix.sagax.notification`
 and enable Communication Notifications there too. Regenerate the
 development and distribution provisioning profiles after that, or let
 automatic signing refresh them on the next archive.
Important: an APNs key is not the App Store Connect API key, even though
both are `.p8` files from the same account. The App Store Connect key
(Users and Access > Integrations, used by `asc` and `altool`) signs tokens
APNs does not accept: APNs answers 403 InvalidProviderToken. The server
logs that case once with this hint.
TestFlight and App Store builds use the production APNs environment.
Only a build run from Xcode on a device uses sandbox. The phone sends its own
environment when it registers and that one wins over
`SAGAX_APNS_ENVIRONMENT`. One APNs key serves both environments.

sections.title: Push notifications for the phone app (APNs): Live Activities (ActivityKit push)
sections.text:
A bot's Dynamic Island / lock-screen Live Activity is started on the phone
with `pushType: .token`. The phone registers each activity's push token
(and, on iOS 17.2+, the push-to-start token) at `POST /api/push/activities`
for that person and bot. When the bot's state changes (working, needs you,
done) and the phone's live stream is not open, the server sends an APNs
push with:
- `apns-push-type: liveactivity`
- `apns-topic: .push-type.liveactivity`
- `event`: `update` or `end`
- `content-state` matching `BotActivityContent` (Date `since` as Cocoa
 reference seconds, Swift's default JSONEncoder)
- optional `stale-date`, `dismissal-date`, `relevance-score`
Priority 10 for needs-you and end (Apple's high-priority budget, rate
limited); priority 5 for working line updates. A 410 / dead token is
pruned; ending a bot clears that person's update tokens for it. Tokens
belong to one person only.

sections.title: Push notifications for the phone app (APNs): On the production VM (Perspicax infra)
sections.text:
The Sagax container already reads its secrets from
` /secrets/sagax` (mounted at `/run/secrets/sagax`, files
`root:10002` mode 0440, the container has group 10002), filled by
`infra/scripts/vm-bootstrap.sh` from the Key Vault. The APNs key follows the
same path. These changes belong to the Perspicax repository and are applied
by the orchestrator, not by this pull request.
1. Put the key in the Key Vault (isolated `az` profile of Perspicax):
 
2. `infra/runtime/docker-compose.yml`, service `sagax`, under
 `environment:` (after `SAGAX_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID`):
 
3. `infra/scripts/vm-bootstrap.sh`, inside the Sagax "on" branch, right
 after the `cat >>"$env_file" <<ENV ... ENV` block that writes
 `SAGAX_IDP_VAULT_KEY_FILE`:
 
4. Deploy as usual (snapshot first), then check the container log for
 `push: APNs on (production by default, topic ca.pulsatrix.sagax, ...)`.

sections.title: Push notifications for the phone app (APNs)
sections.text:
The phone app shows notifications by itself only while it runs or lingers in
the background with its live stream open. Once it is closed, or suspended
for long, only Apple Push Notification service (APNs) can reach it. The
organization server (Sagax in server mode, the `pulsabot` container on the
production VM) therefore sends real APNs pushes.

sections.title: Push notifications for the phone app (APNs): Server settings
sections.text:
| Variable | Value |
 
| `SAGAX_APNS_KEY_PATH` | the `.p8` file, mounted read-only |
| `SAGAX_APNS_KEY_ID` | the 10 character Key ID |
| `SAGAX_APNS_TEAM_ID` | ` ` (the team's 10-character id) |
| `SAGAX_APNS_BUNDLE_ID` | `ca.pulsatrix.sagax` (the default) |
| `SAGAX_APNS_ENVIRONMENT` | `production` (the default) or `sandbox` |
Without `SAGAX_APNS_KEY_PATH` and `SAGAX_APNS_KEY_ID` the server sends
nothing: phones still register, and the first push that would have gone out
logs one line `push: APNs is not configured (...)`; after that, quiet. With
them, startup logs `push: APNs on (...)`.

sections.title: Push notifications for the phone app (APNs): What gets pushed
sections.text:
| Event | Push kind | When |
 
| A person writes to you directly, a bot finishes a turn in your thread | `message` | Nobody saw it (below) |
| Someone nudges you | `nudge` | Always, at once, priority 10, the nudge sound |
| An approval, or a bot waiting on your answer | `approval` | Nobody saw it |
| A bot asks you to take over its computer | `approval` | Nobody saw it. Priority 10 like an approval; the banner has no Allow or Deny (no `requestId`). |
| A turn that could not start (expired OAuth, missing access) | `message` | Nobody saw it |
| An incident the person has to look at | `message` | Nobody saw it |
| A routine of yours finished | `message` | Nobody saw it. The banner names the routine (`Open routine %@`) and opens its report. A bot-to-bot turn stays quiet: the chip in both threads is the notice. |
| A routine of yours failed, or waited half an hour behind a busy bot | `routine` | Nobody saw it |
| An achievement unlocked | `achievement` | No client of yours is connected, and you turned on system notifications for achievements |
"Nobody saw it" is the desktop's own rule (`src/lib/attention.ts`,
`messageAttention`): notify unless you are looking at that conversation in a
focused window. The server does not know which conversation a window shows,
but a window that shows a conversation marks it read
(`POST /api/threads/:id/read`, `/api/groups/:id/read`, `/api/bots/:id/read`).
So when one of your clients is connected (presence), the push waits 8
seconds and is dropped if one of them marked that conversation read; when
none is connected it goes at once (`server/push/decide.ts`).
A phone whose live stream is open (`GET /api/events` with
`x-sagax-push-token`) already has the line: the hub skips APNs to that
device even if another of your phones or the desktop still gets the push.
On the phone, `userNotificationCenter(_:willPresent:)` returns `[]` while
the app is in front, so a push that still arrives (a race, a token that
had not yet been named) shows no banner and plays no sound.
Once a conversation that buzzed the phones is read on any device, the server
sends each phone one silent push (`kind: "read"`, `content-available`,
priority 5, `buildReadSyncRequest`): the phone withdraws that conversation's
banner and recounts its badge. Whenever its unread count drops (or it
loads the fleet), the phone also withdraws banners older than 10 seconds for
bot conversations that are no longer unread or waiting on the person
(`ios/Sources/CompanionCore/DeliveredNotifications.swift`).
Each push follows:
- the phone's Settings > Notifications (notification sounds, the approval
 chime, nudge sound), sent with each registration;
- the person's synced "Notification sounds";
- a bot's notifications muted for that person (Settings of the bot);
- a rate limit of 20 pushes per person in 5 minutes (approvals and questions
 are exempt; a refused push is logged);
- one notification per conversation (`apns-collapse-id` is
 `sagax.t.

sections.title: Ubuntu Desktop: Agent CLI discovery
sections.text:
Applications launched from GNOME do not inherit the same interactive shell `PATH` as a terminal. Sagax
keeps the inherited path and adds existing common locations such as:
- `~/.local/bin`
- `~/.claude/local`
- `~/.volta/bin`
- `~/.bun/bin`
- `~/.asdf/shims`
- `~/.deno/bin`
- `~/.nvm/versions/node/*/bin`
- `/usr/local/bin`
It also probes the login shell in the background. If a CLI still is not detected, set an explicit additional
path before launching the app from a terminal and verify it there:
 `SAGAX_EXTRA_PATH=/your/custom/bin ./release/Pulsa Bot-*-x86_64.AppImage` 
Restart Sagax after installing or signing in to a CLI.

sections.title: Ubuntu Desktop: Build packages
sections.text:
Requirements for building from source:
- Ubuntu 24.04 LTS x86_64
- Node.js 24 or newer
- pnpm 10.34.6 (Corepack can install the version declared by the project)
 
The build creates:
- `release/Pulsa Bot- -amd64.deb`
- `release/Pulsa Bot- -x86_64.AppImage`
The AppImage uses a static runtime and does not require the legacy `libfuse2` package.

sections.title: Ubuntu Desktop: Develop the desktop shell
sections.text:
Development mode uses three processes. Keep each command running in its own terminal:
 
For a package-shaped build without creating `.deb` or AppImage artifacts:

sections.title: Ubuntu Desktop: Download packages
sections.text:
Choose one Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64 package from the latest release:
- Debian package (`Pulsa Bot-amd64.deb`) — recommended; APT installs its desktop dependencies and configures the bundled bot browser's sandbox.
- Portable AppImage (`Pulsa Bot.AppImage`) — does not install system files.
- SHA-256 checksums
Versioned packages and previous releases remain available on the
releases page.

sections.title: Ubuntu Desktop: Enable local control
sections.text:
Installed `.deb` and AppImage builds include the certified Cua Driver 0.33.0 CLI and cursor-theme sidecar.
On GNOME Xorg, open Settings, choose Enable local control (Beta), wait for Ready, then explicitly assign a bot
to This computer. No driver download, terminal command, `chmod`, or daemon setup is required. The owned daemon
starts with `--no-overlay`, so Cua's decorative full-screen X11 cursor surface is never created. Sagax also
uses Electron software rendering on Linux to avoid the reproduced NVIDIA/libGLES GPU-process failure that could
leave an invisible focused app window receiving input.
Cua actions use a private logical cursor. With the decorative overlay disabled, `move_cursor` does not move the
user's physical pointer; approved click and typing actions still target the requested window, while the user's own
mouse remains under their control.
On GNOME Wayland, This computer remains unavailable and an older persisted opt-in is reset to off with private
file permissions. Sign out and choose Ubuntu on Xorg from the login-screen session menu, or continue using Chat,
preview-only capture, Cloud, or Local VM. Wayland re-enablement requires its own real-seat evidence and will not be
controlled by an environment override.
The upstream tag is still marked prerelease and the GitHub release is not immutable. A sigstore bundle is published
beside the archive. Sagax does not verify that bundle; the build trust anchor remains the reviewed digest:
- source commit: `1553a3f360ea12155be3bc77e27c427ca62f967a`;
- archive SHA-256: `166869bd9920338e097050c0114c02d33fa59762a4ac7e690459725a204e91e5`;
- packaged driver SHA-256: `7941c851069ed4b03608a16f2fdd4c905314748765afd6aba45733daab511956`;
- packaged cursor-theme SHA-256: `f516d208440553d8b44e4e6786b20fa2ce995cbbd5895e51803bdb4e0b943b1b`.
Packaging verifies the exact archive size, checksum, member names/types/sizes, and inner hashes before extracting
only those two executables. The app performs no runtime driver download or self-update. Cua's MIT license, the
embedded Inter font's SIL OFL 1.1 notice, full dependency license texts, MPL source locations, and a CycloneDX
inventory ship beside the binary; the reviewed source records live in `third_party/cua-driver`.
The staged `cua-driver` ELF is 57,398,736 bytes and `cua-cursor-theme` is 4,239,272 bytes before Ubuntu compression. The ELF
requires glibc 2.30 or newer plus the standard Ubuntu X11/XInput/xkbcommon libraries already present on the supported
Ubuntu 24.04 desktop; the package verifier executes the exact binary from every artifact layout.
AppImage's pinned SquashFS toolchain can emit root-owned directories as `0755` or `0775`; the package verifier
requires one of those modes consistently across the reviewed resource tree. Before execution, AppImage copies only
the pinned binaries into a private `0700` stage and verifies their hashes again. DEB upgrades repair their exact
package-owned path to `root:root 0755` automatically.

sections.title: Ubuntu Desktop: Install and run
sections.text:
Install a downloaded Debian package with APT so its desktop dependencies are resolved:
 `sudo apt install ./Pulsa Bot-amd64.deb` 
Then open Sagax from the GNOME application launcher. To remove it:
 `sudo apt remove openmausbot` 
The portable AppImage does not install system files:
 
For a downloaded release AppImage, use `Pulsa Bot.AppImage` in place of the versioned path above.
### Bundled bot browser on Ubuntu 24.04
The desktop packages include the browser engine and browser runtime; no separate browser download is needed.
Use the `.deb` package for browser-ready installation on Ubuntu 24.04. Its installer secures the browser's
package-owned files and loads an AppArmor rule for that exact executable. The browser sandbox stays enabled,
and the machine-wide user-namespace restriction is unchanged. Upgrades refresh the same rule; uninstalling
the package removes it. Enabling a bot's browser and approving its actions remain explicit choices.
An AppImage is portable and cannot install privileged system policy. On hosts restricting unprivileged
user namespaces, its bundled browser can still report `No usable sandbox`. Install the `.deb` instead;
do not add `--no-sandbox`, disable AppArmor globally, or allowlist arbitrary executables under your home
directory. See Chromium's explanation of the Ubuntu restriction.
Application data remains local in `~/.sagax`. Electron browser data and window state use the normal XDG
configuration directory (`~/.config/openmausbot` unless the environment overrides it).

sections.title: Ubuntu Desktop: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
### An agent CLI is missing
Run the CLI directly in a terminal, finish its sign-in flow, then restart Sagax. If it lives outside the
common directories above, use `SAGAX_EXTRA_PATH` while testing and report the install location so it can be
considered for automatic discovery.
### A bot needs computer tools
Choose Cloud (Boat) and add a Boat token in App Settings, or use Local VM. Linux This computer remains disabled
on Wayland. On Xorg, enable it from the Local control card first.
### Local control is not ready
On Xorg, press Try again and use the reason shown in the card. The bundled package requires no manual driver
installation or `chmod`; an upgraded DEB repairs its exact package-owned directory modes automatically. On Wayland,
the card directs you to Ubuntu on Xorg and intentionally offers no enable button.
### Screen preview does not start
On Xorg, confirm the session has an active display with `echo "$XDG_SESSION_TYPE"`; it should print `x11`.
On Wayland, confirm `xdg-desktop-portal` and the GNOME portal backend are running, then click Try again to
open a new chooser. Cancelling or stopping sharing never causes an automatic second prompt.
### The AppImage does not start
Confirm the executable bit and architecture:
 
Run it from a terminal once to collect the startup output. Do not install `libfuse2` just for this AppImage; the
package is built with the static runtime.

sections.title: Ubuntu Desktop
sections.text:
Sagax has an Ubuntu 24.04 LTS x86_64 desktop beta. The Electron package embeds the harness server, so
installed builds do not require Node, pnpm, Swift, or a terminal at runtime. For giving a bot the same kind
of Linux desktop on your own server instead of this machine, see byo-vps.md.

sections.title: Ubuntu Desktop: Validate a package change
sections.text:
The verifier checks `.deb` metadata, desktop identity, the exact dormant Cua resource tree and provenance,
SquashFS/DEB directory modes, runtime path policy, and matching binary hashes across all artifacts. The local smoke
launches the unpacked app and AppImage without `--no-sandbox`; CI first reproduces a `0.1.7` in-place DEB upgrade and
then runs the same smoke against `/opt/Sagax/openmausbot`. These lanes prove the embedded server and UI are
usable, verify that an old local-control opt-in is cleared, and assert that
no Cua executable starts on Xorg or simulated Wayland. Low-level runtime tests retain the future private-daemon
contract without activating it in a packaged app. Only a real-seat acceptance matrix can authorize re-enablement.

sections.title: Ubuntu Desktop: What works
sections.text:
- The native Electron window and embedded Sagax server on GNOME Xorg and GNOME Wayland.
- Local Claude, Codex, Grok, Gemini, and other configured agent CLIs.
- Chat, streaming turns, approvals, bot-to-bot communication, and local data storage.
- Connected apps and Boat cloud computers.
