- External documentation and OAuth links in the default browser.
- An explicit, view-only local screen preview on GNOME Xorg and GNOME Wayland. The Wayland path uses the
 native portal chooser and keeps the selected PipeWire stream open until the user stops sharing.
- Explicit opt-in local computer control on GNOME Xorg using the bundled, pinned Cua Driver without its
 decorative full-screen cursor overlay.
- A fail-closed local-control state on GNOME Wayland while its separate real-seat input-safety gate in issue #345
 is resolved.
The local preview does not give the bot control of this computer by itself. On Xorg, local control requires both
the global Enable local control choice and assigning a bot to This computer; every action still enters the
approval flow. On Wayland, local control is disabled and legacy opt-ins are cleared automatically. Automatic Wayland
helper installation, Linux dictation, and ARM64 remain unavailable and fail closed; follow their
progress in issue #29 and the safety hold in
issue #345. Bundled
CUA supply-chain work is tracked in issue #113. Xorg is tracked in
issue #79, and guarded GNOME/Wayland support in
issue #109.

sections.title: Ubuntu Desktop: Xorg and Wayland
sections.text:
The shell, chat, cloud computers, connected apps, and preview-only capture work in both GNOME session types.
The Wayland chooser/select/persistent-stream/cancel/end/retry lifecycle has been validated in a real Ubuntu
24.04 GNOME Wayland session. Sagax detects Wayland before XWayland when both `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` and
`DISPLAY` exist, so capture cannot accidentally bypass portal-mediated behavior.
Open the Computer panel and use the separate Preview this computer card. Capture never starts when the app
or panel opens.
- Xorg: Start preview captures the primary monitor directly.
- Wayland: Choose a screen opens the GNOME portal chooser once. The selected stream stays open until
 you press Stop preview, close the panel, end sharing from GNOME, or quit the app.
Cancelling or ending Wayland sharing returns to a calm Try again state and never reopens the chooser
automatically. Sagax does not capture screen audio, remember the selected monitor after restart, or
offer an Open Settings action on Linux.
Local computer control is independent from preview. It is available after explicit opt-in on Xorg and remains
fail-closed on Wayland. XWayland's `DISPLAY` never bypasses the Wayland safety gate.

sections.title: Markdown editor: Accessibility
sections.text:
The toolbar is a WAI-ARIA toolbar: one Tab stop, arrow keys, Home and End
move between buttons, and every button has a label and its shortcut
(`aria-keyshortcuts`). The text area is labelled by the field's own label.
Escape leaves the editor and puts focus on its frame (focus ring shown), so
the next Tab reaches the next control. Colours come from the app's tokens,
so dark, light and every skin apply.

sections.title: Markdown editor: How it loads
sections.text:
`MarkdownEditor` is in the main bundle and is small. CodeMirror lives in
`MarkdownEditorCore.tsx`, a separate chunk loaded the first time an editor
mounts. Until it arrives (or if it cannot load), a plain textarea with the
same value, label and handlers stands in, so typing is never blocked.
Nothing in the editor reaches the network.
Dependencies: `@codemirror/state`, `@codemirror/view`,
`@codemirror/commands`, `@codemirror/language`, `@lezer/markdown` and
`@lezer/highlight` (MIT). `@codemirror/lang-markdown` is not used: it pulls
the HTML, CSS and JavaScript languages in for embedded code; the markdown
parser is wired directly instead.

sections.title: Markdown editor
sections.text:
Every place in the desktop app where a person writes markdown uses the same
editor, `src/components/markdown/MarkdownEditor.tsx`. The text stays plain
markdown: what is saved is exactly what was typed, through the same handler
and the same request as the plain text box it replaced.

sections.title: Markdown editor: Shortcuts
sections.text:
Mac shown first; on Windows and Linux use Ctrl for Cmd and Alt for Option.
| Action | Mac | Windows, Linux |
 
| Bold | Cmd+B | Ctrl+B |
| Italic | Cmd+I | Ctrl+I |
| Link | Cmd+K | Ctrl+K |
| Inline code (code block for several lines) | Cmd+E | Ctrl+E |
| Heading 1, 2, 3 (again removes it) | Cmd+Option+1, 2, 3 | Ctrl+Alt+1, 2, 3 |
| Numbered list | Cmd+Shift+7 | Ctrl+Shift+7 |
| Bulleted list | Cmd+Shift+8 | Ctrl+Shift+8 |
| Checklist | Cmd+Shift+9 | Ctrl+Shift+9 |
| Quote | Cmd+Shift+. | Ctrl+Shift+. |
| Format | Shift+Option+F | Shift+Alt+F |
| Nest or un-nest a list item | Tab, Shift+Tab | Tab, Shift+Tab |
| Undo, redo | Cmd+Z, Cmd+Shift+Z | Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y |
| Leave the editor | Escape | Escape |
Cmd+K inside the editor makes a link; outside it still opens the command
palette.

sections.title: Markdown editor: Using it in a new field
sections.text:
The text edits are pure functions in `markdown-edits.ts`
(`markdown-edits.test.ts`); the component and every field above have render
tests (`MarkdownEditor.test.ts`, `MarkdownEditor.surfaces.test.ts`).

sections.title: Markdown editor: What it does
sections.text:
- Live formatting while typing. Headings are sized, bold is bold, italic
 is italic, inline code and code blocks are monospace on a tinted band,
 quotes carry a bar, tables are monospace, links are coloured, and a checked
 task (`- [x]`) is struck through. The markdown marks stay visible and dim.
- Write, Preview, Side by side. Preview renders with `ChatMarkdown`, the
 renderer of chat messages, so it shows what the bot's markdown looks like
 in the app. Side by side is in Advanced mode only and is remembered.
- Toolbar. Bold, italic, heading, bulleted list, numbered list,
 checklist, quote, code, link, table, divider line and Format. In Simple
 mode the toolbar keeps bold, italic, bullets, checklist and link; the rest
 is behind the "More" button.
- Lists. Enter continues a list (next number, an empty box for a task,
 `>` in a quote); Enter on an empty item ends the list or moves a nested
 item out. Tab nests a list item under the one above, Shift+Tab moves it
 out. Outside a list, Tab moves focus as usual.
- Auto-pairs. `(`, `[` and backticks close themselves; `*` and `_` do
 where emphasis can start (never at the start of a line, where `*` is a
 bullet, and never inside a word, so `snake_case` types normally). Typed
 over a selection, they wrap it. Backspace removes an empty pair.
- Paste. A URL pasted over selected text makes a link. Tab-separated
 rows (copied from a spreadsheet) become a table, first row as header.
- Format. Tidies spacing without changing what renders: one blank line
 around headings and code blocks and before a list that follows a
 paragraph, `-` for every bullet, `# Title` spacing, no trailing spaces
 (a two-space line break inside a paragraph stays), no runs of blank
 lines. Code blocks and front matter are left byte for byte.
- Counts. Words and characters in the status line, and the cap when the
 field has one (`maxLength`). Fields with their own counter (SOUL.md bytes,
 About me, team instructions) keep it there.
- Task boxes. Clicking `[ ]` or `[x]` in the editor toggles it.

sections.title: Sagax MCP server: Connection discovery
sections.text:
With no configuration, the MCP process probes Sagax's three desktop ports (`8799`, `18799`, and `28799`)
and accepts only a health response that identifies itself as Sagax. This handles the desktop's normal
fallback when another local process already owns port 8799.
Set `SAGAX_PORT` to force one local port, or `SAGAX_URL` to use an explicit HTTP(S) origin. Cleartext remote
HTTP is rejected unless `ALLOW_INSECURE_HTTP=true`; HTTPS should be used outside loopback. An optional
`SAGAX_TOKEN` is sent as a bearer token for authenticated reverse proxies. When a token is set, an
explicit `SAGAX_URL` or `SAGAX_PORT` is required so the credential is never sent while probing unrelated
local ports. `SAGAX_MCP_TIMEOUT_MS` can set an HTTP timeout between 1,000 and 120,000 milliseconds.
In packaged builds, `SAGAX_TOKEN` is required for mutating tools as
described above; it is not a generic reverse-proxy secret.

sections.title: Sagax MCP server: From a source checkout
sections.text:
Start Sagax, then configure the MCP client to run:
 
Packaged desktop builds require a paired session for tools that create,
change, send, switch, interrupt, or run anything. Read-only tools work on
loopback without one. A hosted or shared server with service loopback trust
(self-hosting) needs a
session for almost every tool, reads included. To authorize an external MCP
client:
1. In Sagax, open Settings → Phone → Set up a phone and reveal the
 one-time pairing code.
2. Exchange it locally (remove spaces from the displayed code):
 
 If the desktop selected a fallback port, replace `8799` with the port shown
 in Settings. Copy the returned `token`; the pairing code is single-use.
3. Pin that same port and token in the MCP configuration:
 
The paired client appears with phones under Settings → Phone and can be
revoked there. Do not share the token or commit it to a repository.

sections.title: Sagax MCP server: From the installed desktop app
sections.text:
Release builds bundle `server/mcp-server.js` and can run it with Electron's embedded Node runtime, so users do
not need Node.js or pnpm installed.
macOS example:
 
On Windows, use the installed `Sagax.exe` as `command`, the adjacent
`resources\\server\\mcp-server.js` as the argument, and the same `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1` environment value.
The usual per-user install is under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\\Programs\\Sagax`.
On Ubuntu `.deb` installs, the executable is normally `/opt/Sagax/openmausbot` and the script is
`/opt/Sagax/resources/server/mcp-server.js`. Use the same environment value.

sections.title: Sagax MCP server: Safety and data scope
sections.text:
Transcript reads are paged and capped at 200 messages. Search is capped at 100 hits. Screenshot pixels and
permission grant keys are removed from MCP results. Tool schemas reject unknown fields and malformed values,
and model changes are refused while a bot is working.
The harness itself is local-first and normally binds to loopback. If you expose it through a reverse proxy,
authentication and TLS at that proxy are part of your deployment's security boundary.

sections.title: Sagax MCP server
sections.text:
The Sagax desktop app includes a local stdio MCP server. It lets another MCP client coordinate your
Sagax team while the desktop app and its harness are running.

sections.title: Sagax MCP server: Tools
sections.text:
| Purpose | Tools |
 
| Inspect | `get_system_health`, `list_bots`, `list_channels`, `get_bot_messages`, `get_channel_messages`, `search_messages`, `list_available_models` |
| Create and organize | `create_bot`, `update_bot_profile`, `create_channel`, `update_channel`, `create_task`, `switch_task`, `rename_task` |
| Run work | `send_bot_message`, `send_channel_message`, `wait_for_conversation`, `interrupt_conversation`, `set_bot_model` |
`wait_for_conversation` returns `settled`, `needs-user`, `failed`, `stalled`, or `timed-out`, along with a
small redacted transcript tail. MCP cancellation is honored while a tool is waiting.

sections.title: Sagax MCP server: What it can do
MCP tool names on Grok: never drop a connector tool: Known limit
sections.text:
Tool selection selectors (`mcp: : `) still accept server names of
at most 32 characters (`shared/tool-scope.ts`); a 40-character Perspicax
profile slug cannot be narrowed by a selection. Unselected bots are not
affected.

sections.title: MCP tool names on Grok: never drop a connector tool
sections.text:
Incident (2026-10-11). Bots on Grok on the production server did not have
`cw_psa__query`, `cw_psa__write` or `cw_psa__action` from any Perspicax
profile (`perspicax_profil_ottoline_limited`, `perspicax_quasar_agent`).
Grok names an MCP tool `server__tool` and *skips* a tool whose qualified key it
cannot admit (grok 1.0.50 user guide, `07-mcp-servers.md`, "What Grok admits"):
| Rule | Skipped example |
 
| exactly one `__` in `server__tool` | `cw_psa__query` |
| tool in `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` | `files.read`, `ns:do` |
| no `___` (tool starting with `_`) | `_private` |
| key at most 256 characters | very long names |
The CLI only wrote `Skipping MCP tool` to its own log; the bot saw nothing.

sections.title: MCP tool names on Grok: never drop a connector tool: Post-deploy smoke
sections.text:
1. Gate parity inside the deployed image (fails with exit 1 on a mismatch):
 `docker exec -i -e SMOKE_GATE=/app/dist-server/mcp-gate.js pulsatrix-pulsabot-1 node - < scripts/smoke-mcp-tool-names.mjs` 
2. Live, read-only: in a NEW thread, ask a bot on Grok that has a Perspicax
 profile to list that connector's tools and call `cw_psa__query` (via its
 registered name) for one ticket or system info. Compare the tool list with
 the profile's own catalog (Perspicax `api_search`, or the same profile from
 another MCP client): every tool must be there, `cw_psa__*` under their
 aliases. Then check `GET /api/mcp/tool-names` shows no `mismatch`.

sections.title: MCP tool names on Grok: never drop a connector tool: What Sagax does now
sections.text:
- Explicit alias map, never re-splitting. Grok's ACP support sets
 `mcpToolNames: "grok"`; every connector server (Perspicax profiles, URL
 and stdio servers) is mounted through `server/mcp-gate.ts` with
 `SAGAX_GATE_TOOL_NAMES=grok`. The gate registers each tool under an
 admissible name (`server/mcp-tool-names.ts`) and keeps `alias -> upstream
 name`; a `tools/call` is translated through that map before any check.
 `cw_psa__query` becomes `cw_psa_query` (its description ends with
 `(Connector tool name: cw_psa__query.)`).
- Deterministic, collision-free, never dropping. Invalid characters become
 `-`, `_` runs one `_`, a leading `_` goes; a name that would collide with
 another tool, or exceed 256 characters, gets an 8-hex sha256 suffix of its
 original name. Admissible names always keep their own name.
- Loud, visible failures. Each rename is a `WARNING` and any tool still
 unregistrable an `ERROR` on the gate's stderr; each gate writes
 `DATA_DIR/mcp-tool-names/ .json` (`advertised`, `registered`,
 `renamed`, `unregistrable`, `parity`, `status: ok|renamed|mismatch`),
 served at `GET /api/mcp/tool-names`. Settings > Plugins > a server > Test
 shows each renamed or unregistrable tool on its row. A URL server the ACP
 driver cannot mount is logged instead of skipped silently.
- Parity check. `toolNameParity` asserts a bijection between advertised
 and registered names, every one admissible by Grok's rule. The gate runs it
 on every catalog it relays (report `parity`); CI runs it through the real
 gate process (`server/mcp-gate-tool-names.test.ts`) and the smoke script
 (`scripts/smoke-mcp-tool-names.test.ts`).

sections.title: MCP coverage: Sagax and Perspicax capabilities vs MCP tools: Gap summary by priority
sections.text:
No gap left in the registry. The claim tools came with #497 (merged into this
branch). The Perspicax names follow 1.8.28; the memory v2 names of the draft
behind a switch (Perspicax #326, Sagax #496) are aliases of the same
permissions, so either model is judged.
`approvals:answer` (`answer_approval`), `people:nudge` (`nudge_person`),
`pairing:manage` (`manage_pairing`) and `settings:manage` (`manage_settings`)
are thin wrappers over `act`, so the person's rights and the bot's approval
mode still decide. Perspicax's own Sagax tools (`sagax_bots`, `sagax_send`,
`sagax_thread`, `sagax_routine_run`, `sagax_routine_update`, `sagax_approve`,
`sagax_nudge`) are aliases of the Sagax permissions they stand for.
`sagax_routine_update` is the person's own write through the member API
(`PATCH /api/org/member/routines/{id}`); a bot still uses
`propose_routine_action`, which follows Ask or Auto. The Perspicax gateway tools
(`PERSPICAX_TOOLS`: the memory tools, the `api_*` meta-tools, `identity`,
`flow`, `flow_action`, the `remote_support_*` tools, `review_write`) are listed only on an organization
server linked to Perspicax (`SAGAX_PERSPICAX_TOOLS`) and forwarded by
`/api/internal/perspicax/tool` to the profile mounted in the turn, after the
misuse and safety review. Reading the Perspicax catalog to vet resource names
at turn time (`ApiCatalog`) is not wired yet.

sections.title: MCP coverage: Sagax and Perspicax capabilities vs MCP tools

Inventory of what the Sagax server and the Perspicax gateway can do, against
the tools the Sagax MCP ("agents" server, `server/drivers/agents-catalog.ts`)
exposes to a bot or an AI client. The machine-readable form is the registry in
`server/mcp-permissions.ts`; `server/mcp-permissions.test.ts` fails when a
catalog tool has no permission.
Totals: capabilities 152, covered 152, gaps 0.
Sources read: the agents tool catalog, the internal routes it calls
(`/api/internal/*`), the member API (`docs/org-member-api.md`), and the
Perspicax tool surface (`docs/mcp-surface.md` there): API meta-tools, the
per-API query/write/action tools, the memory tools, flow and review tools.
Reading the table:
- covered: one MCP tool carries it, and it is now gated by the permission
 shown.
- covered (bridge): a Perspicax tool the agents catalog does not list
 natively but a bot reaches through the Perspicax bridge
 (`server/perspicax-mcp.ts`, a profile mounted on the turn). The relay judges
 it with the same permission, so enforce never refuses it by omission.
- MISSING: no MCP tool.
- Tool names are the ones Perspicax 1.8.28 serves (connector
 `mcp/meta_tools.rs`, `mcp/memory_tools.rs`, `mcp/flow_tools.rs`,
 `mcp/sagax_tools.rs`). The per-profile tools are matched by name pattern:
 ` __query` (read), ` __write` or ` __ _write`
 (write), ` __action` (action), ` __read_action` (read), any
 other ` __ ` (an operation's own tool, judged as an
 action). The `-` separator (`cw_psa-query`) is read too.
- Per-resource fine grain (a ticket update in the PSA) is not a separate
 registry row: it is the kind's permission narrowed by a resource rule,
 ` : . ` such as `cw_psa:tickets.update` (see
 `permissions.md`, "Dynamic keys").
- Priority: P0 = coordination safety (claims); P1 = day-to-day work; P2 =
 administrative.

sections.title: Merge order for the MCP permissions branch: #497 is merged into this branch

The first check (2026-10-14) missed one conflict with #497 (native claim
tools): both branches added `PerspicaxMcp.callTool` to
`server/perspicax-mcp.ts`, with different signatures (`tool` here, `name` in
#497) and different answers (`{ status, body }` here, `PerspicaxToolAnswer` in

sections.title: Merge order for the MCP permissions branch: Recommended order
sections.text:
1. The unrelated pull requests (492 to 494, 498 to 507, 509 to 516, 518 once
 it is rebased on main), in any order. They do not interact with this work.
2. 496, then 495. Both merge cleanly in either order, with 497 and with this
 branch.
3. 497 (native claim tools).
4. 517 and this branch (#508), in either order: they merge cleanly together.
 After the last of them, rerun `node scripts/tool-policy/generate.ts` (both
 add rows to `server/tool-policy.generated.ts`), then
 `scripts/testing/index-route-ratchet.test.ts`,
 `scripts/tool-policy/tool-policy-coverage.test.ts`,
 `server/mcp-permissions.test.ts` (it fails while a catalog tool has no
 permission) and `server/drivers/agents-catalog-wire.test.ts`. If a
 catalog golden moves, regenerate it with `UPDATE_AGENTS_CATALOG_GOLDENS=1`
 and set `BUDGET_BASELINE` by hand from the printed sizes.
The permission registry tests are the safety net for steps 2 to 4: a catalog
tool, or a tool Perspicax 1.8.28 serves, without a row in `MCP_PERMISSIONS`
fails them, so no merge can leave one to be refused by omission in enforce.

sections.title: MCP permissions: Adding a tool
sections.text:
Add the tool to the catalog, add its row to `MCP_PERMISSIONS` with a tier,
and update `coverage.md`. The registry test fails while a catalog tool has no
permission. Never rename a key; retire it and add another.

sections.title: MCP permissions: Audit
sections.text:
Both guards write to the server's activity log (category `security`, actions
`mcp.call`, `mcp.shadow`, `mcp.deny`) through `POST /api/internal/mcp-audit`
for the proxy and directly for the relay. Only the whitelisted fields of the
record are kept. If the server cannot be reached, the proxy writes the
`[mcp-audit]` line on stderr.
### Audit volume
Auditing every allowed call costs one local POST and one activity-log line
per tool call, and a turn makes many tool calls (reads, memory, transcript
pages). In shadow mode nothing is refused, so those rows would mostly bury
the denials the shadow period exists to find. The choice:
- `shadow` audits every denial (`mcp.shadow`) and no allowed call by default.
 `SAGAX_MCP_AUDIT_SAMPLE` (0 to 1) audits that share of the allowed calls
 (`mcp.call`), to measure what enforce would write before turning it on.
- `enforce` audits every call, allowed and denied: the record of what ran is
 then the point, and that mode is opted into.
- `off` audits nothing.

sections.title: MCP permissions: Dynamic keys
sections.text:
A per-profile call also gets a resource key, ` : . `,
from its name and arguments:
| Call | Key |
 
| `cw_psa__query` `{ resource: "tickets" }` | `cw_psa:tickets.read` |
| `cw_psa__write` `{ resource: "tickets", action: "update" }` | `cw_psa:tickets.update` |
| `cw_psa__tickets_write` `{ action: "delete" }` | `cw_psa:tickets.delete` |
| `cw_psa__action` `{ action: "merge" }` | `cw_psa:merge.run` |
| `cw_psa__read_action` `{ action: "usage" }` | `cw_psa:usage.read` |
| `cw_psa__find_tickets` | `cw_psa:find_tickets.run` |
A call is allowed when the role holds the kind's permission and no deny rule
matches the key. `SAGAX_MCP_DENY` lists the rules, comma separated: an exact
key, `cw_psa:tickets.*` or `cw_psa:*`. A denied key is reported as
`resource_denied` and the audit row carries `resource`. Segments must be
plain slugs; when a catalog of the Perspicax APIs is passed to the guard
(`ApiCatalog`), a profile it does not list, or a query or write on a resource
it does not list, gives no key. Reading that catalog from Perspicax at turn
time is not wired yet.

sections.title: MCP permissions
sections.text:
One permission per action, named `resource:verb` (`memory:save`,
`claims:acquire`, `routines:propose.action`). The registry is
`server/mcp-permissions.ts`; the inventory is `coverage.md`.

sections.title: MCP permissions: Roles (widest scope per tier)
sections.text:
| Role | read | own | dispatch | claim | admin |
 
| viewer | org | no | no | no | no |
| member | org | self | self | self | no (self-scope exceptions: create, archive or propose deleting a bot of their own, create or manage a room of their own, their own Local VM `vm:exec`, `act` as themselves, a team memory proposal) |
| operator | org | team | team | team | no, plus every member exception (an operator holds at least what a member holds) |
| admin | org | org | org | org | org |
| service | org | self | self | self | no (and never `vm:exec`, `actions:invoke` or `settings:manage`) |
2026-10-27 (#1098): a read reaches the org scope for every role. It changes
nothing, and its source (the Sagax route, Perspicax's memory tiers) shows
only what the person may already read. A call relayed to a person's
Perspicax MCP server that names a tool Sagax does not list is
`mcp:external` (tier own): Perspicax authorizes its own tools, so it is not
refused as `unknown_tool`. A bot the person creates during a turn counts as
theirs for the rest of that proxy's life (`learnBot`).
The `service` role holds claims at `self`: automation can hold work it
started, not take over someone else's.

sections.title: MCP permissions: Rules
sections.text:
1. Deny by default. A tool with no registered permission, a role that is
 not one of the five, or a tier a role does not hold is refused.
2. Scope. Every grant has a widest scope: `self` < `team` < `org`. A call
 reaches a scope (`scopeForCall`): another bot, a room, group or team
 argument means `team`; `scope: "org"` means `org`; otherwise `self`. The
 call is allowed only when the role's grant is at least as wide. Exception
 (2026-10-26): a bot or room the speaking person owns (`SAGAX_MCP_OWN_BOTS`,
 `SAGAX_MCP_OWN_ROOMS`, `scopeOwnersFromEnv`) is `self`, not `team`.
 Since 2026-10-28, `ask_bot` and `delegate_bot` to a bot someone else
 shares with the person at `run` or above (`SAGAX_MCP_RUN_BOTS`) are
 `self` too; any other call naming that bot stays `team`.
3. Audit. One record per audited call: time, principal, role, tool,
 permission, scope, decision, reason, and whether the denial was enforced.
 It never holds arguments, message text or results. It goes to the server's
 activity log (see Audit below), with a stderr `[mcp-audit]` line as the
 fallback. A sink that throws never changes the decision. In `enforce` every
 call is audited, allowed and denied; in `shadow` every denial is, and an
 allowed call only within `SAGAX_MCP_AUDIT_SAMPLE` (see "Audit volume").
4. Mode. `SAGAX_MCP_PERMISSIONS`: `off`, `shadow` (default: denials are
 audited and the call goes through, so existing bots keep working while the
 audit shows what would break), `enforce` (denials are refused with a
 sentence naming the permission). The harness hands the server's mode, deny
 rules and audit sample to the agents proxy it spawns (`mcpPolicyEnv`), so
 both guards judge alike.
5. Identity. `SAGAX_MCP_ROLE` (default `member`), `SAGAX_MCP_PRINCIPAL`
 (default the bot id), `SAGAX_MCP_TEAMS`. The harness sets these when it
 builds the integration; the server remains the authority on what a route
 allows, this layer only narrows.

sections.title: MCP permissions: Tiers
sections.text:
| Tier | Meaning |
 
| read | changes nothing |
| own | the caller's own work: memory, skills, files, widgets, reactions, proposals |
| dispatch | puts other bots, people, routines or cloud agents to work |
| claim | holds on shared work (acquire, renew, release) |
| admin | creates bots, rooms or credentials, runs host commands, settings (2026-10-19: a bot's own rules and docs, its person's logins, computer choice and creating a pairing for the speaking person are `own`, never for a service turn; #1269: `act` and `manage_settings`, which run with the speaking person's own rights, are `own` too, see docs/member-admin-audit.md) |

sections.title: MCP permissions: Tool names
sections.text:
The Perspicax names are the ones Perspicax 1.8.28 serves (connector
`mcp/meta_tools.rs`, `mcp/memory_tools.rs`, `mcp/flow_tools.rs`,
`mcp/sagax_tools.rs`): `api_list`, `api_search`, `api_describe`,
`api_result_query`, `api_lookup`, `api_plan`, `api_upload`, `api_reload`,
`identity`, `flow`, `flow_action`, `review_write`, the memory and work tools,
and the Sagax tools. A Perspicax tool that stands for a Sagax capability is an
alias of its permission (`sagax_send` is `bots:send`); the memory v2 names of
the draft behind a switch (Perspicax #326: `memory_find`, `memory_save`,
`memory_remove`, `memory_suggestions`) are aliases too. A test lists every
name 1.8.28 serves and fails when one has no permission, so enforce cannot
refuse a real tool by omission.
The per-profile tools are matched by name (`profileToolCall`); the
`-` separator of Perspicax's `tool_name_separator` is read too:
| Name | Permission | Tier |
 
| ` __query` | `api:query` | read |
| ` __write`, ` __ _write` | `api:write` | dispatch |
| ` __action` | `api:action` | dispatch |
| ` __read_action` | `api:action.read` | read |
| any other ` __ ` | `api:operation` | dispatch (not known to be a read) |

sections.title: MCP permissions: Where the guard runs
sections.text:
- The agents proxy, for every tool of the agents catalog (the native
 Perspicax tools and the claim tools included).
- `PerspicaxMcp.relay`, for every `tools/call` a bridge relays to a Perspicax
 profile, with the same mode and identity. `PerspicaxMcp.callTool` (the
 native tools' path to Perspicax) relays with `judged`, since the proxy
 already judged and audited that call: it is not judged twice.
Identity is set by the harness when it builds the integration
(`mcpIdentityEnv`): the speaking person, their role (Perspicax admin is
`admin`, manager is `operator`, anyone else `member`) and teams; a turn with
no person is `service`.

sections.title: What a member needs an admin for (audit, 2026-10-19): 1. Bot tool calls (approval cards)
sections.text:
| Tool or action | Where it runs | Before | After | Why |
 
| `sagax-desktop` `run_command`, `write_file`, `browse`, `fetch_url`, ... on the owner's own computer | own | admin card | the owner's card; their permission mode never answers it; since 2026-10-19 their own Always allow made on such a card (`from: origin`, the exact command or path) does | It is their own machine. It is not isolated, so no automatic answer (security review). |
| `sagax-desktop` `read_file`, `list_files`, `search_files` inside the Sagax attachments folder of their own computer | own | admin card | no card, at any level, owner's own turn only, after the safety hold, their rules and their key | The files they sent the bot. Paths normalized (backslashes, `\\?\`, 8.3 short names, case); `..` refused; the folder must look like ` /Sagax/attachments`. |
| `sagax-desktop` `local_vm` | own | owner card at Auto only while autonomy is on, otherwise admin | owner card; unasked at Auto while autonomy is on (unchanged) | The Local VM on their machine is isolated. |
| `sagax-environment` tools (their cloud computer) | own | unasked at Auto while autonomy is on; admin card when autonomy is off | unasked at Auto while autonomy is on; otherwise the owner's card | Their own isolated sandbox. |
| `sagax-environment` `read_file`, `list_files` in `/workspace/attachments` | own | as above | no card, owner's own turn | The files they sent. |
| `sagax-computer` `computer_select` (the bot picks where it works: the person's cloud computer, their own computer, its Local VM or the built-in browser), mounted by Sagax for this turn, for the person it is for (who answers its cards, or the speaker in their own conversation with someone else's bot) | own | admin card on engines that ask first (prod 0.5.27: "Computer select dans Sagax Computer"): the server was in the host-level list | no card, at any approval level, on every engine (Claude already pre-allows it); the safety hold, the person's own deny and ask rules and their security key still come first | There is no menu for the person any more: the bot decides where it works. The commands it runs next keep their own rules (on their real computer, always a card). A computer the organization shares stays `agents` `shared_computer` (admin, delegable). Not mounted this turn, someone else's places, a guest-driven turn or another server's spelling: an admin's card, unchanged. |

sections.title: What a member needs an admin for (audit, 2026-10-19): 3. MCP permission catalogue (`server/mcp-permissions.ts`)
sections.text:
Mode in production: `shadow` (unset): a denial is audited (`mcp.shadow`), nothing is
refused. The tiers matter once a server runs `SAGAX_MCP_PERMISSIONS=enforce`.
A turn no person speaks in (a routine, a webhook: role `service`) never gets
`manage_pairing`, `request_login`, `propose_team_setup`, `rules_update` or
`docs_update`, whatever their tier: they need the person, could create bots
under Full access, or would write lasting instructions from untrusted text.
| Tool | Where | Before (member) | After (member) | Why |
 
| `rules_update`, `docs_update` | own (the bot's own RULES.md and docs) | admin tier (denied) | own | Own data. |
| `request_login` | own (their own vault; the value never reaches the bot) | admin tier | own | Own data. |
| `select_computer` | own (picks among their own places) | admin tier | own | Own destination. |
| `manage_pairing` | own (create: a code bound to the speaking person and capped to their scopes, on an organization server; list stays an admin route) | admin tier | own, self scope (2026-10-26: no longer host level) | Own devices. |
| `propose_team_setup` | own (a card for their own team of bots) | admin tier | own, self scope | A proposal they confirm. |
| `propose_team_memory` | org (memory the section reads) | admin tier | a member of that section, or an admin, confirms the card | The section's own people. |
| `create_bot`, `propose_bot_deletion`, `create_room`, `manage_room` | own (self scope override) | allowed at self | unchanged | Already. |
| `create_agent`, `delete_agent`, `archive_bot` | own (a temporary agent or a bot of theirs) | admin tier | own, self scope (2026-10-26); `delete_agent` on their own agent needs no grant (tool guard `ownerScoped`) | Own bots. |
| `add_mcp_server` | own (2026-10-28: the person's own servers, Settings > Connections; a command runs in their own environment) | admin tier | own, self scope; the route adds to the speaking person's own list on an organization server and refuses a person whose integrations an admin manages | Their own list. The server's shared list stays an admin's screen. |
| `request_credential` | org (server keys) | admin tier | unchanged | Organization secrets. |
| `shared_computer`, `vm_exec` | the person's own computers, the bot's own Local VM | admin tier | own, self scope (2026-10-27/28); the admin card stays for a shared VM or someone else's desktop (section 1) | See section 1. |
| `act`, `manage_settings` | any route, under the person's own rights | admin tier | own, self scope (#1269); never for a turn no person speaks in. The permission tier stays own so the call is not refused outright; since 2026-10-28 (#1098) a write through `act` on their own bots and routes is theirs; `act` on someone else's bot or a route that reaches the organization still waits for an admin card (section 1) | The route checks the person. |

(`/api/tool-grants`), the sign-in lists and the operator's profile in

sections.title: What a member needs an admin for (audit, 2026-10-19): Accepted risks
sections.text:
1. 2026-10-21, decision (told the risk): Always allow on a member's
 server command keeps the program, as on a solo bot ("Programme comme en
 solo"). Finding 1 of the review of #938: on the organization's shared
 server, a rule kept for `npm` (or `git`, `python`) on an admin's card lets
 that bot run any other line of that one program in that folder with no
 card (`npm run deploy` after `npm test`, a script the bot wrote and runs
 with `node`), with the server's rights, until the bot's owner or an admin
 removes it. Accepted as is, not narrowed. What still holds: it is for
 that one bot (never workspace-wide, never another bot of the member), in
 that one folder; a chain, a substitution or a redirect keeps the exact
 line; a held card (safety hold, `dangerouslyDisableSandbox`, Codex
 `additionalPermissions` or network, `requiresExplicitApproval`) keeps the
 whole request; the saver's right (admin, `host.shell`, or the owner's
 `host.commands`) is checked again at each use, and a security key of
 theirs still asks; an engine that reports its shell line beside no input
 (Codex, the ACP engines) is read by that line, and a card with no
 readable arguments offers no rule, so a rule never covers every command.

sections.title: What a member needs an admin for (audit, 2026-10-19): Open points
sections.text:
1. Done 2026-10-19: the four admin keys are delegable (section 4); a
 shared bot's speaker answers their own destination's card; Always allow
 rules on one's own cloud computer and Local VM, listed and revocable in
 Settings > Computer. Done 2026-10-21: permanent grants on a member's bot
 (Always allow on its server command keeps the program for that bot;
 owner and admin see and remove it in the bot's rules).
2. `shared_computer` on an organization server acts on the speaker's own
 desktop: still an admin card.
3. Hardening noted by the security review, not blocking: a link inside the
 attachments folder on the person's computer (only they can create one,
 with a command they approved), case folding on a case-sensitive macOS
 volume, matching a late request to the turn generation.

sections.title: What a member needs an admin for (audit, 2026-10-19)
sections.text:
On an organization server (Perspicax sign-in), this is everything that can
send a member, or a member's bot, to an organization admin. The rule it is
measured against (2026-10-19):
- Own destinations and own data: the person's normal level, never an
 admin. Their cloud computer (server environment, `sagax-environment`),
 their own computer and its Local VM (`sagax-desktop`), their own bots,
 threads, memory, vault and devices.
- Reserved, but delegable in Perspicax (a person or a team, through a
 permission set or "Who has what"): the shared server host, the
 organization's secrets, organization-wide data and settings, creating or
 deleting shared objects.
- Admin only, not delegable: only what would change admin rights
 themselves.
The other guardrails stay whatever the rule: the approval level of each
call, security keys (step-up), confidential conversations, the safety review,
the person's own deny and ask rules, and the audit log.
Where: own = the person's own destination or data; host = the shared
server host; org = organization data, settings or secrets;
rights = admin rights themselves.

sections.title: Bot memory
sections.text:
By default, bots keep notes between tasks. The notes are plain markdown files in a
folder on the computer running Sagax — nothing is stored anywhere else,
and you can open, edit, or delete any of it in any editor. Bot Settings →
Memory shows the same files with a gauge of how much of them actually loads,
an editor dialog that never overwrites something the bot wrote while you were typing,
and a journal of every change with one-click undo.
The Let this bot use memory switch is on by default. Turn it off while the
bot is idle to stop loading `MEMORY.md` into new turns, stop automatic recall
and upkeep, hide native memory tools, exclude memory files from `session_search`,
and stop automatic daily turn logs. Existing files remain for review. A bot
with filesystem access can still edit those files directly; use standing
instructions to forbid that when memory must stay in another source of truth.

sections.title: Bot memory: Conventions inside the files
sections.text:
The files are yours and the bot's, and any markdown is fine. The app itself
reads them as plain text and never requires a structure. The conventions the
bot follows when it writes are:
- Dated entries in `MEMORY.md`. A note the bot adds during a task is one
 bullet with its date and the chat it came from:
 `- 2026-09-10 · from chat "Follow-up" · the user prefers short replies`.
 A person's hand-written bullet without a date is just as valid.
- Superseded, not deleted. When a fact is replaced, the old bullet is
 struck through and dated rather than removed —
 `- ~~the office is in Pune~~ · superseded 2026-09-10` — so the file itself
 shows what changed. Struck lines still count against the budget; trim them
 when the file fills up.
- Daily logs under `memory/log/YYYY-MM-DD.md` are the bot's diary of what
 it did; they are never loaded into a conversation and are meant for you to
 read in the panel or in Obsidian.
- Until dates. A fact that stops being true on a known day ends with
 `· until YYYY-MM-DD` (`memory_update` takes an `until` field for it) and
 stops loading the day after.
- Topic files are ordinary markdown. A topic may begin with a small YAML
 frontmatter block — `title`, `description`, and `aliases` (other words for
 the topic, since notes are found by matching words) — which the topic index
 reads, and may link to another topic with an Obsidian-style `[[wikilink]]`,
 which the app leaves as text. A pointer in `MEMORY.md` to a topic (`see memory/clients.md`)
 is how the bot knows the topic exists.
Nothing about the panel depends on these: an older `MEMORY.md` written in
free form, or one you rewrite by hand, works the same.

sections.title: Bot memory: Dream
sections.text:
The same upkeep pass, nightly and on Tidy up now, also runs a dream.
It re-reads the memory journal and the topic files. Topic files that carry
the same facts become one file. A fact that shows up more than once is
promoted into `MEMORY.md`. A fact that is contradicted (already struck on
an earlier day) or past its `until` day moves to `memory/archive.md`.
The archive is written first: nothing is removed without a copy there.
A line struck today stays, so the tidy-up can still show what it just
replaced. The pass writes a short account at `memory/dreams/ .md`
and a journal row for every file it changes, so Undo puts that file back.
A line with no `readers` mark is left where it was and still loads.
A line marked `readers person` is private: it is never copied into
`memory/company.md`. A line marked `readers company` is a stable fact
about how this person's organization works. `memory/company.md` is not
private memory. Every bot of the same person reads it. A bot of another
member does not.
`memory/procedures.md` records what worked: an approval that was granted,
a task whose steps finished, or a correction from the person that the
next turn followed. Each note has a date and a source. Remove the line
to drop it. No model is retrained from these files.
Every upkeep change is a journal row by Memory upkeep and can be undone.
Upkeep pauses while a backup runs. The model steps need an engine with a
one-shot text call — Claude, Grok, OpenAI-compatible, Mistral and MiniMax,
and the agent engines that speak ACP (Grok CLI, Gemini, Kimi, Droid, Cursor,
OpenCode, Qwen, Hermes, Antigravity and custom ACP agents). On an ACP engine
each call starts the engine's own CLI in a fresh session of its own, never a
chat's, in an empty folder, with no MCP servers and in the ask-first approval
mode; it is refused and dropped the moment the agent asks for a tool, a file
or a permission. The text goes only to the provider the bot already uses.
On any other engine (Pi, for now) the panel says so and only the expiry and
exact-duplicate steps run.

sections.title: Bot memory: Editing
sections.text:
`MEMORY.md` and every topic file can be edited in the panel. A save carries
the hash of the text you opened; if the bot changed the file in between — it
writes with `memory_update` during a task, or with its own file tools — the
save is refused and the panel says so: *Scout changed this file while you were
editing.* Reload shows the bot's version and keeps your draft under the
editor so nothing you typed is lost; Overwrite with mine saves yours over it.
Either way the change is in the journal and can be undone.
Daily logs are read-only in the panel (they are the bot's own record) but can
be deleted. `MEMORY.md` can be emptied but never deleted — the bot expects it
to exist. Topic names are one file name under `memory/`: letters, numbers,
spaces, dots and dashes, ending in `.md`. Nothing nested, nothing starting
with a dot.
The old whole-file `PUT /api/bots/:id/memory` still works for one release; it
has no hash check, so it can overwrite what the bot just wrote. Clients should
move to `PUT /api/bots/:id/memory/file` with `expectedHash`.

sections.title: Bot memory: Group memory
sections.text:
A group chat also has a memory of its own, shared by every bot in it: the
group panel's Memory tab. Each bot of the group reads it at every turn in
that group and adds to it with `group_memory_update` when it learns something
the whole group should keep. It is separate from each bot's own memory:
nothing from a bot's private notes reaches it unless the bot writes it there
on purpose. The group's owner edits it or switches it off; the group's other
people read it. It is stored under `group-memory/ /MEMORY.md` in the
data folder, follows the same 200 lines / 24 KB budget, and is deleted with
its group.

sections.title: Bot memory: Long conversations
sections.text:
Every engine has a context window, and most of them compact their own
session when it fills: they summarize the older part in their own words,
sometimes in the middle of a task, and some say so in the chat. Sagax does
not leave that to the engine. Before a turn, it measures the thread
(the engine's own reading when it reports one, else an estimate) and folds
it itself well before the engine's own compaction point: the two latest
exchanges and the new message stay word for word, everything older becomes
a short summary written by the bot's engine.
That summary is the thread's own memory of its older turns. It is stored
with the conversation on the computer running Sagax, never shown in the
chat and never added to `MEMORY.md`. The next turn starts a fresh engine
session with the bot's full instructions, its `MEMORY.md`, recall, the
summary and the latest turns, so the bot carries on with the same goal and
the same notes. The person sees nothing: no notice, no extra message, only
the usual typing state. The full conversation stays in the app; only what
the engine reads is condensed. Editing an earlier message starts another
branch, which does not inherit a summary of turns it no longer has.
If an engine still compacts on its own (one very long task), Sagax hides
that as well and gives the engine back what its own summary may drop: the
latest turn digests, the thread summary, and the changing part of the
instructions (memory, teammates).
Asking for it with `/compact` still shows a summary card, because the
person asked. For debugging only, `context.autoCompact: false` in
`config.json` turns Sagax's own folding off, and
`context.autoCompactOffBots: [" "]` turns it off for one bot.

sections.title: Bot memory: Memory upkeep
sections.text:
Bot Settings → Memory → Memory upkeep is on for every bot unless switched
off. It keeps the notes in shape without the bot having to decide to:
- Noticing facts. When a 1:1 chat has been quiet for two minutes
 (`memory.captureQuietMs`), or after six turns, one quick model call reads those turns — the person's words and
 the bot's under different rules — beside `MEMORY.md` and the list of topic
 files, and files what is new:
- a core fact the bot needs in every conversation goes to `MEMORY.md`,
 marked `(noticed)`:
 `- 2026-09-25 · from chat "Plans" (noticed) · The person is vegetarian`;
- everything else goes to a topic file for its subject — a person, a
 project or client, food, travel — reusing an existing topic or creating
 one with a header (`title`, `aliases`: the other words someone would ask
 with), so recall finds it later.
 A fact that ends on a known day gets its `until` date; a birthday or other
 yearly date never does. Turns started by another bot or by the harness,
 rooms and failed turns are never read.
 Turns still waiting when the app quits or restarts through its normal
 shutdown are kept as their ids (never their text) in
 `memory-capture-pending.json`, at most 50 chats, and read back from the
 chat at the next start, so what was said just before quitting is still
 noticed. A crash or a forced kill skips that step (on Windows a `SIGTERM`
 is one), and those turns are not captured. A chat deleted or rewound
 meanwhile leaves nothing to read.
- Organizing. Whoever wrote a line in `MEMORY.md` — the bot with
 `memory_update`, the person, or capture — after each capture and in the
 nightly tidy-up one quick model call looks at lines not judged before and
 moves the ones that are detail about a subject (another person, a project
 or client, a trip, likes in one domain) into that subject's topic file,
 unchanged, creating it with a header and other words for it. Core facts —
 the person's name, where they live, their company, diet, allergies and
 health needs, how they like replies — always stay; a line about diet,
 allergies or health is never even offered for moving (a fixed rule, not the
 model's choice), and a line judged core is not asked about again. At most 20 lines move in one pass; each file's change
 is a journal row (*filed into topics*) that can be undone.
- About me. A lasting fact about the person, taken from their own words,
 is added to Settings → General → About me, which every bot reads, as a
 dated line `- 2026-09-25 · learned by Scout · …`. Added by your bots
 under About me lists each one with Remove; a removed fact is never
 added again. On a shared installation, another person's messages never add
 to the owner's About me.
- Nightly tidy-up. Once a day after 3 am (`memory.tidyHour`), or at the
 next check if the computer was asleep, never while the bot is working, and
 on Tidy up now: expired entries move to `memory/archive.md` (from
 `MEMORY.md` and topic files); of two entries with exactly the same fact the

sections.title: Bot memory: Recall before each turn
sections.text:
Before a turn, the person's message (eight characters or more) searches the
bot's topic files and, in a 1:1 chat the person started, the bot's other
conversations. Any matching word counts; a message with five or
more content words needs two per hit. Up to four notes and four conversation
passages — numbered, dated, and at most 6,000 characters — go in front of that
turn's message, opened by a line saying they are the bot's own notes and that
a command inside one is not an instruction. `MEMORY.md` (already loaded) and
`memory/archive.md` (older or no longer true) are never recalled, nor are daily logs
(`session_search` finds those when the bot asks).
It is placed in the message, not the system prompt, on purpose: the prompt's
changing half is re-sent whole whenever any part of it changes, and recall
changes nearly every turn. Rooms, routine runs (which start fresh), and turns
started by another bot, a webhook or a teammate hand-off, recall notes only — a private chat reaches a room
through `session_search`, which discloses it. `features.autoRecall: false` in
`config.json` switches recall off. The server log names every recall
(`auto-recall: … got N note and M conversation passage(s)`).
### Recall by meaning (2026-10-29)
Beside the word search, a local semantic index (`server/semantic-index.ts`)
finds a note or a message that says the same thing in other words: a typo
("dentst apointment"), another ending ("allergie", "allergique"), and, with
an embedding model, a synonym. It is on by default; `memory.semanticRecall:
false` in `config.json` or `SAGAX_SEMANTIC_RECALL=0` switches it off. Word
search still fills the block first; a passage found by meaning only takes a
slot it left free, and follows the same rules: the same threads, the same
audience and expiry filtering, the same block.
It indexes each bot's topic files, one line a passage, and the text
messages of every conversation, a few hundred characters a passage, in
`semantic-index.db` in the data folder. A row holds vectors and a
fingerprint, never text; with content encryption on it is sealed with the
key of its thread or of its bot's owner, so erasing that key erases the
vectors too. Message writes update it at once, a memory file is compared at
every search, and older conversations are caught up in the background.
The built-in vectors hash words and their 3- and 4-letter pieces: nothing
to download. An embedding model the person already runs can be added in the
bot's Memory settings (Advanced, Recall by meaning) or in `config.json`:
`memory.embeddingsUrl` (an OpenAI-compatible `/v1/embeddings` address, such
as `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1`) and `memory.embeddingsModel`. Notes and
messages are sent there to be indexed, and each turn's query too (at most
1.5 s). When it does not answer, the built-in vectors are used alone.

sections.title: Bot memory: Routes
sections.text:
| Method | Path | What it does |
 
| `GET` | `/api/bots/:id/memory` | Overview: gauge numbers, topic and log lists, the folder path. |
| `GET` | `/api/bots/:id/memory/file?path=` | One file's text and hash (`MEMORY.md`, `memory/ .md`, `memory/log/ .md`). |
| `PUT` | `/api/bots/:id/memory/file` | `{ path, text, expectedHash? }` — `409` with the current text when the hash no longer matches. |
| `DELETE` | `/api/bots/:id/memory/file?path=` | Removes a topic or log; refuses `MEMORY.md`. |
| `GET` | `/api/bots/:id/memory/journal?limit=` | Recent changes, newest first. |
| `POST` | `/api/bots/:id/memory/journal/:entryId/revert` | Puts the file back to that row's earlier text. |
| `POST` | `/api/bots/:id/memory/open` | `{ target: "obsidian" \| "folder" }` — opens the folder on this computer; loopback only. |
| `GET` | `/api/bots/:id/memory/upkeep` | Whether upkeep is on, whether the engine can run the model steps, and the last tidy-up and capture. |
| `POST` | `/api/bots/:id/memory/tidy` | Runs the tidy-up now (`409` when upkeep is switched off) and returns its report. |
| `GET` | `/api/profile/learned` | Facts bots added to About me on their own, newest first. |
| `POST` | `/api/profile/learned/:id/remove` | Takes that line out of About me; the fact is never added again. |
All of them need the owner (admin) session, like the other bot-settings routes.

sections.title: Bot memory: The journal
sections.text:
Every change to a memory file that the app can see is recorded — yours from
the panel, the bot's during a task, an import, an undo — in
`~/.sagax/memory-journal/ .ndjson`. It lives *outside* the
workspace on purpose: the bot's file tools point at the workspace, and a
record the bot could edit would not be a record.
Each row says who (bot, person, or import), how (in Settings, during a task,
from which chat, changed outside the app, undo), which file, when, the
before/after hashes, a short diff, and the full earlier text so Undo can put
the file back without anything else. Undo is itself a journaled change, so it
can be undone in turn. Two kinds of row cannot be undone and say so: one
whose earlier text contained a credential (the stored copy is redacted, and
restoring it would write the redaction marker into the bot's memory), and one
whose earlier text was too large to keep.
Bot writes are caught at the turn boundary. When a turn starts, the app notes
what every memory file says; when the turn ends, whatever differs is recorded
as the bot's work for that chat. A file that changed between turns — edited in
Obsidian, say — is recorded as yours, *changed outside the app*. Two of the
same bot's threads running at once are both diffed; a change lands under
whichever thread finished first. Journaling never fails a turn: a row that
cannot be written is logged and dropped.

sections.title: Bot memory: What a bot knows about its other conversations
sections.text:
A bot's 1:1 chats and its rooms are separate conversations, and its memory
holds only what stays true — so on its own, a bot answering in a room had no
idea what it did in its 1:1 an hour earlier, and a morning standup ended in
guesses. Three things close that gap without attaching transcripts:
- The recent-work brief. Every turn's system prompt, 1:1 or room, carries
 a short block: the newest thing the bot said in each of its *other*
 conversations over the last two days — `today 09:05 · 1:1 with Milind ·
 "Invoice reconciliation" · you said: "Sent the three flagged invoices…"`.
 At most ten lines and about 350 tokens; the current conversation is not
 listed. When a brief in a room names a private 1:1 chat, the room gets a
 chip — *Lead's recent-work brief covers 1 private chat with you* — once per
 chat, the same rule as recalled messages.
- One log line per finished turn when memory is on. The harness appends what the bot said
 last, the tools it used, and whether the turn failed to
 `memory/log/YYYY-MM-DD.md`, sourced to the chat or room. The log is never
 loaded into a prompt; `session_search` finds it.
- Recall by time. `session_search` takes `since` (`"24h"`, `"3d"`,
 `"yesterday"`, or a date) and `until`, with or without words, and covers
 the rooms the bot is a member of as well as its 1:1 tasks. "What happened
 since yesterday's standup" needs no keyword. Hits name the room or task
 they came from; a private chat recalled into a room is marked, and the
 room is told.
A daily standup is then a room routine: the chief asks, each member answers
from its brief and pulls detail with `session_search since`, and what was
agreed shows up in each member's next 1:1 brief.

sections.title: Bot memory: What loads, and the budget
sections.text:
At the start of every turn the first 200 lines or 24 KB of `MEMORY.md`,
whichever cuts first, are placed into the bot's system prompt. Nothing past
that line loads, and the bot is only told that the file was cut off. Topic files
and daily logs are never loaded automatically; the bot reads a topic file with
its file tools when it decides it needs it, and logs are for you.
The gauge at the top of the Memory panel is that rule made visible: lines and
size against the budget, amber from 80%, red once anything stops loading —
with the count of lines that are not being loaded, and always the plain
sentence *only the first 200 lines load each turn*.
`MEMORY.md` never fills up. Every write that goes through the harness
(`memory_update`, and capture) keeps the file within the budget in the same
step: when the new entry would push it past, the oldest dated entries move to
`memory/archive.md` — struck-through ones first, then expired ones, then the
oldest live ones — each marked `· moved `. An entry moves whole, with
the lines indented under it (a code block) or, in older entries, the code block
right below it. The archive is written before
`MEMORY.md`, so a line is never out of one without already being in the other,
and `session_search` still finds it. Lines you wrote by hand (no date), health
and safety facts, and the entry just written never move. The bot is told which
entries moved (the first few, and how many), so it can add back anything that
should stay loaded. One entry is at most 1,000 characters and 20 lines, so a
single note cannot push the rest out. The gauge
can only go red when the lines that never move fill the budget by themselves
(or a bot edited the file with its own file tools): then the entry is still
saved, and the bot asks you to trim `MEMORY.md`.
Both limits are `MEMORY_MAX_LINES` and `MEMORY_MAX_BYTES` in
`server/workspace.ts`; the panel, the loader, and the bot's prompt all read the
same two constants.
Two more things load with it:
- Expired notes stay out. An entry that ends in `· until 2026-09-28` stops
 loading the day after that date. The file keeps it (the gauge still counts
 it) until the tidy-up or a person moves it.
- The topic index. Every `memory/ .md` is listed by name under the
 memory block, with its `title`, `description` and `aliases` when the file
 starts with frontmatter — at most 40 topics or 2,000 characters. The files
 themselves still load only when the bot reads them.

sections.title: Bot memory: Where it lives
sections.text:
The folder is the bot's private workspace: the directory its file tools work in
when it has no project folder set. It is created the first time the bot runs a
turn. Bot Settings opens a file in an editor dialog. The files stay plain
markdown on the computer running Sagax, so any editor on that computer can
open the same folder.
Files are written with owner-only permissions (`0600`), atomically (a crash
mid-write leaves the old file intact, never a torn one), and anything that
looks like a credential — API keys, tokens, `password: …` lines, private key
blocks — is replaced with `«redacted N chars»` before it reaches disk. A bot
that helpfully "remembers" a key it read from a `.env` does not get to keep it.

sections.title: Seen by and reactions on messages: Bot reactions
sections.text:
Bots get two agents tools (`server/drivers/agents-catalog.ts`), in every
engine that mounts the agents tools (Claude, Codex, Grok, Gemini, pi, local
models through the chat tools, and the others) and in room turns alike:
- `react_to_message({ message_id?, emoji })`: `message_id` defaults to the
 message the bot is answering (the newest chat line someone else wrote in
 the turn's thread); `emoji` is one of the short list `BOT_REACTIONS`
 (`shared/reactions.ts`): 👍 noted, ✅ done, 👀 looking into it, ❤️ or 🙏
 for a thank-you, 🎉 good news, 😂 a joke. The schema names it as an `enum`
 and the route refuses anything else (`reaction_emoji`); the variation
 selector is ignored, so "❤" is stored as "❤️". A person's own picker is
 not limited.
- `remove_reaction({ message_id?, emoji? })`: takes back the bot's own.
The harness route `/api/internal/reaction` records the bot as the actor
(`bot: `, its name), refuses the bot's own messages (`reaction_own`),
is idempotent (the same emoji twice changes nothing), keeps one reaction per
bot per message (`reaction_one`; remove first to change it), allows three
adds per turn (`reaction_budget`), and writes no message. It acts only on the
turn's own thread, so a confidential thread's reaction stays in it. On a live
voice call the tools are not shown, the guidance is left out and an add is
refused (`reaction_call`): the bot answers by voice.
When to react (`REACTION_PROMPT`, its own part of the system prompt, the maintainer
2026-10-18): sparingly, most messages get none; never instead of an answer
the person needs (a question gets words); never a reaction and a sentence
that says the same thing. A plain "thanks" or "ok" gets ❤️ or 👍 and no
text; a small task done gets ✅ instead of a "Done" sentence. A turn that
only reacts writes no reply bubble, and a reply that only repeats the
reaction placed in the same turn on the message it answers (that emoji
alone, or an aside such as "*(no further text needed)*") is not written
either (`echoesOwnReaction`, `server/index.ts`); a real sentence, even in
parentheses, or a reaction from an earlier turn keeps the reply.
The chip looks like a person's: emoji and count, the bot's mascot and name
in the tooltip (desktop) or the "who reacted" sheet (iOS). Like every
reaction it is a quiet `message.patch`: no notification, no unread.

sections.title: Seen by and reactions on messages: Reactions
sections.text:
A message carries `reactions: [{ emoji, actors: [{ id, kind, name }], at }]`
(`shared/reactions.ts`): one entry per emoji, `kind` is `person` or `bot`,
`at` is when the emoji first landed (it orders the chips). Messages stored
with the older `{ emoji, by }` entries are read through `normalizeReactions`
and rewritten on their first change.
`POST /api/threads/ /messages/ /reactions` with
`{ emoji }` toggles the caller's own reaction (`mode: "add" | "remove"` is
accepted too). Rules:
- The caller is always the actor; a body naming someone else is ignored.
- Who may call it is who may read the thread: a hidden bot, thread or room
 is 404, a conversation between two people is the pair's only, a read-only
 room member may react.
- `emoji` must be one emoji sequence (400 `reaction_emoji`); only chat
 messages take one (400 `reaction_kind`); 24 distinct emojis per message at
 most (409 `reaction_full`).
- The change is a persisted message patch, sent live as `message.patch` to
 everyone who sees the thread. It is quiet: no notification, no unread.
In the app (`src/components/Reactions.tsx`): a smiley in the message's hover
bar opens a picker with 👍 ❤️ 😂 🎉 👀 🙏 ✅ ❌ and a search in a small
built-in emoji set (`src/lib/emoji-list.ts`); the "…" menu starts with "Add
reaction" (E). Chips under the message show the emoji and the count,
highlighted when the viewer reacted; a click toggles the viewer's own; hover
or focus lists who reacted, a bot with its mascot.

sections.title: Seen by and reactions on messages: Seen by
sections.text:
Every thread keeps one read position per participant: `{ messageId, at }`
keyed by the person's principal id or `bot: `
(`server/read-receipts.ts`, table `thread_reads`). A person's position moves
when their focused app shows a message (`POST /api/threads/ /read`), a
bot's when its turn consumed the message. Positions only move forward and are
never written to the transcript.
Under a message, `SeenByRow` (`src/components/SeenBy.tsx`) shows:
- the muted label "Seen by" (fr "Vu par", pt-br "Visto por");
- the avatars of the people and bots who have read up to it, oldest first,
 stacked, five at most, then "+N";
- on hover or keyboard focus of an avatar, a tooltip with the name and the
 read time ("Sam Taylor · 2:46 PM"); the same words are its aria-label.
Each reader appears once, under the last message they have seen that they
did not write. A room shows everyone; a 1:1 with a bot shows the bot until it
answers. The viewer is never shown. "Send read receipts" off still hides a
person both ways in a conversation between two people.

sections.title: Seen by and reactions on messages
sections.text:
Status: 2026-10-18. Applies to a 1:1 with a bot, a room, and a conversation
between two people, on a solo server and an organization server alike.

sections.text:
