on port 8810, so do not expose it from a public server. It ships only in a
git checkout: the Docker image does not contain it.
 `node --experimental-strip-types companion/src/index.ts`

sections.title: Self-hosting the Sagax server: What works headless (and what doesn't)
sections.text:
Runs fully on a server:
- every engine CLI (Claude, Codex, Grok, custom ACP engines — install and
 log them in on the server)
- chats, rooms, bot-to-bot coordination, routines (they keep running with
 every laptop on the planet closed — this is the point)
- connected apps / custom MCP servers, webhooks, Company Brain
- computer use on cloud or container computers (the bot's computer runs
 server-side anyway)
- text-to-speech (with a key), the web UI (the server serves it itself)
- a browser for bots, once the engine is installed on the server
 (`pnpm omb browser install`, or nothing to do in the Docker image,
 which ships it): each bot gets its own isolated, persistent session.
 Watching it live from the app is the next step (docs/plans/browser-engine.md).
Desktop-only for now (needs the Mac/Linux app):
- dictation/voice, controlling the host desktop

sections.title: Tout est modifiable par les bots (sagax_settings): Comment ça marche
sections.text:
- Outil : `sagax_settings` (`action` list, get ou set ; `key`, `target`,
 `value`). `list` (avec `family`) donne les clés : rien n'est figé dans
 l'invite du bot.
- Droits : la route de l'écran est rejouée avec la session de la personne
 (`server/bot-act.ts`). Un membre ne peut pas faire par bot ce qu'il ne
 peut pas faire à la main : la route répond son refus, que le bot relaie.
- Décision (`shared/settings-actions-policy.ts`), dans l'ordre :
 1. une classe que la personne protège par clé de sécurité : carte signée ;
 2. autrui, organisation : carte, à tout niveau, Full compris (comme un
 paiement) ; secret, en lot et suppression aussi, sauf quand ils ne
 touchent que l'environnement de la personne (le niveau décide) ;
 3. pas le travail du propriétaire (la personne ne possède pas le bot qui
 parle ou ce qui change) : carte ;
 4. bot à Ask ou Auto-accept edits : carte ;
 5. élargit les droits (niveau d'approbation, mode du propriétaire,
 règle allow, valeurs par défaut des nouveaux bots, outils, applis ou
 coéquipiers du bot qui parle lui-même, où travaillent les bots) :
 un niveau est appliqué jusqu'à celui du bot qui parle, jamais Full ni
 Custom sans carte ; le reste demande la carte ;
 6. sinon appliqué tout de suite.
- Secrets (#1545, 2026-10-28) : le bot ne voit jamais la valeur d'un secret.
 Il pose, remplace ou utilise un secret par référence :
 `{"$secret": "generate", "length": 32}` (fait par le serveur) ou
 `{"$secret": "copy", "from": , "field":
 "password"}` (pris dans le coffre de la personne), résolus sur le serveur
 juste avant la route ; la carte et le journal gardent la référence. Les
 secrets de la personne (coffre, clés, 1Password, portefeuilles, secrets
 de webhook) suivent le niveau du bot comme le reste de son
 environnement ; les secrets de l'organisation gardent sa carte.
- Moteurs d'un serveur d'organisation (#1545, 2026-10-28) : ajouter un
 compte, installer, vérifier de nouveau, mettre Claude Code à jour,
 renommer et libérer l'espace ne touchent que la personne : le niveau du
 bot décide (plus de carte en Full pour un admin). Déconnecter, retirer, ou
 changer le programme, le dossier ou les outils d'un moteur qu'un bot d'une
 autre personne, ou le modèle par défaut de l'organisation, utilise (autrui)
 garde la carte à tout niveau : le travail des autres s'arrêterait.
- Demande de la personne au bot principal (2026-10-20) : quand le bot
 principal de la personne fait le changement parce qu'elle l'a demandé
 dans son message du tour (`quote`, ses propres mots, vérifiés dans ce
 message par `shared/primary-request.ts`), les règles 4 et 5 ne
 s'appliquent pas et une suppression passe aussi : niveaux d'approbation,
 règles « toujours permettre » et leur retrait, sur n'importe quel bot de
 la personne. Une clé de sécurité choisie, un secret, autrui, un lot et
 l'organisation gardent la carte. Full compris sur un serveur
 d'organisation (2026-10-20), aux règles de la route : l'organisation

sections.title: Tout est modifiable par les bots (sagax_settings): Console Perspicax (exposée à Sagax)

sections.title: Single stream orchestration (thread mode off): Design
sections.text:
### Data model: segments are threads
A bot's stream is its threads that a person had with it, oldest first
(`shared/single-stream.ts`, `isStreamSegment`, `streamSegments`): never a
routine run, a hidden AI-client conversation, a confidential thread, a
bot-opened thread or a parallel task. Nothing is copied or moved. Turning
threads back on shows the same segments as threads; turning them off again
merges them. That is the migration: existing threads of a bot appear in the
stream in chronological order with no data written, fully reversible.
"New topic" creates a thread (`POST /api/bots/:id/tasks { stream: true }`):
a fresh engine context. The person sees a divider ("Nouveau sujet" / "New
topic") in the same stream, never a new place.
### Server orchestration (`server/single-stream.ts`)
- Marker. A send from a client with threads off carries `singleStream:
 true` (`singleStreamTurnField`); the server marks the thread
 `streamSegment: true` (server-private, never on the wire). A send with
 `false` clears it, so thread mode on is unchanged. A send that says
 nothing (older build, phone, relay) leaves it as it is. A confidential,
 hidden, routine, parallel or bot-opened thread is never marked;
 `makeTaskConfidential` drops the mark and the digest.
- Digest. A person's turn in a marked segment (no teammate, routine,
 webhook, peer ask or call) gets an "Earlier topics" block in the volatile
 half of its system prompt: one entry per other segment of the same
 person's stream, newest first, with a digest (summary, decisions, open
 items, files and links) for the newest 8 and a one-line index (title,
 date, id) for the next 40, then a count. Those topics leave the
 recent-work brief of that turn, so nothing is said twice.
- Cost. Per segment digest at most 900 chars; whole block at most 6,000
 chars (about 1,500 tokens), logged on every stream turn
 (`[stream] ... chars (~N tokens)`). A digest is extractive by default
 (first ask, latest ask and answer, quoted facts and identifiers from
 `keyFacts`, files and links: free, never invents) and cached in memory
 per segment change. The bot's own engine writes a model digest (the
 compaction path's `generateText`, 20 s bound, fallback to extractive) at
 most once per stream turn, in the background, for the newest stale
 segment, and right when a new topic closes the previous one. It is stored
 on that segment (`segmentDigest`, server-private, anchored to its newest
 message).
- Recall on demand. `recall_topic` (agents MCP, read-only,
 `topics:recall` permission) lists the stream's topics or returns one
 topic's transcript in 12,000-char pages, newest page first, paging back
 with `before`. It is offered only in a stream turn
 (`SAGAX_SINGLE_STREAM`), so a thread-mode catalog is unchanged, and its
 route (`/api/internal/recall-topic`) re-checks: depth 0, the calling
 thread is a marked segment, the topic is one of `streamCandidates`.
 Anything else reads as missing.
### Privacy boundaries

sections.title: Single stream orchestration (thread mode off): Fresh topic on return (2026-10-18)
sections.text:
the decision: coming back to a bot lands on a new, empty topic, with the
earlier ones folded behind one "Earlier topics" line, and the bot keeps all
of it (digest, `recall_topic`). The rule (`shared/fresh-topic.ts`, same
cases on iOS): a fresh topic when the topic the bot opens to is quiet past
the threshold (default 4 h, Settings > Appearance > Conversation) or the
person was away from the bot or the app longer than that; never over a
running turn, a waiting approval or question, an unread answer, teammates
working or queued messages; a person who left a moment ago stays where they
were. The topic is a client draft until its first message
(`POST .../tasks { stream: true }`, then the send). Notifications, links and
search hits open their own topic. Section "Fresh topic on return" in
`AGENTS.md` has the full rules and tests.
Release note text:
- FR : « Retour dans un chat : un sujet neuf. Après 4 h d'absence ou de
 silence (réglable dans Réglages > Apparence > Conversation), revenir à un
 bot ouvre un nouveau sujet vide ; le bot garde tout l'historique et les
 sujets précédents restent à un clic, sous « Sujets précédents ». »
- EN: "Coming back opens a fresh topic. After 4 h away or quiet (Settings >
 Appearance > Conversation), coming back to a bot opens a new, empty topic;
 the bot keeps the whole history and earlier topics stay one click away,
 under Earlier topics."

sections.title: Single stream orchestration (thread mode off): One conversation: THE rule (2026-10-28)
sections.text:
After several fixes that did not hold (#719, #722, #763, #975, #1026, #1028,
#1116, #1162, #1207, #1435), the maintainer asked for the reference design's
experience once and for all: with threads hidden a bot is ONE continuous
conversation, on every device. The reference design keeps exactly one
transcript per bot (its "threads" are tasks opened beside it; the only
"new" is "Reset this conversation"); routines, calls, notifications and
other devices all write into that one transcript, in time order, and the
history loads upward.
Why the fixes did not hold: three clients had three definitions of "the
conversation" (the server's `mainThread`: the thread the person last wrote
in; the desktop's `streamHomeThread`: the newest segment with content; the
phone: the thread last opened on that device), and each path that creates or
opens a thread (routines, webhooks, send_prompt, peers, voice, notifications,
search, activity rows, bot commands, continuation, incidents) had a chooser
of its own. Every new feature added one more.
Now there is one rule, in one file, `shared/single-stream.ts`:
`conversationThread(tasks)` = the newest open segment of the person's
stream. A segment is a conversation a person had with the bot: never a
routine run, a results thread, a hidden AI-client conversation, a
confidential thread, a bot-opened thread, a parallel task, an archived or a
closed thread. The cases are `shared/single-stream.vectors.json`, run by the
TypeScript test and by the phone's `SingleStreamTests.swift`.
Who reads it:
- Server, `conversationThreadFor(bot, person)` (`server/index.ts`): the
 only chooser. `WireBot.mainThreadId` (per viewer on an organization
 server), a routine's report (`resolveResultsThread`, and a run whose
 destination is gone), a webhook's post, `send_prompt` and `sagax_send`,
 `ask_bot` and `delegate_bot` (`peerThreadFor`), a call that names no
 thread, a send that names no thread, the Primary Bot's incident answer
 (mirrored as its message into its conversation at the end of its "Team
 incidents" turn, with the link to that thread). A webhook's run works in
 its own task like a scheduled run (it used to take the live chat: a new
 topic per event). A run's task is tagged `routineRunId` at creation. A
 turn continuation is a bot-opened job. A legacy " · Results" thread
 is marked `routineResults` when met. "New topic" over a topic nobody wrote
 in yet answers with that topic (no empty topics pile up, on any device).
- Desktop: `botOpensTo` reads `mainThreadId` first, then the same rule over
 the window's tasks. `openBotThread` is the one gate for every way into a
 thread: an earlier topic scrolls the conversation back to it
 (`focusMessage` with `segment`), a thread outside the stream opens beside
 it (`SideThreadPanel`), never in its place. The window follows the
 conversation (a newer topic from another device, a reconnect). `newTask`
 creates a stream topic. `ChatView` draws one timeline: the earlier topics

sections.title: Single stream orchestration (thread mode off): Parallel tasks and agent work stay in the stream (2026-10-26, #1145, #1170)
sections.text:
- A parallel task asked from any segment of the stream gets no row under
 the bot with threads hidden (`threadsWhenTreeHidden`,
 `parallelTaskInStream`). Its approvals join the composer's approval box
 and its questions are answered above the composer, each sent to the
 task's own thread (`useParallelCards`), so the person never leaves the
 conversation. Its answer is posted in the conversation, as before. With
 threads shown, every thread stays listed and reachable.
- Work a bot sends over the agent API (`send_prompt`) lands in the bot's
 single chat with that person, folded into one exchange chip (`peerAsk`;
 `src/lib/bot-exchange.ts`). A person's AI client is another agent
 (2026-10-29): its sends stay out of the stream, in its own conversation
 with the bot, like a peer's (`shared/agent-conversation.ts`).

sections.title: Single stream orchestration (thread mode off): Tests
sections.text:
- `shared/single-stream.test.ts`: segment rule and order, exclusions.
- `server/single-stream.test.ts`: digest extraction and caps, model digest
 fallback and timeout, composed block budget, recall pages, candidates.
- `server/drivers/agents-catalog-single-stream.test.ts`: the tool appears
 only in a stream turn and is a read.
- `server/single-stream.e2e.test.ts`: marker, new topic, digest in the
 prompt, background model digest, `recall_topic` list and read, refusal of
 a confidential topic, hidden and confidential exclusions, thread mode on
 unchanged, a topic made confidential later.
- `server/org-private-threads.e2e.test.ts` PT-5: per-person streams on a
 shared bot.
- `src/lib/single-stream.test.ts`, `src/lib/use-segment-transcript.test.ts`,
 `src/components/ChatView.stream.test.ts` (earlier topic above the live one,
 dividers, New topic, confidential alone, threads on unchanged, default),
 `src/state/notification-open.test.ts` (notification and search hit into an
 earlier topic), `src/lib/thread-preferences.test.ts` (default off, "1"
 kept).

sections.title: Single stream orchestration (thread mode off): What exists today (investigation, 2026-10-17)
sections.text:
- Thread mode is Settings > Appearance > Show threads, the renderer key
 `omb-show-threads` (`src/lib/thread-preferences.ts`, `SHOW_THREADS_DEFAULT
 = true`; synced on an organization server through `/api/me/preferences`,
 `shared/user-preferences.ts`). Unset is on; the switch writes "1" or "0",
 so an explicit choice is distinguishable from the default. iOS keeps its
 own fallback (`ios/App/Features/Sidebar/HomeMenus.swift`,
 `SidebarHiddenViews.swift`).
- Threads off today hides every thread control: no picker in the header
 (`TaskPicker` returns null), no "new thread" in the sidebar row or bot menu,
 `ComposeToPicker` opens the existing chat. There is no "new chat" while
 threads are off; ⌘N opens the compose picker. Threads still get created
 behind the scenes (an older build, another device, a teammate, a bot's
 `start_thread`, a routine, an AI client's hidden conversation). The app
 opens the bot's main thread (`server/main-thread.ts`, the open thread the
 person last wrote in) and, when a deep link or notification lands on
 another one, shows "Back to conversation" (`ThreadsOffReturnLink`,
 `src/components/thread-home.ts`). That is the "where did it go" problem.
- the reference design keeps one continuous conversation per bot; sub-agent work
 (Sagax: hidden AI-client conversations, #291; parallel tasks) stays out of
 the chat and reports back into it.
- Context today: Sagax folds a long thread itself
 (`compactConversation`, `server/context-budget.ts`,
 `server/compaction-summary.ts`): two latest exchanges verbatim, the rest
 summarized by the engine's tool-free `generateText` with a deterministic,
 extractive fallback, stored on the task (`contextSummaries`, server-private).
 Every 1:1 turn also carries automatic recall (`server/recall.ts`, FTS
 passages from memory and the person's other conversations, 6,000 chars),
 a recent-work brief (`server/recent-work.ts`, one line per other
 conversation over 48 h, 1,400 chars) and `session_search` /
 `session_read` on demand. All of them are narrowed by
 `privateRecallFilter` (confidential threads feed nothing; on an
 organization server, the same person's threads only).
- Sub-agents and side work: parallel tasks (`parallelOf`, a card and a
 reply in the asking conversation), `start_thread` (bot-opened jobs,
 `openedBy`), the side thread column ("Ouvrir à côté",
 `src/lib/side-thread.ts`), hidden AI-client conversations.

sections.title: Sharing a whole team: Adding a shared team
sections.text:
Import is additive: everything becomes new records in a new team (numbered if
the name is taken). Nothing in the file can change a bot, group chat or team
you already have.
- Bots start on Ask, with no connected-app access and the installation's
 default model. A suggested approval level in the file is recorded, never
 applied.
- Skills arrive switched off; routines arrive paused.
- Each connection becomes a new MCP server that is switched off with
 empty values, named after the connection (`crm`, or `crm-2` when `crm` is
 already taken, so it can never pick up credentials you already have). Your
 organization's MCP policy still applies; a refused connection is listed and
 the rest of the team is added. Finish connections in Plugins → MCP
 servers.
- Starter notes are written once, through the normal memory writer.
- Preset bots in a file appear in New bot under Imported presets; a
 bot made from one gets the preset's skills switched off
 (presets.md).
- A preset file (skills and presets, no bots) adds its presets to New bot and
 nothing else. A file with only skills has nothing to add here and is
 refused with a pointer to the organization shelf (Templates → From
 {Organization}, see org-library.md).
If any step fails, everything the import created is removed again.

sections.title: Sharing a whole team
sections.text:
Share team… saves one team as a single file (` - .openmaus.json`).
Someone else adds it in Templates → Import, or an organization uploads it
in Admin → Packages and its desktops add it from Templates → From
{Organization} (org-library.md). Open it from the team's menu in the sidebar (right-click
the team name), or from Templates → Share.

sections.title: Sharing a whole team: The file format
sections.text:
`openmaus.package` version 2, defined in `shared/package-format.ts`, the one
module the app, the import preview and Admin all validate with. It still
reads version 1 files (JSON and the BotMRR Markdown playbook). Older apps
refuse version 2 files with their existing "not supported" message; Admin can
produce a version 1 download for them. A file is at most 4 MB. Example files
and their expected hashes live in `shared/package-fixtures/`.
The HTTP route is `POST /api/teams/export` with
`{"format":"package","version":2,"team":"Sales desk"}` (admin scope). Optional
fields: `name`, `tagline`, `summary`, `release`, `notes`, `skills` (`"all"` or
names), `includeMemory` (default `false` over the API), `avatars` (data URLs
by bot id) and `dryRun` (count without recording keys). The response is
`{document, filename, redacted, skipped, summary, choices}`. With
`skills: "all"` the export puts in the skills that fit and lists the rest in
`skipped`; a list of names is shared exactly or refused. Every `400` from a
version 2 body also carries `choices: {skills}` (every skill name on the
team's bots), so a client can offer a different choice. `includeDefaultsPreset:
true` adds the New bot defaults preset, and `kind: "library"` (instead of
`team`) saves a preset file; both are described in presets.md.
A body without `version: 2` keeps the original whole-installation Markdown
export.

sections.title: Sharing a whole team: Versions and identity
sections.text:
The first time a team is shared it gets a package id (from its name) and each
bot, group chat and routine gets a key. Later shares of the same team reuse
them, even after renaming the team or anything in it, and suggest the next
version (1.0.0, then 1.0.1, …). A team first added from a shared file keeps
that file's package id and bot keys, so "import the published release, edit,
share again" produces the next release of the same package. The record lives
in `published-teams.json` in the data folder.

sections.title: Sharing a whole team: What goes in the file
sections.text:
- Bots. Each bot's name, title and description, its standing instructions,
 its colour and mascot, and its picture (downscaled to at most 256 × 256 and
 64 KB; the dialog stops adding pictures after about 2 MB of them).
- Skills. All skills on the team's bots by default, or the ones you tick.
 Only the `SKILL.md` text travels, never scripts or other files. A file
 holds at most 30 skills per bot and 60 per team, and one skill per name.
 When you have not chosen, the dialog puts in what fits (switched-on skills
 first) and lists the rest under Left out, including a name two bots
 hold with different content. The skill boxes then start ticked on what
 went in, less any skill a bot had to leave out over its 30 (even when
 another bot's copy went in), so unticking any box is always a choice that
 fits. When you tick more than fits, it says why and keeps every skill box
 so you can change the choice.
- Playbooks, group chats (members and who answers by default) and the
 team's shared instructions.
- Routines, including group chat goals. They always arrive paused.
- The Chief of Staff.
- Connections. For each remote MCP server a bot uses: its address and the
 names of the values it needs (for example `Authorization`). The values
 themselves never travel. Hosted servers often keep their key in the address
 itself, so an address loses any sign-in part and `#fragment`, and keeps its
 query and `;matrix` parameter names with the values emptied (`?key=`,
 `;key=`, and `key=` inside a path segment). Any path segment, parameter
 name or subdomain label (anything left of the last two host labels) that
 looks like a key is replaced with `redacted`. A part looks like a key when,
 after `%XX` escapes are decoded, it holds a run of 16 or more letters,
 digits, `-` or `_` that mixes letters and digits, or 24 or more letters or
 digits in a row, such as a token, a hex key or a server id. Words joined by
 hyphens with a short number, such as `github-mcp-server-2024`, stay as
 they are. The rule is deliberately broad, so the dialog lists each
 connection's full address before you save and names any address it
 changed.
- Starter notes. Each bot's `MEMORY.md` and topic notes. Include
 starter notes is ticked, because a team is shared whole; untick it if the
 notes hold private details about you. Daily logs never go in.
- Connector requirements (which connected apps the team expects), as
 labels only.
- Your New bot defaults as a preset, only when you tick Include my New
 bot defaults as a preset: their name, look, standing instructions, skills
 and (with starter notes) notes, never their model, folder, computer,
 approval level or connected apps. See presets.md.

sections.title: Sharing a whole team: What never goes in the file
sections.text:
Chat history, keys and passwords, model choices, computers, and who can see
each bot. The file format has no field for any of them. Local MCP servers
that run a command on this computer are left out, as are routine attachments.
Text can still contain a secret someone typed into it. Before the file is
written, every text part is checked with the same detectors the app uses for
its logs. Anything that looks like a key or password is replaced with a
marker, and the dialog lists which parts were changed. The Admin upload runs
the same check again and refuses a file that still contains one.
The dialog shows, before you save, exactly what the file holds (counted by the
server from the same export), and afterwards what was removed or left out.
There is no confirmation step: Save file is the decision.

sections.title: In-chat terminal: destinations: Destinations
sections.text:
A destination (`TerminalResource`) is a place a person may open the
terminal on. Two kinds (`scope`):
| Provider | Scope | What it is | Who may open it |
 
| `sandbox` | personal | The person's cloud computer (their server environment: Docker or, on a hosted organization server, Kubernetes through the provisioner) | The person, for their own bot (an admin: from any bot) |
| `local-vm` | personal | Organization: the Local VM on the person's computer, through their Sagax app. Solo: this server's Local VM of the bot | Same |
| `desktop` | personal | "Cet ordinateur". Organization: the person's computer through their Sagax app, when their Where bots work is their computer or the bot works there. Solo: this computer, only when the server is the Sagax app on it | Same |
| `ssh`, `unraid` | server | A host of the server from `config.json` (`terminalShell.hosts[]`, `terminalShell.unraidSshAlias`, `SAGAX_UNRAID_SSH_ALIAS`, `vps.sshAlias`) | Organization admins (a solo server's operator) |
| `test` | server | Vitest echo shell (`SAGAX_TERMINAL_TEST=1`) | Same |
A personal destination has the single id `mine`: it always means the
environment of the person who lists or opens it, so a card answered by
someone else opens THEIR environment under THEIR rights, never the owner's.

sections.title: In-chat terminal: destinations: How each destination runs
sections.text:
| Destination | Path |
 
| `sandbox` | The provisioner's `/v1/sandboxes/ /tty` upgrade (signed, size in the URL): `docker exec` with a TTY (`sandboxd-docker.ts execTty`) or the Kubernetes exec API with `tty=true` and its resize channel (`server/sandboxd-k8s/sandboxd-k8s-client.ts execTty`), as the sandbox user in `/workspace`. Keystrokes and resizes are framed (`server/sandbox-tty-frames.ts`). |
| `local-vm`, `desktop` (organization) | A bridge operation (`terminal_open`, `vm_terminal_open`) with a one-time ticket; the app connects back (`GET /api/desktop-bridge/ /terminal/ `, session cookie + bridge secret, same person) and runs the shell (`electron/desktop-terminal.mjs`): the login shell, or `docker exec -it -u cua` into the Local VM (`electron/local-vm.mjs terminalCommand`, which holds the VM against its idle stop). |
| `local-vm`, `desktop` (solo), `ssh`, `unraid` | A local PTY from the system's `script` command (`electron/script-pty.mjs`): `docker exec -it -u cua`, the login shell, `ssh -tt`. |
The widget sends keystrokes as binary WebSocket frames and its size as a
text frame `{"type":"resize","cols":..,"rows":..}`; every destination
follows the size.

sections.title: In-chat terminal: destinations
sections.text:
Sagax has one interactive terminal: the one in the conversation. There is no
terminal button or menu entry. The bot proposes it as a card when it is
useful (the person wants to connect to a machine, to debug live, or a step
needs their own typing); the person approves it, and an xterm opens in the
thread. Credentials and connection strings never reach the client.

sections.title: In-chat terminal: destinations: Security and audit
sections.text:
- Approval card required; nothing runs before the allow. The bot cannot type
 unless the person turns on bot input.
- The person's rights are checked on list, on offer, and again at open.
- WebSocket attach uses the authenticated upgrade path (voice mode, desktop
 viewer). Closing the widget ends the session; 15 minute idle close; 3 live
 sessions per person.
- `terminal-sessions.jsonl` (DATA_DIR): `session.requested`,
 `session.destination` (the person changed the destination),
 `session.refused`, `session.denied`, `session.opened`, `session.ended`,
 each with the person, bot, conversation and destination. A terminal on
 the person's computer is also in their Computer tab's activity
 (`desktop-bridge-audit.jsonl`); the Kubernetes provisioner audits
 `sandbox.tty`.

sections.title: In-chat terminal: destinations: The bot's tools
sections.text:
- `list_terminal_resources`: what this person may open here, and the default
 (where the bot works now).
- `offer_shell_terminal { reason, provider?, resource_id? }`: stages the card.
 Without a destination, the card proposes where the bot works (its
 Workspace, or the place Auto chose this turn); else the person's cloud
 computer, Local VM, computer, in that order.
Both are member-scope tools (`server/member-tool-scope.ts`): the list is
already filtered for the person and the card only stages a request.

sections.title: In-chat terminal: destinations: The card
sections.text:
The card shows the bot's destination and, when there is more than one, a
Destination menu with every other destination this person may open.
The allow sends the pick (`terminalDestination`) and the widget's size
(`terminalSize`). The server opens the pick only when the card offered it
AND the registry allows it for the person answering
(`server/terminal-resources/registry.ts`, `terminalResourceAllowed`); a
refusal leaves the card open.

sections.title: In-chat terminal: destinations: The widget
sections.text:
The terminal takes the whole width of the conversation column and refits its
grid when the column changes (`src/lib/chat-bubble-width.ts`, fit addon). Its
font stack leads with the bundled Symbols Nerd Font Mono, limited to the icon
ranges, so prompt themes (Powerlevel10k, Oh My Posh, Starship) draw their
icons (`src/components/terminal/terminal-font.ts`, license in
`third_party/nerd-fonts-symbols`).
Detach moves the same terminal (same xterm, same WebSocket, no new
connection) into a floating window (`src/lib/floating-windows.ts`,
`src/components/floating/`): several at once, stacked, focus on click, each
closes on its own and brings the terminal back to its chat row. The session
(`src/components/terminal/terminal-session.ts`) lives while the chat row or
its window holds it, and ends a moment after both let go. Terminal windows
are not reopened after a restart (the shell session is gone); their position
and size are remembered per session.

sections.title: Tool policy (securable tool layer): Adding a route
sections.text:
`scripts/tool-policy/tool-policy-coverage.test.ts` fails when a route has no row, and when a row's route is gone. It runs in the vitest shards (`vite.config.ts` includes `scripts/**/*.test.ts`). To fix it:
1. Run `node scripts/tool-policy/generate.ts`. Reviewed rows are kept; new routes get the default classification.
2. Review the new rows (tier, scope, defaultEnabled) and commit them.
The route list comes from the server sources (`scripts/tool-policy/route-inventory.ts`). Sagax routes are code, not a registry. `server/request-auth.ts` is left out because its path rules are the auth gate, not routes.
Status: B1 declares the policy only and nothing enforces it yet. B2 adds grants and the guard (docs/agent-api.md).

sections.title: Tool policy (securable tool layer): B2.1: guard before the card
sections.text: An `agents__ ` (or `mcp__agents__ `) permission request is checked before the card or Full access answers it: the bot's grant, then the grant of the person its turn speaks for. Audit rows (`agents. `, admin activity): `card` (pre_card, with guard decision and `speakerPrincipalId`), then `declined`/`expired` when nobody approves; an approved call is audited by the call itself (now with `speakerPrincipalId`). Enforce: `refused` and denied without a card. Shadow (default): recorded only.

sections.title: Tool policy (securable tool layer): Grants and the guard (B2)
sections.text:
`server/tool-grants.ts` stores grants in ` /tool-grants.json`. Each grant has a subject (a bot or a user), a scope, who granted it, an optional expiry and a revocation. A grant at a higher tier covers the lower tiers of the same area.
`server/tool-guard.ts` makes one decision per agent tool call:
1. A default-enabled read or write is allowed.
2. Anything else needs a grant for the caller.
3. A bot's call also needs a grant for the person its turn speaks for, so a bot never reaches past its speaker.
Writes still raise the approval card. The decision is recorded on every agent-api audit row as `guard`, `guardAllow`, `guardMode`, `scope` and `readOnly`.
`SAGAX_TOOL_GUARD` sets the mode:
- `shadow` (default): audits the decision and changes nothing.
- `enforce`: refuses with `not_granted`.
- `off`: skips the guard.
In shadow mode the audit shows what enforcing would refuse. Today that is `create_agent`, which is admin tier and has no grants yet.

sections.title: Tool policy (securable tool layer): Grants routes (B3a)
sections.text:
Admin scope only (gate + handler). Policy rows are `tool-grants:admin`, never default-enabled, so no agent tool can grant itself anything.
- `GET /api/tool-grants[?kind=bot|user&id=…]`: every row (active, expired, revoked) with `state`.
- `POST /api/tool-grants` `{subject:{kind,id}, scope:" : ", expiresAt?}`: a bot must exist; admin-tier grants need an expiry within 30 days.
- `POST /api/tool-grants/ /revoke`: keeps the row. Both writes go to the admin activity log (category `rights`).
Per bot (2026-10-15, the bot editor's Permissions page; `server/routes/bot-runtime-settings.ts`): the bot's owner (with `bots.tools` on an organization server) or an admin.
- `GET /api/bots/ /tool-grants`: that bot's rows only, with `state` and `mayGrantAdmin`.
- `POST /api/bots/ /tool-grants` `{scope, expiresAt?}`: the subject is the bot in the path. 2026-10-26: the owner grants every tier, admin included, for a scope that stays in their own environment; a scope whose area reaches past it (`shared/grant-reach.ts` `ORG_REACH_AREAS`: org, members, people, teams, admin, config, engines, keys, workers, fleet, billing, usage, tool-grants...) stays an admin's (403 `org_scope_admin_only`). An admin-tier grant ends within 30 days. The GET answers `mayGrantAdmin: true` and, for a member, `adminOnlyAreas`.
- `POST /api/bots/ /tool-grants/ /revoke`: only a grant of that bot (another bot's or a person's is 404). Both writes are audited as above.
Their policy rows are `tool-grants:admin`, never default-enabled. An admin still reviews every person's grants in Settings > General > Advanced ("People's tool access", shown only when some exist).
A person's own grants (2026-10-26, `server/routes/my-tool-grants.ts`, Settings > "Mes accès aux outils"): the subject is always the signed-in person (`{kind: "user", id: }`), the grant the guard checks as the speaker of their bots' turns.
- `GET /api/me/tool-grants`: their rows with `state`, `mayGrantAdmin` and `adminOnlyAreas`.
- `POST /api/me/tool-grants` `{scope, expiresAt?}`: no admin needed for a scope of their own environment, any tier; past it, 403 `org_scope_admin_only` (an admin keeps `/api/tool-grants`). An admin-tier grant ends within 30 days.
- `POST /api/me/tool-grants/ /revoke`: their own grant only (anyone else's, or a bot's, is 404).
No person (a local service, a bot's act session, an AI client): 403. Policy rows `tool-grants:admin`, never default-enabled, so no agent grants itself or its speaker anything. Every write goes to the admin activity log (category `rights`).
The guard's mode stays `shadow` by default. The Journal (Approvals > Journal, `docs/approval-levels.md`) shows each agent tool call with the guard's verdict, including what enforcing would refuse.

sections.title: Tool policy (securable tool layer)
sections.text:
Every HTTP route the server answers has one row in `server/tool-policy.generated.ts`. The types and the matcher are in `server/tool-policy.ts`.
| field | meaning |
 
| `method`, `kind`, `route` | The guard the handler matches: an exact path, a prefix or a regex source, and its method (`ANY` when the handler has no method guard). |
| `tier` | `read`, `write` or `admin`. |
| `readOnly` | `true` only for a GET that deletes nothing. |
| `scope` | ` : `, the grant a caller needs. |
| `defaultEnabled` | Whether agent tools may use the route without a grant that names it. It is never `true` for admin. |
| `destructive`, `billing` | Billing stays admin. Destructive rows are admin except the personal provider routes below. |
Default classification (`classifyRoute`):
- read: GET.
- admin: DELETE, a deletion verb (`delete`, `remove`, `wipe`, `purge`, `reset`, `revoke`, `archive`), org, admin, billing, usage, fleet, engines, keys, credentials, roles, members, import and export.
- write: everything else, including a route with no method guard.
The personal provider routes (`/api/me/providers` and the older
`/api/me/voice-keys` alias) are the person's own environment. Their handlers
derive the owner from authentication and never accept another person's id.
Their reads and writes, including removing their key or endpoint, are enabled
without an admin grant. The normal approval rules still apply to bot writes.
A request that matches no row is treated as write, off by default (`UNKNOWN_ROUTE_POLICY`).

sections.title: Tool selection: Approvals and access
sections.text:
Selection narrows available tools. Existing approval modes, guest restrictions,
integration permissions and host-control confirmation still apply. Auto or
Full approval does not re-enable an excluded tool. MCP discovery and calls are
both filtered, including URL-backed servers and zero result budgets.
This is tool availability, not a sandbox for commands, file access or
credentials. Allowing a shell tool still allows that tool's existing authority.
Bot-proposed profile changes cannot edit this owner setting.

sections.title: Tool selection: Engine support
sections.text:
| Engines | Available selection |
 
| Pi, Grok CLI, Grok API, OpenAI compatible, Mistral, MiniMax | Native and app-supplied MCP tools |
| Claude, Codex, Gemini, Kimi, Droid, Cursor, OpenCode Go, Qwen, Hermes, Custom ACP, Antigravity | App-supplied MCP tools; keep `native:*` in Allow and do not exclude native tools |
| Boat native | Meaningful tool restrictions are unsupported |
Grok CLI's native contract is verified on version 1.0.41. Other versions
refuse native restrictions until their contract is verified. Inherited Grok
profile restrictions still apply. Grok accepts simple `[agent]` name/definition
entries, including trailing comments, and an explicit `--agent-profile` file.
Quoted or dotted keys, inline agent tables, multiline TOML, conflicting
profile sources and CLI tool overrides refuse scoped turns when their existing
restrictions cannot be safely resolved. Scoped Grok disables its managed MCP gateway;
unexpected native MCP servers prevent the prompt from starting. Scoped Claude
requires a modern CLI with strict MCP isolation and cannot inherit its native
MCP configuration. Scoped Codex checks its effective MCP configuration before
starting the prompt. Each Codex MCP mount keeps independent private gate
settings on new and resumed threads; custom servers retain approval prompts.
Unsupported restrictions and malformed saved selections stop the turn with a
setup error. The settings warning is deliberate: it does not claim an engine
can enforce a restriction that its contract does not support. Native selection
for the other CLI engines remains a later contribution requiring verified
provider contracts.

sections.title: Tool selection: Names and examples
sections.text:
Use the tool's original, case-sensitive name, before any model-specific alias:
 
`native:*` includes the engine's native tools. `mcp:mail:*` includes all tools
on the configured server named `mail`. Partial wildcards, such as
`native:read*`, are invalid. A valid name that is not available selects
nothing; it does not fall back to all tools. The Allow and Exclude lists each
accept up to 256 selectors, with at most 1024 characters per selector.
Pi drafting, with Only allow listed tools checked:
 
Grok CLI drafting:
 
Pi with one custom MCP tool:
 `mcp:mail:read_notes` 
Select the `mail` server in the existing MCP servers card too. A selector
does not enable a disabled server, connect an account, or grant integration
access.
Grok CLI with one custom MCP tool needs its native lookup and call tools
explicitly selected:
 
Grok uses those two helpers to discover and call the selected MCP tools.
Their results and calls are checked against the same original selectors.
Pi sends the selected MCP schemas directly to the model.

sections.title: Tool selection
sections.text:
Open a bot's Access → Tool selection settings to reduce the tools sent to
its model. This is useful for local models with a small context window.
- All current tools keeps the existing engine and integration defaults.
- Custom selection, with Only allow listed tools checked, offers only
 the tools in Allow. An empty Allow list selects no tools.
- Uncheck Only allow listed tools to keep the current catalog except for
 tools in Exclude. Exclude always wins.
Enter one selector per line, then choose Save tool selection. Changes take
effect on the next turn. Finish the bot's active tasks before saving. A failed
save never grants newly enabled tools. Changes that remove tool access can
remain active in the running app even if saving fails; retry the save to keep
them after a restart. Duplicating a bot preserves its selection from the moment
the copy is created.

sections.title: Server environments (organization mode): A person's own MCP servers and GitHub account
sections.text:
Settings > Mes connexions (`server/routes/person-connections.ts`) lets each
person add MCP servers of their own and connect their GitHub account. A
command they add runs here, in their own environment, never on the Sagax
host: the engine starts Sagax's stdio proxy (tool server `sagax-stdio`)
holding a turn capability that names the person and the server; the Sagax
server keeps one process per person, server and thread through the
provisioner's signed stdio stream (`/v1/sandboxes/ /stdio`, upgrade
`sagax-stdio`; the command and its variables ride the first line, whose
SHA-256 the signed path names) and relays the JSON-RPC frames
(`server/sandbox-stdio-mcp.ts`). At most 8 such processes per person run at
once; an idle one stops after 10 minutes.
Their GitHub connection (`server/github-connect.ts`) is written into
`/workspace/.config/gh/hosts.yml` and `/workspace/.git-credentials` (0600,
`credential.https://github.com.helper store`) when they connect and again
at the first tool call of each turn, so `gh` and `git` in the environment
work as them. Disconnecting removes both. The image carries `gh`, `node` and
`npm` for this (a change needs the sandbox image rebuilt). Public internet
egress stays open, so github.com, api.github.com, codeload.github.com,
objects.githubusercontent.com, raw.githubusercontent.com, ghcr.io and
api.githubcopilot.com are reachable; only private destinations are dropped.

sections.title: Server environments (organization mode): Deploy
sections.text:
`deploy/docker-compose.sandbox.yml` adds the provisioner, the pull-or-build
service for the sandbox image and the Sagax server's settings, all under the
`pulsabot` profile:
 `docker compose -f compose.yaml -f deploy/docker-compose.sandbox.yml --profile pulsabot up -d --build` 
Smoke test on a machine with Docker (creates one temporary environment and
deletes it, with its egress rules):
 
The desktop (computer use, Chromium, the live view through the real viewer
route, pause, resume and usage) has its own smoke test:
 
The image with the desktop is about 397 MB (arm64), 38.5 MB more than
without it; `--build-arg WITH_DESKTOP=0` leaves it out.
Settings > Local VM no longer offers a VM per bot on an organization server,
and a bot's cloud backend cannot be a per-bot VPS there (409 `org_user_sandbox`).
Cloud there, including a cloud routine and a room, is the person's one
server environment. The bot computer routes do not open a shared machine
(the same 409).

sections.title: Server environments (organization mode): Desktop
sections.text:
Each environment can show a small Linux desktop (1280x800): Xvnc (an X
server with its VNC server), openbox, a gradient background (hsetroot), a
launcher bar (tint2: Chromium, Terminal, Files, open windows, clock),
Chromium, xterm and pcmanfm, driven by `/usr/local/bin/sagax-desktop` in the
image. Without the background and the bar the screen was black with only a
cursor. Nothing of it runs until it is
needed: a plain shell turn starts no X server.
- Computer use: bots get the desktop bridge's shape, `computer_list_tools`
 then `computer_use` with `screenshot` (JPEG), `get_screen_size`, `click`,
 `move`, `drag`, `type_text`, `key_press`, `scroll` and `open_url` (the cloud
 computer's vocabulary). Each call is one exec of a fixed `sagax-desktop`
 argv (xdotool, scrot), never a shell line; text and addresses travel in
 `SAGAX_*` variables. The first call starts the desktop. Where it runs
 follows the bot's Works on and the routine rules above: the person's own
 computer when that is the target, else this desktop. A bot whose Computer
 setting is off gets no computer use here either.
- VNC: listens on `127.0.0.1:5901` inside the sandbox's own network
 namespace only and asks for a password (VncAuth only). Two passwords: the
 full one controls the screen, the view-only one only watches; both are
 replaced each time the owner opens the view, unless a view is still open
 or was opened in the last 30 s (then the same ones, so it keeps working).
 Opens are serialized per person, and `sagax-desktop start` takes a lock:
 two at once used to race on the password file and answer 502.
- Live view: `GET /api/desktop-viewer/sandbox/me` (and its
 `/websockify` WebSocket), the Computer tab and the full-window viewer. The
 target is built from the caller's own session principal: there is no id
 that names another person's desktop, an admin or the server's console has
 none, and a person signed out by Perspicax is refused. Opening the view
 starts the environment and its desktop and hands the view-only password;
 "Prendre le contrôle" (`?control=1`, a button in the middle of the Computer
 tab's screen, shown like Play / Pause / Stop only after the pointer rests
 on the screen about 2 s, on keyboard focus or on a tap) opens the desktop large (92vw by 88vh, letterboxed) and hands
 the full one there, while the tab's square stays view-only; while such a
 view is open, the bots' `computer_use` there is refused, never queued
 (`server/sandbox-control.ts`), and "Rendre le contrôle" or closing the
 window (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+Esc, or Escape outside the screen) hands it back. The WebSocket never
 starts anything: the Sagax server frames the RFB bytes itself
 (`server/ws-bridge.ts`) and reaches the VNC port only through the
 provisioner, a signed HTTP upgrade (`/v1/sandboxes/ /desktop`) spliced
 to a `docker exec` relay inside that one sandbox. No port is published, no
 network path opens between Sagax and a sandbox. A view in control counts as

sections.title: Server environments (organization mode): Lifecycle
sections.text:
- Lazy: mounting the tools creates nothing; the first tool call creates the
 network, the `/workspace` volume and the container, then starts it.
- One per person: the capability a turn's tools carry names the person
 (fixed at mount, never read from the request). The provisioner is
 addressed by an opaque key,
 `sha256(instance, principal id)`; its API has no bot parameter. Objects are
 named `sagax-user- ` and labelled `com.pulsatrix.sagax.sandbox.user= `
 and `sagax-user= `.
- Idle stop: after `SAGAX_SANDBOX_IDLE_MINUTES` without a command (default
 10). The next call starts it again; `/workspace` persists.
- New image: a stopped environment created from another image than
 `SAGAX_SANDBOX_IMAGE` (an earlier deploy) is recreated from the current one
 when it starts again, keeping `/workspace` and its network. A running one
 is never replaced behind its owner's back, except when the owner opens the
 desktop and it has none (`sagax-desktop` missing, exit 127) and no command
 runs there; otherwise the view says to stop it and open the desktop again.
- Capacity: at most `SAGAX_SANDBOX_MAX_RUNNING` run at once (default 2; a
 paused one counts, it keeps its memory). A
 new one stops the least recently used idle one, or the call is refused with a
 clear message when every running environment is in use.
- Sign-out: when Perspicax signs a person out (back-channel logout,
 disabled or removed), their environment is stopped at once and deleted
 (container, network and volume) after `SAGAX_SANDBOX_DELETE_GRACE_HOURS`
 (default 72). A person back in before then keeps it. Pending deletions are in
 `user-sandbox-deletions.json` in the data folder and survive restarts.
- Reset: Settings > Organization > Your server environment > Reset deletes
 it, `/workspace` included, and creates a fresh one, after a confirmation.

sections.title: Server environments (organization mode): Resource defaults (8 GiB host)
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Meaning |
 
| `SAGAX_SANDBOX_MEMORY_MB` | 1536 | per environment, no swap (the desktop with Chromium measured about 260 MiB) |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOX_CPUS` | 1 | per environment |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOX_PIDS` | 512 | per environment (Chromium's processes and threads count) |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOX_TMP_MB` | 512 | tmpfs `/tmp` (counts against memory only when used) |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOX_DISK_MB` | 2048 | soft quota on `/workspace` |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOX_MAX_FILE_MB` | 512 | largest single file |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOX_MAX_RUNNING` | 2 | running or paused at once (3 GiB at most) |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOX_IDLE_MINUTES` | 10 | idle stop |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOX_DELETE_GRACE_HOURS` | 72 | delete after sign-out (Sagax side) |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOX_SUBNET_POOL` | `10.213.0.0/16` | must not overlap the VNet or other Docker networks |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOX_EGRESS_DENY` | empty | extra CIDRs to block |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOX_RUNTIME` | empty | `runsc`, `sysbox-runc` |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOX_IMAGE` | required | built from `deploy/sandbox/Dockerfile` |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOX_INSTANCE` | `default` | same value on both services |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOXD_URL` | empty | Sagax side; empty means no environments |
| `SAGAX_SANDBOXD_KEY_FILE` | `/run/sagax-sandboxd/key` | both services |
| `SAGAX_DOCKER_GID` | 999 | group of `/var/run/docker.sock` on the host |
`SANDBOX_BACKEND` defaults to `docker` and leaves this table in force. Set it
to `kubernetes` on the provisioner that should call the Kubernetes API
(`server/sandboxd-k8s/sandboxd-k8s.ts`). The compose provisioner stays `docker`. Sagax
runs both and sends a person to Kubernetes only when
`SAGAX_SANDBOX_CANARY_PEOPLE`, `SAGAX_SANDBOX_CANARY_BOTS` or
`SAGAX_SANDBOX_ROUTE=kubernetes` says so. `SAGAX_SANDBOX_ROUTE=docker` sends
everyone back to Docker. The https URL is `SAGAX_SANDBOXD_K8S_URL` and the
CA file is `SAGAX_SANDBOXD_TLS_CA`. Images must sit under
`SAGAX_SANDBOX_K8S_REGISTRY` and, by default, carry a digest. The manifests
are one tree, `deploy/k8s/` (`provisioner/`, `sandboxes/`, `helm/`, `tofu/`).
The cutover is ops/sandboxes/cutover-rollback.md.
Variables and the SOC 2 map for the provisioner are in
sandbox-kubernetes.md. A Kubernetes pause drops the
Pod (the memory is released) and still holds the capacity slot; a Docker
pause keeps the memory. Copy one person's Docker volume to their PVC, or
back, with `scripts/sandbox-workspace-migrate.ts`. The source is left in
place and a second run with the same checksums writes nothing.

sections.title: Server environments (organization mode): Security model
sections.text:
- No Docker socket in Sagax. Only `sagax-sandboxd` (the provisioner, same
 image, `node dist-server/sandboxd.js`) mounts it. It is read-only, has no
 capabilities, no new privileges, 192 MB and 64 pids, and sits on an
 `internal` network shared with the Sagax server alone. It publishes no port.
- Signed calls only. The provisioner writes a 256-bit key to the
 `sandboxd-key` volume (mode 0440, read-only for the Sagax server). Each
 request carries an HMAC over method, path, timestamp, nonce and body digest;
 a 30 second window and a nonce cache refuse replays.
- Narrow API. `ensure`, `stop`, `DELETE`, `exec` and status for one 32-hex
 key. The provisioner can only create the fixed spec of
 `sandboxContainerSpec()`, checked by `assertSandboxIsolation()` before every
 create, and only touches objects carrying its labels and its instance; a
 same-named object it did not create is refused.
- Each sandbox: uid 1000, read-only root, no capabilities,
 `no-new-privileges`, Docker's default seccomp and AppArmor profiles, never
 privileged, no host mounts or devices (only its own volume on `/workspace`),
 tmpfs `/tmp`, memory without swap, CPU, pids, open files and file size
 limits, private IPC and cgroup namespaces, no published port. Optional
 stronger runtime: `SAGAX_SANDBOX_RUNTIME=runsc` (gVisor) or `sysbox-runc`
 when the host has it. The image has no setuid binary and no sudo.
- Network: one bridge network per sandbox, a /28 from
 `SAGAX_SANDBOX_SUBNET_POOL` (default `10.213.0.0/16`), no inter-container
 traffic, no IPv6. At start the provisioner runs a one-shot helper (host
 network, `NET_ADMIN`, fixed script) that adds, for the pool only: a
 `DOCKER-USER` jump to a chain dropping private, link-local and reserved
 destinations (`10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/16`, `100.64/10`, `127/8`,
 `169.254/16` including cloud metadata, Azure WireServer `168.63.129.16`,
 multicast) and an `INPUT` drop for anything from the pool to the host itself.
 Public internet stays open. If the policy cannot be applied, the provisioner
 refuses to create environments (`SAGAX_SANDBOX_REQUIRE_EGRESS_POLICY=false`
 turns that off for a lab only).
- Disk: `/workspace` has a soft quota (`SAGAX_SANDBOX_DISK_MB`): over it,
 `write_file` is refused and Settings shows it; one file is capped by
 `SAGAX_SANDBOX_MAX_FILE_MB`. For a hard cap, put `/var/lib/docker` on xfs
 with project quotas.

sections.title: Server environments (organization mode)
sections.text:
On an organization server (`SAGAX_IDENTITY=perspicax`), each person gets one
isolated Linux environment on the server: their "server environment"
(`user-sandbox`). Shell, file and browser tools run there whenever the turn
does not target the person's own computer (`user-desktop`). There is never
one environment per bot, and an organization server never runs a bot's tools
on the Sagax host or inside the Sagax container. A cloud routine and a room
whose computer is Cloud use that same environment. A team computer does not
open a shared machine.
| Target | When | Where |
 
| `user-desktop` | the bot's Works on (or the conversation's pin) is Local VM or This computer | their own computer, through the desktop bridge (`sagax-desktop`, see AGENTS.md "Desktop bridge"), while their Sagax desktop app is connected |
| `user-sandbox` | organization mode, any other turn | one person's environment (below) |
| `host` | solo server | this machine, unchanged |
| `none` | organization mode without a provisioner | nothing is mounted |
The choice between the two is `resolveBotWorkplace` (`server/desktop-bridge.ts`),
from the bot's Works on: Auto and Cloud ("Cloud (server environment)") use the
server environment, the default; Local VM and This computer use the person's
own computer, and when their desktop app is not connected nothing runs there
and the bot and the composer say so. Routines use the server environment
unless the bot works on the owner's computer, it is connected and the owner
allowed routines on it; room follow-ups no person asked for use it too. Files
a person attaches in that turn are copied to `/workspace/attachments/`.
Whose environment (`sandboxPrincipalForTurn`, matching private threads and
"the speaker pays"):
| Turn | Environment |
 
| a conversation (1:1, private thread with a shared bot) | the speaker, the person talking; a bot hop keeps the person its source turn spoke for |
| a routine, and any thread or hop a routine starts | the bot owner (routines run as the owner) |
| a room turn answering a person | that person (the latest person who spoke in the room) |
| a room follow-up no person ever asked for | the room's creator (`group.createdBy`, else its first listed person) |
| nobody known | nothing is mounted (fail closed) |
A teammate's files and commands therefore never land in the bot owner's
environment, and a person's work follows them across every bot they use. A
bot's follow-up after a person's message keeps that person's environment
rather than the creator's: the work they asked for and its files stay
together, and nothing they wrote moves into someone else's environment.
Code: `server/user-sandbox-routing.ts` (targets, owner), `server/user-sandbox-tools.ts`
(`run_command`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `list_files`, `browse`,
`computer_list_tools`, `computer_use`, mounted as the MCP server
`sagax-environment`), `server/user-sandbox-manager.ts` (lifecycle on

sections.title: Server environments (organization mode): The engines' own tools
sections.text:
Running the engine CLI itself inside the person's environment was not
feasible safely now (it would need the CLIs, their credentials and a route
back to the Sagax loopback inside a sandbox whose egress policy forbids
exactly that). So on an organization server every turn sets
`withholdHostTools` (`server/drivers/host-tools.ts`):
- Claude Code: `--disallowedTools` adds `Bash`, `BashOutput`,
 `KillShell`, `Monitor`, `Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `MultiEdit`,
 `NotebookEdit`, `Glob`, `Grep`, `LS`, `WebFetch`, `EnterWorktree`,
 `ExitWorktree`, `Workflow`, `DesignSync`. Deny rules, so subagents get them
 too. `WebSearch` (run by Anthropic) stays.
- Codex: `features.shell_tool=false`, `features.unified_exec=false`,
 `features.view_image=false`, a read-only sandbox asking for approval, and
 every command, patch or permission request is declined before any card or
 Full-access auto-accept.
- Chat engines (OpenAI-compatible) and the Boat agent never run anything
 on this machine.
- Grok Build, pi, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Kimi Code, OpenCode, Hermes
 Agent: each one's own tool profile leaves it Sagax's MCP tools only
 (AGENTS.md, "Engines on an organization server", has the mechanism per
 engine), in an empty folder Sagax owns, and a request to run a command
 or change a file is declined before any card.
- Droid, Cursor Agent, Antigravity, a custom ACP agent are refused on an
 organization server (409 `host_tools`, with the engine's reason on its
 card and in the picker) rather than run in the container: Droid's ACP
 mode ignores its tool selection, Cursor's service picks its own tools.
Running an engine inside the person's own environment instead (the CLI in
the sandbox, its egress policy around it) is still not built: none of the
engines above needs it, and the two refused ones would bring their own
service login into it.
Shell, files and pages then go through `sagax-environment`.
The engine CLIs therefore live in the Sagax server image, not in this one:
`engines.lock.json` pins them and an organization build (`ENGINE_SET=all`,
Perspicax's `build-push.sh`) installs every one of them there
(Engines baked into a server image).
`deploy/sandbox/Dockerfile` carries no engine. Being installed does not lift
the rule above: an engine that cannot withhold its own tools (Droid, Cursor
Agent, Antigravity, a custom ACP agent) is still refused on an organization
server.
`scripts/smoke-host-tools.ts` starts the real Claude Code CLI with the
driver's flags (no model request) and checks its tool list has no `Bash`.
`scripts/verify-org-host-tools.ts ` drives a real ACP CLI through
its driver against a fake model on 127.0.0.1 and checks the tools it offers
the model, that a shell or file request does not act, and that the Sagax
MCP tools still work.

sections.title: Voice mode with xAI: A call recovers by itself
sections.text:
A call must never hang, go silent, lose a turn or drop. Each part that can
fail recovers on its own:
- The listen socket (page side). When `/voice/listen` drops (a Wi-Fi
 switch, a sleep, the server restarting), the page opens it again after
 250, 750 and 2,000 ms, then every 5 s for the rest of the call; the count
 starts over once a socket is ready (`src/lib/voice-mode/stt-stream.ts`,
 `RECONNECT_BACKOFF_MS`, `RECONNECT_EVERY_MS`). Only the utterances already
 finished and still waiting for their words are uploaded whole; the one
 being spoken is sent again from its first frame on the new socket, with
 its words, interim, finalize and probe state reset. Late words of an
 utterance the timeout settled are no longer awaited, so they never eat the
 next turn's words. A socket that never opened (an old server) gets the
 backoff only, then the call uploads.
- xAI's speech to text (server side). The page's socket outlives xAI's
 (`server/voice-listen-session.ts`). When xAI's socket closes, the server
 opens a new one behind the same page socket (250, 750, 2,000 ms) and sends
 the page `{"type":"reconnected"}`; the page sends the open utterance again
 and uploads the finished ones that were waiting. Only when those three
 tries fail does the page socket close (1011), and the page reconnects on
 its own. A reopened socket counts as working only once xAI sent words on
 it or it lived 10 s (accepting then closing at once still fails), and
 more than 6 reopens in a minute close the page socket too, so a flapping
 socket is never reopened forever. Like the streaming voice, xAI's socket is rotated at 540 s, once
 nothing was heard or sent for 3 s (no utterance open); audio that arrives
 while the next socket opens is held and sent to it, so the page never
 notices.
- A failed upload. A whole-turn upload is tried twice (a refusal once),
 each try given up after 20 s (`TRANSCRIBE_TIMEOUT_MS`). When both fail,
 the call reports `transcribe-failed`: the bar shows "That didn't come
 through" and the call says "That did not get through. Could you say it
 again?". A turn is never dropped silently. The iPhone does the same when
 it uploads a turn.
- A stalled voice. A clause spoken over POST `/voice/stream` with no
 first byte, or no next chunk, for 8 s is aborted with an error
 (`SPEECH_STALL_MS` in `api.ts`); the player has its own 10 s backstop for
 any sentence whose audio stops coming (`READ_TIMEOUT_MS`). The player then
 plays the next clause, and the call is never stuck "busy".
- Audio contexts. The output and the capture contexts are resumed when
 the system suspends or interrupts them (`statechange`). A player whose
 audio clock stopped resets its schedule when it goes idle, so the next
 answer does not wait on audio that will never play.
- The microphone. A track that ends (unplugged, taken by the system)
 or a `devicechange` that removes the call's microphone opens the capture
 again (`MIC_REOPEN_MS`: at once, then 0.5, 1.5 and 3 s, the later tries on

sections.title: Voice mode with xAI: A call turn runs fast (2026-10-29)
sections.text:
Measured in production before this: about 5.8 s from the end of speech to
the first words (1.9 s of turn setup over a conversation of about 183,000
tokens, a cold engine, 3.8 s to the first token), more on a large model,
and lines said meanwhile piled up. Now (`server/voice-turn.ts`):
- A fast model. Every call turn, and the warm that starts its process
 when the call is accepted, runs on a fast model: the bot's own fast model
 when it set one, else the fast tier of its engine (Haiku on Claude Code,
 a fast Grok on Grok), else the fast tier of another engine the payer can
 use (`pickVoiceModel`, server/model-auto.ts, the same tiers Auto uses). A
 bot pinned to a model gets it too; a request that needed another
 engine's connector keeps that engine. No fast model anywhere: the bot's
 model.
- A short context, in a session of its own. The call never resumes the
 conversation's engine session. Its first dispatch (the warm) closes an
 idle process the thread kept and starts a new session; the first spoken
 turn carries a short view of the conversation (`voiceTranscript`: the
 conversation's own summary, or a quoted summary of what is older, then
 the latest 12 messages, 6,000 bytes in all); every later turn resumes
 that session with its words alone, plus anything that reached the
 conversation meanwhile that the call did not write or hear (a task's
 result). The call session's cursor lives in memory (`VoiceTurnSessions`);
 the conversation's cursor and handed-message record are left alone, and a
 call turn neither folds the conversation nor waits for it. A new call on
 the thread before a hang-up keeps the warm process and session.
- The conversation learns what the call said. Its next written turn
 resumes its own session on the bot's model: an engine that records what
 its session was handed gets the call's lines as unseen messages; another
 gets them in front of the words (`callLinesBlock`, the newest 24; memory
 only, a restart loses it). A conversation that had no session before the
 call starts one from the usual rebuild.
- Real work is handed off. The call instruction (`VOICE_CALL_DELEGATE_LINE`)
 tells the bot that it answers on a fast model from a short view: for
 code, a long search or read, many tool steps, it says in one sentence it
 is on it and calls `start_thread` with `report_back`. That parallel task
 runs on the bot's main model, its brief carrying the conversation (its
 summary and latest turns at the rebuild budget, `callHandoffHistory`),
 and its result is posted back into the conversation, where the call
 announces and reads it (`howToSpeakTopicResult`).
- No pile-up. A barge-in still cuts the answer (the page stops the turn
 its words cut, `expectedUtteranceId`), and a stale answer is still never
 spoken (the speech fence). Lines said while the bot cannot take them
 (a turn being stopped) wait in the queue, and every waiting line of the
 same call drains as one turn (`callLineGroup`, server/steer-queue.ts)

sections.title: Voice mode with xAI: A live call, like a phone
sections.text:
The person presses the call button on a bot. When the server reports
`GET /api/bots/ /voice/status` `available: true`, the call runs in voice
mode on any desktop (macOS, Windows) or browser, server mode included
(`src/components/voice-mode/LiveCall.tsx`, engine `src/lib/voice-mode/call.ts`).
Without it, a solo Mac keeps the older call (the macOS dictation helper and
the configured TTS provider, half duplex). That call marks its turns like
the live call (`useVoiceCallMark`, `src/lib/voice-mode/call-mark.ts`): each
send carries `voiceCall`, the server knows the thread is on a call (so
`end_call` is offered and hangs it up after the goodbye), and it speaks only
`spokenPart` of an answer.
- Full duplex. The microphone stays open for the whole call. While the bot
 speaks, the person can talk over it: on the first voiced frame (32 ms) the
 bot is ducked within 10 ms to about -6 dB (it may still be a cough,
 `DUCK_SOFT`), then to 12% once the voice is confirmed (128 ms), and it
 stays ducked, nothing cancelled,
 while the call checks that this is the person talking to it
 (`call-machine.ts` `bargePending`). The bot is cut (its voice fades out in
 12 ms, every queued sentence is dropped, and its running turn is
 interrupted with `/interrupt` if it is still writing) as soon as the
 streamed words are real words (not a sound the recognizer spelled, not a
 backchannel such as "mm-hmm", "uh-huh", "hum", "euh") and, with Only my
 voice, match the voiceprint; or, when no words have come yet, after
 400 ms of voiced speech (`BARGE_IN_CONFIRM_MS`). Worst case for a real
 barge-in: ducked by 42 ms, silent by 412 ms (400 ms plus the 12 ms
 fade, `call.test.ts`); usually sooner, when xAI's first words arrive
 first. With Only my voice the check of the voiceprint adds the
 embedding's time, and a clip too short to judge waits for more audio. A
 cough, a chair or a "mm-hmm" never cuts the answer: when the turn ends
 without real words (or in another voice) the bot is unducked and goes on.
 Short words that end before the check ("stop") still cut the bot before
 they are sent. What the bot had written stays in the transcript, marked
 interrupted, and the new words become the next turn.
- Turns. Silero VAD v5 (on this computer, `models/silero-vad-v5.onnx`)
 gives a voice probability per 32 ms frame; `turns.ts` starts a turn after
 about 190 ms of voice and ends it after an adaptive silence. Settings >
 End of turn picks the range: Short (420 to 800 ms), Normal (560 to
 1100 ms, 700 to start) or Patient (800 to 1500 ms). The streaming words
 move it: an unfinished clause (no final punctuation and a trailing "and",
 "to", "the", "de", "pour"..., a trailing comma or filler, or one or two
 words) waits 500 to 1000 ms longer. The socket asks xAI to keep fillers
 (`filler_words=true`), so a trailing "euh" or "um" is seen; they are
 removed only from the text the bot gets (`shared/voice-mode.ts`
 `stripFillers`), and a turn of fillers alone is no turn. A candidate too
